en: Śrīḥ!
The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara:
The Section on Royal Duties (Rājadharmakāṇḍa)
Auspicious Invocation: Oṃ, salutation to Vighnarāja, the bestower of the fruit of freedom from obstacles.
That King Govindacandra established his foot upon the path of justice, in the homes of the virtuous, among elephants, and upon the heads of kings—
all that was indeed due to the wondrous power of the counsel of Lakṣmīdhara.
In the eleventh chapter, the one of meritorious intellect recites the collection of the duties of kings.
The Declaration (the indication of the subject matter):
Praise of the King; first, his consecration, then his virtues;
then the ministers, then the fortresses, and thereafter the rules for the construction of buildings.
The consolidation of the kingdom, the treasury, the army, and then the ally; the protection of the princes, and counsel—these indeed constitute the sixfold policy.
Then follow the rites for the consecration of the procession and the ritual for the festival of the gods;
thereafter, the great festival of Kaumudī and the ritual for the raising of the banner.
On the Mahānavamī day, there is worship and the ritual for the emblem;
then the release of a bull and the stream of wealth—these are the festivals in sequence on the eleventh.
[2] 1 — Now, the praise of the king; regarding this, Manu says:
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how his supreme success is achieved.
For when this world was without a king and assailed from all sides by fear,
the Lord created a king for the protection of all this.
Having extracted the eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and from Candra and Vitteśa—
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in splendor.
Like the sun, it scorches both eyes and minds;
and no one at all on earth is able even to look upon it.
By his power, he may become fire and wind; he may be the sun, the moon, or the King of Dharma (Yama); he may be Kubera, Varuṇa, or the great Indra.
Nārada said: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms—
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Dhanada.
When, for some reason or even without cause, a king falls under the sway of anger and consumes his subjects, he is then called "fire."
When a king, desiring victory and with weapons raised, relies upon his own prowess and marches against his enemies, he is then declared to be Indra.
When the king, free from the heat of anger and appearing joyful,
goes to see his subjects, he is then said to be in the *some* state.
When the illustrious king, seated upon the throne of justice, wields the rod of punishment impartially toward all beings, then he is Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
But when the lord of the earth favors supplicants, elders, the wise, servants,
and others with gifts, he is then called the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
Manu says:
A king should conduct himself with the splendor and conduct of Indra, Arka, Vāta, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, Agni, and the Earth.
Just as Indra sends down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should one practicing the vow of Indra shower that kingdom with the fulfillment of its desires.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should he draw taxes from the kingdom; for that is indeed the proper vow of the sun.
Just as the wind moves having entered all living beings, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "wind-like" vow.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must everything be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do his subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow.
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is known as the Agneya vow.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings.
Nārada said:
He is without beginning and without end, the lord of the earth among bipeds;
for, being radiant and pure, he has not strayed from the path.
How is it that the king is not a deity— he by whose word an impure man becomes pure, and who instantly makes the pure impure?
Therefore, one should not despise him, nor revile him, nor treat him with contempt;
one should abide by his command, for death would result from its transgression.
The majesty of kings is their command, and that is established in their speech;
whatever they may say, whether it be false or true, that is the law for those engaged in legal proceedings.
This one named Rājan moves upon the earth as the thousand-eyed Indra in person;
these subjects must not remain standing in defiance of his command.
Because he holds the office of protection, because of his sovereignty, and because he is seen to favor all beings, whatever the king does is authoritative; such is the established rule.
Just as a husband is always worthy of honor by women even if he is devoid of virtues,
so too is a lord of men worthy of honor by his subjects even if he is devoid of virtues.
Since subjects do not deviate from the path out of fear of the kings' commands,
legal procedure (vyavahāra) should therefore be understood as the proclamation of the king's governance.
For the sake of stability, rulers of the earth have established rules of conduct;
therefore, they say that the royal decree is weightier even than those rules of conduct.
Subjects are purchased by the king through his ascetic merit; thus, the monarch is their master.
Therefore, one must abide by his word, for their conduct is dependent upon him.

‘Cāritravidhayaḥ’ refers to the methods for establishing shares and other arrangements made by the king; ‘rājaśāsanam’ is the royal edict; ‘vārttā’ is the livelihood consisting of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth.
Manu says: “A ruler of the earth must not be disregarded as a mere human being, even if he is a child.”
For this is a great deity who dwells in human form.
Fire burns only the man who approaches it too closely;
but the fire of a king consumes the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-born Śrī, in whose prowess lies victory,
and in whose anger resides death— for he is composed of all splendor.
Whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
therefore, the king quickly sets his mind upon his destruction.
Therefore, that lord of men should apply whatever dharma he desires toward those who are dear to him, or whatever is undesirable toward those who are not dear; he should not question that dharma.
Regarding the application of punishment, Manu says:
"Having considered the place and time, as well as the power and learning [of the offender],
he should inflict punishment according to his ability upon men who act unjustly, in accordance with what is deserved."
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is remembered as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be righteousness itself.
When properly maintained through careful deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when implemented without due deliberation, he brings about destruction on every side.
[7] Regarding the term "king," Gautama says: "Others, except for Brahmins, should sit below him as he sits above; they too should respect him. Bṛhaspati says:
"Because he pleases his subjects by means of the fourfold army..."
Shining with that form, he is called a king.
Aṅgiras:
Because he purifies the king— who has committed a sin— by means of a severe punishment and by way of instruction, he is therefore called a *guru*.
‘Pāpam’ refers to the evildoer; ‘from avana’ means from protection. In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa:
“In a land without a king, security and prosperity do not prevail.”
Moreover, in a kingless state, an army cannot withstand its enemies.
As cows without a herdsman, as a forest without debtors,
and as rivers without water, so is a kingdom without a king;
it would be like blinding darkness, where nothing at all could be discerned.
If there were no king in the world to distinguish between the good and the evil, [the strong would devour the weak].
Thus ends the praise of the king.
2. Now, regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*): therein, in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, it is said:
"On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable asterism, one should perform the bath named after the asterism."
At a moment endowed with excellent qualities and free from all portents of ill omen.
When a fixed sign is conjoined with a benefic, situated in a quadrant, and endowed with an upacaya house,
there shall be a king who is the very soul of Śaṅkara in Pārvatī, the land of Kaśmīra.
Then, one endowed with all auspicious marks should be consecrated as the new king;
at that time, a city should be established there, crowded with banners and flags.
Likewise, the royal highways should be made free of dust by means of auspicious waters;
and the citizens, having bathed and being dressed in fine garments, should carry auspicious objects in their hands.
[10] One should likewise go to the king’s residence accompanied by the chief courtesans,
as well as by the leading citizens, musicians, and those preeminent in virtue.
The city should be made beautiful with graceful dancers,
and at the time of the bath, a great clamor should likewise be raised.
With the sounds of musical instruments, conchs, and auspicious proclamations, and with the presence of sūtas, māgadhas, and bards.
Having first performed the great propitiatory rite (māhāśānti), the meritorious and auspicious rite for Vaināyaka,
as well as the excellent rite for the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti), he likewise offered the third oblation.
The family priest, having fasted and being well-versed in the Śruti and Smṛti,
should satisfy the thirteen great mantras in the sacrificial fire.
And likewise the Gaṇa, the Apratiratha, the Satya and Dharma Gaṇas,
as well as the Āyuṣya, the Abhaya, and the supreme Svastyayana.
Furthermore, he [should recite] the Vaiṣṇava mantras, as well as those of Indra,
and always those of Savitṛ, Brahmā, Rudra, and Varuṇa.

The thirteen great mantras are: “ṛtāṣāḍ,” “gaṇaḥ,” “īdṛg anyā gṛhe,” and so forth; “apratirathaḥ,” “āśuḥ śiśāna”; “satyagaṇaḥ,” “āgāt satyam”; “dharmagaṇaḥ,” “yās te agne ghorās tanuvaḥ”; and the two for fearlessness and auspiciousness, “yatra indra” and “svastidā.
Likewise, the king, having bathed, should be bathed again with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) like a deity.
Then, with jars made of clay, copper, silver, or gold, filled with water.
The Śūdras, stationed in the western direction, should bathe [the image] with water;
then the Vaiśyas, standing in the southern direction, should bathe it with milk.
Then the Kṣatriyas stationed in the eastern direction [offered] with curd;
then the Brahmins stationed in the north [offered] with nectar and clarified butter.
Thereafter, the head of the king should be purified by the twice-born with earth from a mountain;
his two ears should be diligently cleansed with earth from an anthill.
The neck of the mountain should be cleared of earth from the position of Śakra,
and likewise the heart [of the mountain] should be cleared of earth from the door of the royal palace.
Then, the back should be cleansed by kings with clay from a temple,
and likewise the right arm with clay extracted from an elephant's tusk.
The nose should be gradually cleaned with earth attached to a bull's horn;
then the region of the hips should likewise be cleaned by Vaiśyas with earth from a brothel.
When the sides are to be cleaned, they should be cleaned in due order with earth from a riverbank;
then, when the shudras are to clean his knees, they should use earth from a horse-stable.
[12] One should always [anoint] the calves with earth from Gokula and the feet with earth from a lake,
using all medicinal herbs, all seeds, perfumes, and gems.
He should be bathed with all kinds of flowers, all kinds of fruits, and likewise with yellow pigment (rocanā);
then, seated upon the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana), he should be bathed with all the radiant waters.
In accordance with their capacity, men, placing the family priest at their head,
should consecrate the king according to the words of the astrologers.
By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise by the foremost of Śūdras,
as well as by women devoted to their husbands and by those with sons, as if toward their own children.
Then, having bathed, with his limbs anointed, having performed the libations to the gods and the sacred fires,
he put on a crown, wore garlands, bound his turban, and was fully adorned.
One should behold a hundred auspicious signs and one hundred and eight meritorious ones;
for the sake of pacification, all this should be performed in due order at the principal site.
Having performed the remainder and then offered the oblations, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Thereafter, having first worshipped Vināyaka, the king should be consecrated.
Then, in due order, he [honored] the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— the planets, the blue lord of serpents (Nīla), Agni, the Brahmins, and the domestic priest.
Having dedicated it to the gods and the ancestors, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins;
and there, one properly grants fearlessness to all beings.
Then, for this reason, he should release all animals held in their respective places;
he liberates those situated in their bonds and enclosures according to the sacred teaching.
He abandons those who are thorns— even those who are cruel— such as the killers of cows, Brahmins, and others,
as well as elephant-killers, even if they are well-trained.
The king himself should be seated by the priest upon a beautiful and auspicious lion-throne covered with a tiger-skin.
Seated upon his throne, he should look upon the assembled subjects,
having honored the royal umbrella and weapons, as well as the leaders of the gaṇas and the horses.
Having mounted his decorated elephant and distributed his stores of wealth,
he circumambulated the city, entered it, and returned once more to his home.
Having paid honor to the leading citizens present in the assembly, he should dismiss them;
and when they have departed, he should gratify the actors and dancers with wealth.
He should feed all the brahmins, as well as the poor, the helpless, and his kinsmen;
thereafter, together with the great assembly, according to the traditional customs of former kings.
The king takes his meal after distributing [portions] to the royal servants;
then, having sipped water and taken betel-leaf in his mouth, he may enjoy himself for a moment.
Then, together with a few of those residing in the inner apartments,
he should guard himself with great effort, and thereafter enjoy as he pleases.
By this very procedure,
the king should always perform the rite of consecration with effort on the day of his coronation, year after year.
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa:
When that clamor of the people had gradually subsided, the lord of men, having bowed to his seated preceptor, spoke thus to the family priest: [14]
O Blessed One, you ought to command all the rites and their necessary equipment for the consecration of Rāma.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha, the best of the twice-born,
commanded those diligent attendants standing before the king with palms joined in reverence.
"The appointed officials;
gold and other gems, jewels, and even all medicinal herbs;
white garlands, parched grain, and honey and clarified butter separately."
Unwashed garments, a chariot, and all types of weapons;
a white-colored horse and an elephant endowed with auspicious marks.
Both yak-tail fans, the banner, and the white parasol;
and a hundred golden jars, radiant as fire.
A bull with golden horns in its entirety, a tiger skin,
and whatever else may be desired, as well as anything that is pleasing to the mind.
"Have the lord of the earth stationed in the fire-chamber at dawn,
and have the gates of the inner apartments as well as the gates of the entire city closed."
Let them be honored with sandalwood, garlands, and likewise with strings of flowers;
and let there be an offering of curd and milk, excellent in substance and quality.
One shall obtain the fruit of a hundred thousand excellent Brahmins;
let the preparations for the perfected mantras and so forth be arranged at dawn itself.
"Tomorrow, as soon as the sun has risen, there shall be the recitation of auspicious blessings;
let the Brahmins be invited and let the seats be prepared."
Let the banners be commanded to be raised, and let the royal highway be sprinkled with water;
let all the citizens and the courtesans likewise be well-adorned.
Let them remain in the second courtyard of the royal palace—
*kakṣyā* meaning an inner enclosure or court.
In temples and shrines, various kinds of food offerings should be presented along with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
And various arrangements of garlands should be set out separately.
Let the warriors, firm in their long-standing resolve, armored and clad in clean garments,
enter the magnificent palace of the great king.
Having thus given his command,
Vasiṣṭha reported to the king, whose mind was well-pleased, that everything had been accomplished, further gladdening him.
Likewise,
all the materials for the consecration have been prepared,
as well as water brought from the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
And water was brought from other sacred rivers,
as well as all kinds of seeds, perfumes, and various jewels.
A vehicle yoked with men, darbha grass, flowers, water,
unwashed garments, and a golden pitcher.
Furthermore, golden jars, beautifully adorned and filled with the sprouts of milk-trees mixed with fruits, were prepared.
Rasa, gorocanā, parched grain, curd, ghee, honey,
as well as earth from sacred fords, water, and living beings.
Two beautiful fly-whisks with handles of lovely jewels, as pure as moonbeams and well-adorned,
were prepared for the sake of the illustrious Rāma.
Resembling the orb of the full moon and adorned with glorious garlands,
a royal parasol was prepared for Rāma’s consecration as crown prince.
And my excellent elephant, the royal mount, awaits me.
A royal mount fit for a king,
a white horse of the finest breed prepared for Rāma’s sake,
and eight auspicious maidens adorned with every ornament.
Courtesans endowed with beauty and youth and well-adorned,
white flowers, a cow, a sword, and a bow as well.
A pale-white bull with a hump, well-adorned with a golden chain;
a lion-throne covered with tiger-skin; and a kindled sacrificial fire.
All musical instruments, bards, panegyrists, and heralds; teachers, Brahmins, cows, and auspicious beasts and birds.
The citizens and country-folk, along with the guilds and the assemblies of merchants—
these and many others, being joyful and speaking kindly.
Likewise, there are the words of Daśaratha addressed to Rāma:
"O eldest, you have been commanded by me; born of my senior wife, you are equal to me in virtues.
You are a son worthy of me, even as I am worthy of my senior and peerless wife."
O father, your beloved son named Rāma has been born as the eldest by virtue of his own qualities;
by these very qualities, O dear one, you have won over these subjects.
Therefore, under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, you shall obtain the position of crown prince.
Likewise:
When the domestic priest had departed, Rāma, with his mind restrained,
then approached Nārāyaṇa together with his large-eyed wife.
Then, holding the vessel containing the sacrificial oblation over his head according to the prescribed rite,
he offered the clarified butter into the blazing fire for the sake of the Great Deity.
Having consumed the remainder of that sacrificial oblation and having made a resolution within himself,
he should meditate upon the divine Nārāyaṇa on a bed of kuśa grass spread upon the sacrificial ground.
Restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, the son of the best of men lay down together with Vaidehī in the glorious temple of Viṣṇu.
Then the people heard that Rāma, having observed the fast together with Vaidehī, was lying down according to the prescribed rites upon the ground strewn with darbha grass.
Thus concludes the ritual for consecration.
[18] 3 — Now, the qualities of a king.

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The king should be far-sighted, highly energetic, capable, free from envy, affectionate toward his devotees, generous, a refuge for all beings, sharing with others, truthful in speech, free from malice, profound, intolerant of injustice, wise, majestic, skilled in providing remedies, not procrastinating, dexterous, patient, knowledgeable of targets, skilled in the knowledge of the application and collection of place, time, and materials, secretive in the execution of counsel, one who keeps his own vulnerabilities concealed while knowing the vulnerabilities of others, a firm striker, light-handed, victorious over cold, heat, and fatigue, one who has conquered passion, hatred, greed, and envy, beloved by the subjects, a provider of favor to the distressed, a giver of food to Brahmins, and one who seeks prosperity and fame."

‘Long-sighted’ means one who knows the true nature of future affairs. ‘Profound’ means one whose outward expressions of anger, joy, and so forth are unperceivable. ‘Impatient’ means one who cannot endure the prosperity of others. ‘Not slow-acting’ means one who does not procrastinate. ‘One whose secret counsel is hidden’ means one who knows the true nature of his plans by inferring them from their results. ‘One with closed vulnerabilities’ means one whose weak points are covered against those whom others might attack. ‘Beloved by the subjects’ means one who causes delight among the people.

Gautama says: “The king rules over all, with the exception of the Brahmins. He should be one who acts rightly and speaks rightly; he should be well-trained in the three Vedas and in *ānvīkṣikī* (logic) and the other sciences; he should be pure, have his senses under control, be endowed with virtuous associates and proper means, and be impartial toward his subjects. He should also promote their welfare. ‘Rules’ (*īṣṭe*) means he is the sovereign lord. ‘*Ānvīkṣikī*’ is the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*). Yājñavalkya says:
One who possesses great energy, is liberal in his aims, grateful, a servant of the elders,
humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure.
One who is not dilatory, possessed of mindfulness, not mean-spirited, nor harsh;
likewise, one who is virtuous, free from vice, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.

That lord of men was likewise trained in the protection of his own weak points through the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī) and the science of government (daṇḍanīti), as well as in the science of commerce (vārtā) and the triple Vedas (trayī).
‘Mahotsāhaḥ’ means one of great exertion; ‘sthūlalakṣyaḥ’ means one who is liberal in expenditure. [20] Kātyāyana says:
He should be disciplined, endowed with scriptural knowledge, and possessed of both treasury and valor.
A king should be devoted to Brahmins, characterized by a disposition for generosity, and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Free from arrogance, malice, slander, fickleness, and anger; confident yet humble, not overbearing, sociable, and pleasant to behold.

Prosperity attends to the utmost degree that wise man who has his senses under control, who has conquered himself, who wields the rod of punishment against those who deserve it, and who acts only after careful deliberation.

‘Stambhaḥ’ (arrogance) is the refusal to bow before others. ‘Upatāpaḥ’ (affliction) here refers to the oppression of subjects. ‘Paiśunyam’ (slander) is the disclosure of the faults of others. ‘Pragalbhaḥ’ (boldness) is the absence of fear in an assembly.
Viṣṇu says: A king who is happy through the happiness of his subjects and distressed by their distress [is truly a king].
Endowed with fame in this world, he is honored in heaven after passing away.
Yājñavalkya says:

A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward his affectionate kin, and wrathful toward his enemies; he should behave toward his circle of servants and his subjects as a father does.
Manu says: He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies,
straightforward toward friends, and endowed with forbearance toward Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning grains,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
Kātyāyana says:
Kings who remain established in their own duty shall attain the state of Śakra;
but those who are always devoid of proper conduct shall dwell in the Avīci hell.
That king who goes under the sway of anger without having properly understood [the consequences] shall dwell in a terrible hell for half a kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
The superintendent of liquor, fallen from heaven, dwells in the form of a king;
he must constantly perform that by which he may attain the ultimate reality.
Thus end the qualities of a king. [22] 4 — Now, the ministers.
Regarding that, Yājñavalkya says, following the phrase "there, the lord of men":
"He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
with them, and then with a Brahmin, he should deliberate upon the kingdom, and after that, by himself."
‘Maulān’ means hereditary, descended from father and grandfather; ‘śucīn’ means pure, proven honest through tests.
Manu says:
“Hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, and of noble birth.”
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who have been thoroughly tested.
[23] ‘Those who have attained their mark’ means those whose actions have been fully observed.
Even a task that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so the highly prosperous kingdom, especially when undertaken without assistance?
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions,
he should act for his own benefit by attending to the affairs of all of them separately.
But above all others, the king should consult with a learned Brāhmaṇa regarding the supreme counsel endowed with the sixfold policy.
Always placing full confidence in him, one should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, one should then carry out the task.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Therefore, the king himself should choose assistants who are of noble birth—
brave, born of a high lineage, endowed with strength, and possessed of prosperity."
[He saw] virtuous people endowed with beauty, goodness, and qualities, possessed of patience,
capable of enduring afflictions, full of great energy, knowers of the Dharma, and sweet-spoken.
One should employ such assistants as these in auspicious undertakings: those who offer beneficial counsel to the king, who are devoted to their master, and who are full of affection.

[24] Regarding the adherence to the qualities of a king, Kātyāyana says: "One should appoint as a minister for deliberating on affairs a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with these very same qualities, who is devoted to the king, and of noble birth."
Where the ministers, courtiers, and physicians speak only what is pleasing,
the king there quickly falls away from his kingdom, his dharma, and his happiness.
One should not give way to anger at his words,
for these [words] must always be spoken by them as that which is just and well-established.
‘Ministers’ [are to be employed] in royal affairs; ‘courtiers’ in matters such as penance; ‘physicians’ in medical treatment. In the Mahābhārata it is said:
"Those servants who are suitable for those respective tasks should be properly stationed after they have been thoroughly tested."
A protector of the earth ought not to appoint a servant without first examining him.

Likewise: A king who desires his own welfare should not station by his side men who are childish, nor base, nor lacking in wisdom, nor those who have not conquered their senses, nor those of ignoble birth.
Virtuous, of noble birth, brave, wise, and free from envy;
men who are not mean-spirited, pure, and skillful—such should be the attendants at one's side.
Every day, the lord of men should examine his servants through trustworthy spies who share similar character and are confident; for such people reveal what is in the mind.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One who is of noble birth, endowed with virtuous conduct, proficient in the science of archery,
skilled in the training of elephants and other disciplines, and gentle in speech."
He is an expert in omens, in the knowledge of portents, and in medicine;
he is grateful for services rendered, heroic, capable of enduring hardship, and upright.
A Brahmin or a Kṣatriya who knows the rules for military arrays and tactics, and who can distinguish between the worthless and the essential, should be appointed as the king’s commander-in-chief.

“An expert in the rules for military arrays (*vyūha*): an *vyūha* is the arrangement of an army in formations such as a wheel (*cakra*) or a staff (*daṇḍa*). “Its *tantra*” is the treatise on it; one who knows the various types of arrays through that [treatise] is meant.
“One who is tall, handsome, skillful, pleasant-spoken, and not arrogant;
one who wins the hearts of all—such a person is appointed as the chamberlain (*pratīhārī*).”
An envoy should speak exactly as instructed, be proficient in the local dialects,
eloquent, patient with hardships, articulate, and knowledgeable in the distinctions of place and time.
Having understood the place and the time, that messenger who speaks at the proper moment what has been done by the rulers of the earth shall be a true envoy of the king.
Tall, robust, brave, firm in devotion, and undisturbed— such guards, who are ever-enduring of hardship and loyal, should be appointed by the king.
One who is unassailable, free from cruelty, and firm in devotion to the king becomes a betel-bearer,
or a woman possessing those same qualities.
"Incorruptible," meaning unassailable by others;
one who knows the true principles of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), is skilled in [the requirements of] place and time,
and is expert in statesmanship— such a person should be appointed as the Minister for Peace and War (*sāndhivigrahika*) by the king.
The "six measures of policy" (*ṣaḍguṇāḥ*) are peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge; he is a knower of their application and their various methods.

He should be known as one who understands income and expenditure, knows the world, is skilled in the production of regions, recognizes what has been done and left undone by his servants, and is a protector of the people.
‘Akṣarakṣitā’ means a protector of the dice. One who is handsome, young, tall, firm in devotion, of noble lineage, brave, and capable of enduring hardship is proclaimed as a bearer of the sword.
A king’s archer should be brave, endowed with strength, skilled in elephants, horses, and chariots, capable of enduring all hardships, and pure.
He was skilled in the knowledge of omens and portents, an expert in the training of horses,
a knower of the true principles of equine Ayurveda, and one who understood the specific characteristics of different types of terrain.
One who knows strengths and weaknesses, possesses steady vision, speaks kindly,
is brave, and is highly educated is proclaimed to be a worthy charioteer.
One who is incorruptible, pure, and skillful, the best among those who know medical science,
and knowledgeable in the rules of the treatises on soup— such a person is praised as the superintendent of the kitchen.
Those who know the rules of the science of cookery, who are unassailable, of noble birth,
and whose hair and nails are kept short— such men should all be maintained in the kitchen.
One who is impartial toward both enemy and friend, proficient in the treatises on dharma,
a preeminent brahmin of noble birth, shall serve as the judge of legal affairs.
In that assembly, the chief members of the twice-born who were to serve as judges should be of such a character:
proficient in the scripts of all countries and learned in all the scriptures.

The wise declare that the scribe of the king is the superintendent of all departments; [he should write] auspicious documents provided with a heading, perfectly complete, arranged in even lines, and beautiful.
He who indeed writes the syllables is known as the excellent scribe;
he is skilled in expedient means and speech, and proficient in all the treatises.

O best of kings, a scribe should be one who can express many meanings with few words; he should be skilled in the means—conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force—and proficient in speech. He must understand the true intent of statements and know the distinctions between place and time.
[28] O best of kings, the scribe should be one who is not to be bribed by the king’s favorites.
Men who know the true nature of others, who are tall in stature, and free from greed,
should be appointed as officials for legal matters to summon people.
The king should appoint such persons as gatekeepers,
who are experts in the proper handling of iron, garments, skins, and other such items, as well as precious gems.
One who discerns the core from the worthless, who is incorruptible and ever pure,
and who is both skillful and vigilant, is proclaimed as a worthy superintendent of wealth.
The ruler of the earth should appoint men who are like treasurers at all the gates of income,
and likewise at the gates of expenditure.
One who has mastered the eight branches of medical treatment through mutual consultation,
who cannot be led astray, who is a protector of the Dharma, and who is born of noble lineage— such a person shall be a physician.
He is to be known as the master of life; his word must always be carried out by the king, O monarch, just as it is carried out by ordinary people.
One who knows the rules for training elephants, is skilled regarding wild breeds,
and likewise is patient with the king's afflictions, is praised as an elephant superintendent.
One who possesses these very qualities, and especially one who is well-seated on an elephant, is recommended for all the king's undertakings.
‘Svāsana’ means one who possesses a firm seat.
One who knows the rules for training horses, is skilled in medical treatment,
and serves as the superintendent of horses for the lord of the earth is praised as a *svāsana*.
One who is incorruptible, brave, wise, and of noble birth,
who is diligent in all duties, is remembered by the king as the proper superintendent of the fort.
One who knows the rules of the science of architecture, possesses a light hand, has overcome fatigue,
is far-sighted, and is brave is proclaimed as a master builder (sthapati).
Whether weapons are released from a machine, released by hand, not released at all, or held while being discharged,
the preceptor of missiles who remains unperturbed and skilled is distinguished as superior.

"Discharged from a machine" refers to arrows and the like; "discharged by hand" refers to spears and the like; "not discharged" refers to swords and the like; "held after being discharged" refers to staffs and the like.
An elder, born of a noble family, well-spoken, descended from his father and grandfather, pure, and disciplined—such a person is desired as the superintendent of the king's inner apartments.
Women over fifty years of age and men beyond seventy should be appointed by the king as attendants in the inner apartments for all duties.

One who knows the principles of storage and classification, who is ever vigilant, skilled in the armory, and diligent in his duties—[such a person should be appointed]. "Storage" (*sthāpanā*) refers to the placement of weapons and machines in their appropriate locations; "classifications" (*jātayaḥ*) refer to the internal distinctions among weapons and so forth.
[30] O upholder of the royal lineage, the actions of a king are immeasurable;
having understood these actions to be superior, inferior, or middling, the monarch [should act accordingly].
He should employ [officials] among men who are superior, inferior, or middling;
for by the reversal of duties, a king meets with destruction.
“Because of the inversion of duties and actions”: by assigning a low task to one who is superior, or a high task to one who is mediocre, a king perishes.
Having ascertained their assignment, personal effort, devotion, learning, valor, lineage, and conduct, the ruler of the earth should determine the livelihood of his men.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not have a greedy retinue; a king may well be greedy himself, but it is better that he be so alone than with a [greedy] retinue, for faults arise from the retinue and lead to destruction; therefore, one should seek out such a retinue beforehand.
Having spoken of ministers endowed with learning and virtue, Manu says:
"One should also appoint others who are pure, wise, and steadfast."
He should appoint well-tested ministers who are trustworthy and capable of collecting wealth for the state.
He should appoint as many diligent,
capable, and discerning men as are required for his duties.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “The protection of the royal family, the preservation of the treasury, and the safeguarding of cows and Brahmins constitute his duties for the next world. Because these tasks are common to all his dependents, he must specifically employ scouts and secret agents, as well as the application of counsel; since these are for that purpose, the king’s livelihood—whether direct or indirect—must be exclusively free from fault. Therefore, those on the side of the servants who are afflicted by the defects of anger, greed, pride, or fear; those who have been flattered, then insulted; those who have been falsely accused; those deprived of their gifts, honors, and positions; those whose entire property has been seized; and those ruined by their own faults—these must be constantly scrutinized. Regarding those devoted to dharma and artha, one should strive to ensure they do not hear of their own territory nor cause dissension in the enemy’s territory, employing means such as conciliation (sāma) and the rest. Those skilled in counsel should be appointed among counselors, those heroic in the use of force among military officers, those constant in dharma among high-ranking officials and the king himself, those free from greed among those in charge of collecting revenues, and those of noble lineage among the border guards. Pure individuals should be employed in financial matters, and others should be assigned to other tasks according to their suitability.”

‘Of all’ refers to the ministers. ‘Saṃparāya’ means war; that which is useful for it is ‘sāṃparāyika’. ‘Because of the commonality of action’ means because of the single task consisting of protecting the kingdom. A ‘spy’ (cāra) is one who moves about in disguise to know the conduct of the countryside. A ‘counter-spy’ (praticāra) is one who moves in disguise and knows the conduct of that [spy]. ‘Those entrusted with counsel’ (mantrapraṇidhayaḥ) are those who seek out the king’s secret plans. The meaning is that these are like snakes related to the enemy king and are to be suspected. ‘Because they have that as their purpose’ means since the knowledge of such conduct is precisely the purpose of the spies and others. ‘Direct activity’ (pratyakṣā vṛttiḥ) is observing the matter oneself. ‘Indirect’ (parokṣā) is knowing the conduct through spies. ‘Exclusively’ (ekāntataḥ) means by relying on only one of the two types of activity. ‘The side of the servants’ (bhṛtyapakṣāḥ) refers to the servants—those who were previously honored but later dishonored. ‘Accusation’ (abhyākhyānam) is the public proclamation of faults. ‘Deprived of gifts, honors, and positions’ means those deprived of gifts, deprived of honors, and deprived of their positions. ‘Those ruined by their own faults’ means those corrupted by their own defects. For that reason, ‘these and others’ must ‘be constantly scrutinized. One should strive regarding the duties and other matters pertaining to ‘them. ‘Non-disclosure of one’s own domain’ means the non-leaking and non-publicizing of the secrets of one’s own territory. ‘In great matters,’ they must be protected ‘within oneself. ‘Constantly devoted to dharma’ means righteous people. ‘In the collections’—the word ‘of wealth’ (arthasya) is to be supplied. ‘In the border regions’ (prānteṣu) means in the frontier districts of one’s own territory; ‘native’ (maula) means those born in that region.

Viṣṇu: “One should appoint reliable persons to mines, salt-works, toll-stations, and elephant forests; righteous persons to religious duties; skillful persons to financial matters; brave persons to military affairs; fierce persons to fierce tasks; and eunuchs to women. Manu:
“For their sake, one should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth.”
He should employ pure men at the mines and workshops, and timid men within the inner apartments.
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy agents;
he should be intent on providing shelter in this world and behave toward men like a father.
He should appoint various wise supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry them out.
‘The annual tribute’ (*sāṃvatsarikaṃ baliṃ*) refers to the tax to be collected once a year. Likewise:
“And he should appoint a messenger who is proficient in all the scriptures.”
One who understands gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements, who is pure, skillful, and of noble birth.
Devoted, pure, skillful, mindful, knowledgeable of place and time,
handsome, fearless, and eloquent— a messenger such as this is praised by kings.

The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of discipline depends on punishment; the treasury and the kingdom depend on the king; and peace and its opposite depend on the envoy.
For it is the messenger indeed who unites those who are divided and also divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated from one another.
He should discern, through secret gestures and movements,
the other's facial expression, hint, and action, as well as what he intends to do regarding his undertakings.
Having understood in its true essence everything intended by the enemy king,
one should apply such effort as will not cause harm to oneself.
In the Mahābhārata:
"A protector of the earth must never kill a messenger under any circumstances;
for the slayer of a messenger shall enter hell along with his ministers."
[34] In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "The virtuous declare that messengers are not to be killed; many punishments for a messenger have been prescribed:
disfigurement of the limbs, flogging with a whip, shaving the head, and likewise the branding of marks."
For they declare these punishments for a messenger; indeed, the execution of a messenger is not seen as a punishment.
Thus [ends the section on] ministers.
Now, regarding the conduct of a subordinate, the Fish Purāṇa states that the Fish spoke:
I shall tell you how the mind of a king should be followed by his dependents;
listen as I speak.
O son of the Sun, having understood what must be done with your whole being according to your own power,
you should never speak, setting aside his words.
That which is agreeable and pleasing to him should be spoken in the assembly of people;
that which is disagreeable but beneficial should be spoken to him when he is in private.
[35] O King, when the mind is composed, one should speak what is true to the matter;
for one's own interest should be spoken by friends, and never indeed by oneself.
One must strive diligently to ensure that no duties are neglected;
furthermore, one appointed to a task must not cause any loss of wealth.
One should not disregard his pride, for he will become dear to the king;
likewise, one’s dress, speech, and conduct must conform to the king’s.
One should not engage in royal pastimes nor avoid what is disliked by them; one must remain wary of those who have become enemies of the superintendent of the harem or have been cast out from it.
O King, one should not go about praising [the king] without the sovereign's command;
one should carefully conceal any lack of affection and any insult.
Whatever may be a king's secret, that one should not disclose to the world; O best of kings, whatever has been told by the monarch, whether secret or non-secret, must be kept so.
One should not proclaim that in the world; thus one will become dear to the king.
Or, when another [command] is being issued, one should rise up with haste.
A wise man should say to the king, "What shall I do?
and having ascertained the state of the matter, he should act accordingly.
If this is done constantly, lightness of character will certainly arise;
therefore, one should speak what is pleasing to the king, but not excessively or repeatedly.
He should not be of a laughing disposition, nor should he have a frowning face;
he should neither be an over-talker nor a non-speaker, and likewise, he should not be envious.
He should never be self-conceited in any way,
nor should he ever proclaim the misdeeds of the king.
One should wear the garment, weapon, or ornament given by the king;
one who desires prosperity should not give those items to another person while still wearing them.
One should not eat excessively, nor should one indulge in sleeping during the day;
likewise, one should never enter through an unannounced door.
And one should not look at the king while he is on unsuitable ground;
rather, one should then sit to the king's right side or his left.
Furthermore, sitting in front or behind [the teacher] is censured;
as are yawning, spitting, coughing, anger, and leaning against a support.
A wise person should avoid frowning, spitting, or belching in his presence; nor should he himself proclaim his own virtues there.
Having purified their hearts and resorted to supreme devotion, they should skillfully employ only others for the purpose of proclaiming their own virtues.
The attendants of kings must always remain vigilant;
they must avoid deceit, greed, slander, atheism, and meanness.
Fickleness must always be abandoned by those who live in dependence upon a king;
rather, one should unite oneself with learning, sciences, and arts through one's own effort.
[37] Thereafter, one should attend upon the king for the sake of prosperity, which increases one's fortune;
and his sons, favorites, and ministers should always be paid homage.
One should never place trust in his ministers;
one should not speak to him unless asked, though one may speak at will in times of emergency.
A servant must always ascertain what is beneficial and wholesome speech, well-deliberated with those who wish him well, as well as the master's own state of mind.
A man who understands his wife's mind should serve his husband for the sake of happiness; one who desires prosperity must also discern his husband's favor and displeasure.
One should abandon a king who has become disaffected, but one should cause him to carry out his duties while he is still devoted;
for if he is disaffected, he will bring about destruction as well as the rise of the enemy.
Having increased one's hopes, he brings about the destruction of the fruit;
though free from anger, he appears angry, and though gracious, he is not without purpose.
He speaks with slow and hesitant words and cuts off his livelihood;
yet, delighted by partial statements, he does not otherwise acknowledge [the truth].
In all acts of devotion, he behaves as if asleep;
during discourses, he casts blame and interrupts the speech.
He feels ashamed even when his own virtues are being proclaimed;
moreover, he casts his gaze elsewhere while a ritual action is being performed.
This indeed is the characteristic of one who is dispassionate; now hear the characteristic of one who is attached:
he becomes pleased at the mere sight [of the teacher] and accepts his words with respect.
He offers him a seat and inquires after his welfare and other such matters;
and when seeing him in seclusion, he does not hesitate to disclose secrets to him.
Upon hearing his conversation, one’s face becomes joyful; one welcomes even unpleasant words spoken by him. Furthermore, one accepts even a small gift with great respect.
Likewise, during intervals between conversations, he remembers [it] with a joyful countenance.
Thus, O descendant of the Solar Lineage, one who is devoted should perform service;
even if he has previously been indifferent, one should not abandon him when in times of distress.
Those who do not abandon a friend, a servant, or even a master in times of calamity— even if they are devoid of merit and immeasurable—
go to the realm frequented by the hosts of gods and the boundless garlands of Indra.
Thus ends the conduct of dependents.
fortresses.
Yājñavalkya says:

One should dwell in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; therein one should construct fortresses for the protection of the people, the treasury, and oneself.
‘Paśavya’ means beneficial for cattle. ‘Jāṅgala’ is characterized by high ground. Manu says: “Jāṅgala is rich in crops, inhabited mostly by Āryas, and free from impurity.”
One should dwell in a pleasant country that has submissive vassals and provides a means of livelihood.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "It shall consist mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, be unassailable by others,
contain some Brāhmaṇas, and likewise perform many types of labor."
A land that is not dependent on rain for its waters, which is delightful, filled with devoted people,
free from oppression by taxes, and likewise abounding in flowers and fruits.
That dwelling was inaccessible to enemy armies even in times of calamity;
it shared equally in the king’s sorrow and joy, and remained ever dear to him.
Free from reptiles and devoid of wild beasts and thieves—
a king should dwell in such a territory as may be available.
Manu says: One should dwell in a city by taking refuge in a desert-fortress, an earth-fortress, an earthen-fortress, a wooden-fortress, a man-fortress, or a mountain-fortress.
‘Dhanva’ is a desert region; ‘mahīdurga’ is terrain that is extremely low and high; ‘vārkṣa’ is a forest fort.
Bṛhaspati says: For the protection of oneself, one’s wife, one’s wealth, and one’s people, as well as for the preservation of accumulated stores.
The king should cause a fortress to be built, equipped with ramparts and gates.
[41] Manu says:
One should take refuge in a mountain fortress with every effort;
for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Likewise: "A single archer standing upon a palace can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight a hundred thousand. Therefore, a fortress is superior."
Bṛhaspati said:
[A kingdom] is provided with the fuel and juices of living beings, with canes, young grass, food, and vehicles,
and with various machines and weapons, as well as with smooth and brave men.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas and Kṣatriyas who maintain the sacred fire-offerings,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
Irrevocable taxes shall be granted to them, and houses and lands shall be bestowed;
having recorded this in their own royal edicts, they should be made exempt from the king's authority.

They should always perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), desire-based (kāmya), pacificatory (śāntika), and nourishing (pauṣṭika) rites according to the Purāṇas, as well as discipline in cases of doubt.
Wherever the ground is even or undulating, in whatever manner it may be,
the halls, towers, moats, and other such features should be constructed accordingly.
Then the subjects should construct houses there on all sides:
the twice-born, physicians, merchants, artisans, craftsmen, and guards likewise.
One should likewise arrange for platforms, standing places, exits, crossroads, pits, and quadrangles, as well as assembly halls, marketplaces, and cow-pens.
‘By the perfected ones (siddhaiḥ)’ means by those who are devoted. ‘The stages (bhūmayaḥ)’ is a transposition of case endings; it refers to the specific nature of the one to be propitiated.
Thus [are explained] the difficult points.
Now, regarding the construction of the city, it is stated therein in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"There should be a gate-tower (*gopura*) provided with doors, which is exceedingly beautiful."
Mounted upon an elephant adorned with banners, the king should enter the city by that [gate].
And likewise, four market-streets should be constructed there;
at the front of one of those streets, a firm temple for the gods should be built.
The royal palace is ordained at the front of the second street;
the court of justice (dharmādhikaraṇa) should be established at the front of the third street.
And at the very front of the fourth street, a gateway (gopura) is prescribed;
one should have the city made either rectangular, square, or circular.
One should likewise cause a triangle lacking corners, one with a barley-corn center,
one in the shape of a half-moon, and one in the form of a thunderbolt to be made.
On the banks of rivers, they praise the half-moon shape because of that [natural contour];
elsewhere, it should be constructed with great effort by one who understands.
A *gopura* is a city gate. *Āyata* means long. *Sraktihīna* means devoid of corners.
Bṛhaspati says:
one should construct a separate residence within the fortress, provided with water and trees.
To the east of that, he should construct an assembly hall facing the east, endowed with auspicious characteristics.
It was provided with garlands, incense, and wine, endowed with heroes and jewels,
furnished with deities in the form of images and paintings, as well as fire and water.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"The king shall have a treasury built to the south of the royal palace;
and on the southern side of that, the elephant stable is ordained."
The stable for elephants should be constructed facing either the east or the north;
likewise, the armory is prescribed for the south-eastern quarter.
[44] And the kitchen, O knower of dharma, as well as other workshops,
and the house of the domestic priest should be situated to the left of the royal palace.
And for those who know the mantras and the Vedas, as well as for the physician, a share in that very same place is likewise ordained; and there, a storehouse is established.
Likewise, the place for the cattle and for the horses is established here;
a row of horses facing north is ordained.
O knower of dharma, those horses should be kept facing eastward; indeed, those turned toward the west are censured. Thus should they be maintained by the night-watchmen throughout the entire night.
One should keep cocks, monkeys, and especially baboons,
as well as a cow with her calf, within the stables.
Goats should be diligently maintained by one who seeks the welfare of horses;
furthermore, the removal of their dung from the stables of cattle, elephants, horses, and other animals [should be performed].
When the sun, the god of gods, has set, the king,
having understood the situation, then directed his charioteers to their respective positions there.
He should provide dwelling places for all of them in due order—
both for the warriors and for the artisans— without distinction.
[45] He should provide auspicious dwellings in the fortress for those who know the proper time for mantras,
as well as for veterinarians of cattle, horses, and likewise elephants.
The king should indeed provide for them abundantly, for in a fortress afflictions are powerful;
a place within the fortress is ordained for both the *kuśīlava*s and the Brahmins.
Without a fortress, even a great army cannot achieve its purpose; therefore, within the fortress, defensive engines equipped with various weapons must be constructed.
Protection must be provided by the king for those who have killed a thousand men;
furthermore, the gates of the fortress must be kept secure by the monarch.
O King, a storehouse for all types of weapons is highly recommended here— namely, bows, projectiles, and javelins.
Then there were arrows, swords, and likewise armor;
clubs, balls, and mallets, along with iron bars.
And of many stones, as well as mallets,
tridents, sharp-edged spears, and iron clubs, O King.
O best of men, [he was covered] with spears along with tridents, with javelins, with battle-axes,
with discuses, and with armor together with shields.
There were piles of spades, ropes, and reeds, as well as baskets, weapons for harming, sickles, and heaps of charcoal.
And here is left a collection of all the implements of the artisans,
as well as all musical instruments and medicinal herbs.
There was an abundant accumulation of fodder, fuel,
molasses, all kinds of oils, and likewise dairy products.
[46] Then, from all sides, there were fat, marrow, and sinews together with bones,
as well as ox-hides, drums, and grains.
Likewise for clouds, cotton cloths, barley and wheat,
for all jewels, all garments, and even for all metals without exception.
Of *kalāya* beans, mung beans, black gram, and chickpeas, together with sesame seeds;
likewise of all grains, as well as of soil and cow dung.
The king should store in his fortress hemp, resin, lac, borax, and whatever else may be required.
In the jars, venomous serpents, as well as predatory lions and the like, and wild beasts and birds, should be placed; and they must be kept from harming one another.
O illustrious one, the king must diligently establish separate and well-guarded locations for those who are hostile.

Likewise: A king should always reside in a well-guarded fortress, equipped with mechanical weapons, watchtowers, and ramparts, supplied with all kinds of grain and medicinal herbs, and surrounded by merchants.
Likewise: "O King, the ancient masters have described this as a digestive formulation (kṣudyoga) for half a month, consisting of śirīṣa, udumbara, śamī, and bījapūra fruits, saturated with ghee."
[47] Kaśeru, utpala roots, and likewise sugarcane root—
this supreme monthly preparation is a medicinal gruel (maṇḍa) prepared with the aforementioned milk and ghee.
Having obtained the bone of a man slain by a weapon, one should use it as the fire-drill;
with a variegated bamboo stick, one should then produce fire there.
O King, wherever the rite is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder three times within the house, no other fire shall blaze there; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, there should be the bone of a cotton plant and a snake's slough;
incense for the expulsion of snakes is always recommended in the home.
O King, a house that is smeared with sea salt, rock salt, barley, and earth scorched by lightning is not consumed by fire.
During the day, the fire must be guarded in a secure place, especially when the wind is blowing.
Thus ends the construction of the city.
Now, regarding the purification of the external ground, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa; Indra said:
What kind of city should be constructed, and what kind of town is auspicious? O best of gods, in what location should it be built? This is what I wish to know.
[48] Brahmā said: In a region where all medicinal herbs grow, which brings happiness to all the worlds,
and in a place sloping toward the northeast, the city of Śakra and other structures should be constructed.
In a place free from gravel and stones, devoid of thorny bushes,
firm, free from dust, and not overgrown with kusha grass and the like;
The earth is endowed with a fragrant scent, characterized by a sweet taste,
free from outcasts and the fallen, and devoid of fragments of earthenware bowls.
Abandoned by the dwellings of gods, free from affliction, and delightful;
with upward-sloping banks, easy to ford, and devoid of unevenness.
That earth is pure when purified by burning and other rites, and it is auspicious when accompanied by Caṇḍeśvara or joined with Sarveśvara; otherwise, the earth brings fear.
When the earth is inverted in its previous color and deviates from the rules regarding its location, time, and other factors as set forth in the sūtras,
it brings fear to the sovereign, the merchant guild, and the city.
A land afflicted by misfortunes such as pestilence, crowded with malevolent spirits like Pūtanās,
marked by banners [of war], and productive of all kinds of evils, must be avoided.
That earth which has not been abandoned for a year, where black grain grows, and which provides satisfaction, should be known as a giver of auspiciousness.
The goddesses here must always be protected and worshipped according to their respective portions;
one should arrange their stations and perform their consecration (adhivāsa).
Caṇḍeśvara is a particular attendant (gaṇa) of Mahādeva. “Adhivāsa” means installation. Likewise:
First, the enclosure on the ground should be made with four staffs.
Having taken a cow with its calf, as well as a water-jar, grain, and gold;
One should visualize the Earth upon that [lotus], adorned with Meru as its pericarp, clothed in garments, containing gold within, and accompanied by mango leaves.
Having thus worshipped the three-eyed God of gods, who is endowed with forest-dwelling habits and surrounded by oceans;
Having meditated upon Kumāra and the others, Śiva and the others, as well as the primordial Great Earth,
the Sun and the other world-protectors, the Nāgas, the groups of deities, and so forth;
Having first performed the worship, one should afterwards offer the bali-oblation to the directions;
having recited the Svapnamāṇavaka mantra, one sleeps there at ease.
At the end of the night, having observed an auspicious dream, an omen, or an auspicious bird, the teacher and the thread-holder should lay out the lines in the identified direction.
"‘The dreaming boy’ [is described] by the verse beginning with ‘That which while awake...
Between the Citrā and Svātī [nakṣatras], when there is a conjunction of Puṣya and Pitrya (Maghā),
the remaining [asterisms] situated between Uttarā and Dhruva are established according to the tradition."

The meaning is that the direction which lies between the rising of the two constellations Citrā and Svātī, and likewise which is joined straight with the constellations Puṣya and Maghā, is the eastern direction.
[50] In the absence of those, the twice-born should determine the east by means of birds;
thus, when the directions have been purified, he should perform the laying of the cord (sūtrapāta).
Having honored the preceptor, the master builder, and the best of the twice-born,
one should first establish the temple of the deity, the residence of the preceptor, and the dwelling of the Brāhmaṇas.
The preceptor, however, should construct the royal palace and the remaining houses according to the order of the social classes;
the city should be made circular, oblong, triangular, or square.
Just as it is adorned with the splendor of marketplaces according to the division of locations,
so too should a temple be constructed either in front of the royal palace or elsewhere.

The auspicious Maṅgalā, endowed with a beautiful thread, associated with the deities, and surrounded by the host of Śiva’s Mothers, should be fashioned with a bow; she bestows all accomplishments at her center and extremities.
One should never place Hari in the southeast, south, or southwest;
nor Viṣṇu in the west or north; and one should not install Śiva in the northwest.
When [the rite] is performed, the performer perishes and that place becomes desolate;
the deity is not worshipped there in that auspicious, native place.
In various sūtras I shall explain that by which peace and auspiciousness may come to cities,
towns, and the gate-towers and other structures of the gods.
In difficult paths, Śiva is praised when facing the enemy and situated in an auspicious sector;
when in front of the enemy, the city protected on all sides by him prospers even in a fortress.
Therefore, O Śakra, a fortress should be constructed in cities, towns, and other settlements;
for Mahālakṣmī and others, along with Caṇḍikā, bring about security.
Auspicious, yet appearing in inauspicious forms, the slayer of Mahiṣa with a face like Śiva’s,
she brings happiness to all the worlds, abiding according to the distribution of her stations.
Mahālakṣmī is praised in the east; Mahiṣāpahā is in the southeast;
Śivā is said to be in the south; and Carcikā is in the western city.
In the north, the five [images] beginning with Śubhadā and Kṣemā bestow peace upon the city;
nine Caṇḍikās should be established in the capital, and five indeed in the fort.
Likewise:
"The city, protected by deities and endowed with all constituent elements,
should be constructed with seven or five inner cities and adorned with pavilions."
Auspicious chambers endowed with beauty should be constructed in front of the pavilion;
thus, it shall be provided with a temple and possessed of a golden hue.
A city is proclaimed to be provided with nine fortifications;
a town is endowed with marketplaces and crowded with deities and the like.
Listen now to that city, Pattana, where there are marketplaces for gold, jewels, clothing, woolen cloth, and leather goods, as well as for the sale of liquor and other such items.
One should construct a compact and level marketplace, beautifully adorned like a merchant's stall; it may bear the name of a deity or one's own name, and as a port, it shall grant all desires.
[52] O Supreme God, one should cause an excavation to be made by means of mud pits and the like;
between the two [structures], a temple for the deity and so forth should be constructed.
But when the deity is devoid of divine splendor, one should resort to the auspicious "equal-vision" (samadṛṣṭi);
for when the deity is perceived through its physical marks (cihna), there is no definitive determination by vision alone.
When the mind is equanimous, the perception of the task is likewise auspicious;
one should not act with deficiency or excess when obstructed by serpents, lions, and the like.
In this manner, one should construct a beautiful shop for the son within the enclosure wall;
it should be four cubits in size, level, well-aligned with its measuring lines, and very handsome.
The city should be made with level roads and level exits from the streets;
its crossroads should be clean and always graced with worship.
The duties of other deities are encompassed by their own respective offices;
among these other deities, those who know the mantras bring auspiciousness to each of their own regions.
In this world, those who give much are distinguished according to the excellence of their acquisitions;
likewise, among the twice-born and others who are lifelong celibates, those devoid of sacred mantras are not auspicious.
Likewise, O Śakra, Carcikā and the others are terrifying when devoid of mantras;
so too, O twice-born ones, are the gods when positioned in front, behind, or on both sides.
Those who desire the welfare of the king and the kingdom must relinquish even a hundred hands;
they must not obstruct the king's vision, but should protect the queens with great effort.
If the eight staffs are made too wide, the king perishes;
therefore, a beautiful sight should always be provided within the archway.
A gateway (toraṇa) eight cubits high, richly adorned and made of stone or wood, is recommended for the Goddess; as are ponds, wells, water, and groves.
Likewise, a garden established in the northeast or the north-eastern direction bestows auspiciousness;
it shall grant all desires to the goddesses and the Mothers.
Whatever may arise from inauspicious planetary influences, from fate, or from the passage of time—
all that becomes auspicious when performed in a temple of the deity.
The constant recitation of the *bali* mantra and the ritual for the Mothers shall be auspicious;
they grant all desires to cities, towns, villages, and the cities of Brahmā.
There dwelt those who were knowers of the Vedas, endowed with the power of the knowledge of Brahman;
that city, named Kamalā, brings happiness to all the worlds.
For where one, two, three, or four Vidyās are established—
namely Rudra, Devī, Vijayā, and Gāyatrī— the Wheel exists by its own nature.

Houses should be constructed in rows, situated on auspicious paths and aligned straight; they should be located along excellent routes toward the east and north, provided with water, and endowed with deities.
For the sake of worshipping Brahmā and the Thirty-three gods, one should provide monasteries and other such facilities;
one should also establish places for recitation for Śiva and the Creator (Brahmā).
Whether in a pure city, O child, or in a royal capital, a port, a fortress, or a marketplace,
an auspicious vision of Mahālakṣmī brings great blessings.
Of Mukha, Liṅga, and Gaṇeśa; especially of Dhanada (Kubera), of Śrī in her gentle form, and of Svāmīśa and Śubha.
[54] One should cast one's gaze upon fierce Rākṣasa goddesses and not otherwise;
either outside, near a forest, or on the banks of a river or a mountain stream.
And the supreme [image] should be made in a palace, or else in a sacred ford (tīrtha) or following the market stalls;
[these forms are] Vārāhī, Bhairavī, Ugrā, Nārasiṃhī, and Trivikramī.
One must carefully avoid looking at cities, ports, and houses; a fierce gaze seizes the kingdom, and a cruel gaze seizes the city and its like.
The gaze of the Man-lion and the Boar would destroy beloved people;
therefore, one should maintain an auspicious gaze that is even and directed everywhere.
Even in marriage, an auspicious aspect is equally beneficial; it is not otherwise.
Therefore, with great effort, a gentle aspect from the gods is praised.
The aspect of planets possessing gentle forms upon the ascendant brings auspiciousness;
likewise, such gentle aspects upon cities, towns, and fortresses bring auspiciousness.
O King, in this manner, an auspicious aspect should be cast upon a city or a fort that is joyful;
however, for the sake of auspiciousness, one should avoid aspects from those of fierce form.
In the invocation or in water, a fierce gaze brings about auspiciousness.
Thus concludes the purification of the site.
[55] 6 — Now follows the ritual procedure for the building work.
In that regard, Sūta said in the Matsya Purāṇa:
(On the fruit of time) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the determination of the proper times for building a house.
Having recognized an auspicious time, one should then begin the construction of the dwelling.
The man who has a house built in Caitra incurs disease;
in Vaiśākha, he gains wealth and jewels; and in Jyeṣṭha, he likewise meets with death.
In Āṣāḍha, one obtains excellent servants and fine clothing;
in Śrāvaṇa, there is the gain of friends, but likewise loss in Bhādrapada.
In Āśvayuja there is the loss of one's wife; in Kārttika, wealth and grain;
likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa, food; and in Pauṣa, fear of thieves.
One shall frequently obtain gain; one should predict fire for Māgha, and gold for Phālguna—thus is the fruit according to the time recorded.
[56] (The results of the lunar mansions):
Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Mūla, the three Uttarās,
Ārdrā, Svātī, Hasta, and Anurādhā are commended for the commencement of building a house.
(The Result of the Days of the Week: All days of the week are auspicious, with the exception of Sunday and Tuesday.
(The Fruit of Yoga:
One should avoid [these actions] during Vyāghāta and Śūla; one should not perform them during Vyatīpāta and Atigaṇḍa, nor during the Viṣkambha, Gaṇḍa, Parigha, and Vajra yogas.

(The results of the Muhūrtas: One should begin the construction of a house during the Muhūrtas known as Maitreya, Māhendra, Gandharva, Abhijit, Rauhiṇa, Vairāja, and Sāvitra, which correspond to the asterisms Svāti, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj.
(The Result of the Ascendant):

Having obtained strength from both the Moon and the Sun, and with the ascendant aspected by benefics, the raising of pillars and other such works should be undertaken; otherwise, one should avoid them.
(The Examination of the Ground):
This same [procedure] should apply to palaces; it is likewise recommended for wells and ponds.
One should first examine the ground, and afterwards design the building site.
White, red, yellow, and black—land of these colors in successive order is recommended for the Brahmin and the other castes; therefore, an examination must be performed.
[57] For Brahmins, it is recommended that [the food] have a sweet taste; for a Kṣatriya, however, it should be astringent;
likewise, for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is praised as being both astringent and pungent.
In a pit measuring one cubit (ratni) in depth, having smeared it thoroughly on all sides with cow-dung, one should place clarified butter in an unbaked earthen bowl and prepare four wicks.
For the purpose of examining the ground, one should kindle a full fire facing all directions;
one should observe its radiance starting from the east and proceeding in successive order according to the castes.
That site known as Sāmūhika which shines forth on all sides bestows auspiciousness upon all castes in both palaces and houses.

A pit measuring one cubit (ratni) in depth should be examined by filling it with earth that was previously excavated; if more earth is required to fill it, one obtains prosperity; if less, there is loss; if exactly the same, the result is neutral.
Or else, one should sow all kinds of seeds in a ploughed field;
even those [seeds] will sprout there within three, five, or seven nights.
One should always avoid any other ground except for the best of the eldest [earth];
having examined it with the five products of the cow and medicinal waters, one should then sprinkle it.
Having fashioned a grid of eighty-one squares with lines made of gold,
or having smeared it with a fivefold paste, one should trace it all around with a thread.
There are ten lines extending eastward and ten extending northward;
in all divisions of the site-plan (vāstu), nine squares each are to be recognized.
[58] (Worship of the Deities):
Having divided the site into eighty-one squares, the architect, in all types of sites,
should worship the deities occupying those squares— thirty and fifteen respectively.
Thirty-two are to be worshipped on the outside, and thirteen are to be worshipped within;
I shall declare them by name, so listen to their locations.
One should worship them according to the prescribed rite in the northeast corner and the others:
Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Kuliśāyudha.
Sūrya, Satya, and Bhṛgu, as well as Ākāśa and Vāyu;
Pūṣan and Vitatha, and both Gṛhakṣata and Yama.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and likewise Pitṛgaṇa;
Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Jalādhipa.
The Asura, Śoṣa, Pāpa, Roga, Ahi, and Mukhya;
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Sūrya, Aditi, and likewise Diti.
These thirty-two are on the outside; now hear of the four within.
A wise person should worship those situated in the four corners, beginning with Īśāna.
Āpa, Sāvitra, Jaya, and likewise Rudra;
in the center is the four-footed Brahmā, and eight [deities] are situated near him.
One should know all those who are separated by one [in order]; hear them from the east onwards by name:
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Vivasvat, and Vibudhādhipa.
Mitra, then Rājayakṣman, Pṛthvīdhara in sequence,
and the eighth, Apavatsa— these are recorded as being situated around Brahmā.
Āpa, Apavatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti—
this is the group of the Padikas, thus [arranged] completely in the corners.
In the middle of that [space], however, there are the calves and the two-footed ones on all sides;
now I shall describe the bamboo strips and the cords individually.
To Vāyu from the disease, to the Pitṛs from Śikhin,
to Mukhya from Bhṛśa, and likewise to Vitatha from Śeṣa.
From Sugrīva to Iti, from Mṛga to Parjanya—these lineages have been fully described; in some places, however, they are indeed called Rajjus.
The convergence of these [lines], as well as the middle point, the equal [point],
and that which is situated at the corner of the trident— this is declared to be the vital point (marman).
In the installations of pillars and always during the procedures for measuring with a balance,
a person should carefully avoid damaging them with stakes, walls, or similar obstacles.
In every case, the site is specified as extending through the lineage of the ancestors;
fire is established in the head, and water is situated in the mouth.
Pṛthvīdhara and Aryaman are established upon the two breasts;
Āpavatsa, however, should always be worshipped by the wise upon the chest.
Diti and Parjanya are in the two eyes; Aditi and Jyautiṣka are in the two ears;
and the Lord of Serpents and Indra, stationed on the shoulders, should be worshipped with great effort.
Likewise, Satya, Rogā, and the others— five in each arm—
and Rudra and Rājayakṣmā are stationed together in the left hand.
Savitṛ, the son of Savitṛ, likewise took refuge in his right hand;
Vivasvat and Mitra were established within his belly.
Pūṣan and Rājayakṣman are located at the wrists of the two hands;
likewise, the two Asuraśīrṣas are situated on the left side.
Likewise, on the right side is Vitatha together with Gṛhakṣata;
Yamāmbupa should be known to be on the two thighs, and Gandharva and Puṣpaka on the two knees.
Bhṛgu and Sugrīva are in the two calves; Dauvārika and Mṛga are situated in the buttocks; Jaya and Śakra are in the penis; and likewise, the Pitṛs are in the feet.
Brahmā consists of nine parts in the center and is worshipped in the heart;
however, in a temple, Vāstu is remembered by Brahmā as consisting of sixty-four parts.
There, Brahmā occupies four squares; then, one square each in the corners.
Outside in the corners there are eight, and on both sides there are situated [squares] measuring one and a half.
Twenty are their two-footed [verses], and sixty-four are recorded as their four-footed [verses].
Regarding the commencement of a house, one should observe where itching occurs on the body of the owner.
One should remove the thorn from there, whether by means of a palace or even by means of Bhava;
for that which possesses a thorn brings fear, whereas that which is without a thorn destroys fear.
One should avoid in every way a site that has missing or extra limbs;
one should apply this rule everywhere in cities, villages, and regions.

‘Śubhanirīkṣitaṃ’ means observed by auspicious planets. ‘Aindavaṃ’ refers to Mṛgaśiras. Regarding ‘dīptau pūrvādīti’: starting from the eastern direction and proceeding clockwise, the proper lighting of the wick brings happiness to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, respectively; this is the meaning. ‘Khātapūraṇaiḥ’ means by the very fillings of the excavated pits associated with them. ‘Pitṛvaṃśāntarāyataḥ’: the Vāstupuruṣa is as long as the lineage extended from the ancestral group up to the fire (vahni). ‘Ambupo’ is the lord of waters. ‘Puṣpakaḥ’ is Puṣpadanta.
