In the phrase ‘jayaśśakra’, the word *jaya* denotes Śakra. ‘Tadvat koṇeṣv ekapadā’: in the eighty-one-square Vāstu diagram, those deities who occupy a single square in the corners should be understood here in the same way. ‘Bahiḥkoṇeṣu cetyādi’: in the four outer corners, there are eight deities in the squares on both sides; ‘sārdhā bhavanti’ means they exist together with the four principal deities.
(The characteristics of the four-winged house,
etc. O best of the twice-born, I shall describe by name and according to their actual form the four-winged house, the three-winged house, the two-winged house, and the single-winged house.
Sūta said:
I shall describe the four-winged house (catuśśāla) according to its forms and names. The four-winged house is surrounded on all sides by four doors and vestibules (alinda).
That auspicious [mandala] named Sarvatobhadra is found in the abode of the gods and kings;
however, when it is devoid of the western gate, they call it Nandyāvarta.
That which is devoid of a southern gate is called Vardhamāna; that which is devoid of an eastern gate is renowned by the name Svastika.
They declare that the *rucaka* is devoid of the northern door;
and that which lacks the eastern hall (*saumya-śālā*) is the *triśāla* known as *dhanyaka*.
Bringing security and prosperity to men and bestowing the fruit of many sons,
it is renowned as "Sukṣetra" (the Excellent Field), being devoid of the first lunar mansion, Śravaṇā.

A house with three wings (triśāla) that lacks the southern wing is conducive to wealth, fame, and long life, and it destroys sorrow and delusion; however, that which lacks the eastern wing [is not so].
That which causes the destruction of a family among men and brings about the fear of all diseases,
being deficient in its final [syllable], is known as *pakṣaghna*.
It destroys friends, kinsmen, and children, and likewise brings the fear of snakes;
however, from the southern and western wings, it bestows wealth, grain, and fruit.
The western-northern wing (paścimottara-śālaka) should be known as that which brings security and prosperity to men, as well as bestowing the fruit of sons; it is also called Yamasūrya.
That [formation] brings fear of kings and fire to men and causes the destruction of the family;
when there are two *śāla* formations in the north and east, it is called the *daṇḍa* (staff) formation.
That which is called Cāpa, having two halls— the southern and the eastern— is a source of fear from untimely death and brings about the threat of foreign armies.
If the hearth is situated to the east or west, it brings fear of poison, weapons, and fire, as well as the threat of defeat; it is an omen of death.
It brings widowhood to women and causes manifold fears;
through these two northern halls, it produces terror for men.
Wise men should always avoid houses with two wings, with the exception of the Siddhārtha type.

‘Alinda’ refers to the porch at the entrance. ‘Saumya-śālā’ refers to the northern gate-hall. ‘Excluding Siddhārtha’ means setting aside that two-hall structure which is joined with the southern and the other two halls.
(The Characteristics of the Houses of Kings and Others) Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the residence of the lord of the earth.
That is said to be of five kinds, according to the distinction between the superior and the others.
A width of one hundred and eight cubits is considered the best;
for each of the other four [sizes], the width is reduced by eight cubits.
The length for all five [types] is said to be increased by one-fourth;
I shall now describe the fivefold residence for the crown prince.
In that [measurement], eighty [units] are reduced by six and then again by six in detail;
furthermore, it is stated that the length in all five [directions] is increased by one-third.
[64] I shall describe the fivefold abode of the General;
it is sixty-four units in total width, decreasing by six units at each stage.
In these five [measures], the length shall be increased by one-sixth.
Now I shall describe the five types of dwellings for practitioners of mantra.
The width should be sixty cubits, diminished by four in each of the four directions;
the length is increased by one-eighth, and this applies to all five types as well.
I shall describe the five types of residences for the neighboring kings, ministers, and common people;
they consist of forty-eight, thirty-six, and thirty-two [units] respectively, decreasing by four each time.
A length exceeding by one-fourth [the width] is recommended for these five:
the houses of artisans, chamberlains, and Vaiśyas constitute the five types of houses.
For those measuring twenty-eight cubits, the width is successively reduced by that same amount;
the length is said to be double [the width], and it is exactly the same for the middle-sized [shrines].
I shall describe the five types of residences for messengers, laborers, and others:
the length is one-fourth greater [than the width], and the width is twelve [units].
For the astrologer, the preceptor, the physician, the member of the assembly, and the family priest, there shall be a reduction of one and a half [parts] from the width in successive order.
I shall also describe for them the fivefold abodes in sequence:
they are forty [yojanas] in width, and decrease by four [yojanas] in succession.
Among these five, the length shall be greater by one-sixth.
I shall now describe the common five types of houses for the four castes.
Of the thirty-two [fingers], four are subtracted in succession up to sixteen; beyond that, it is even less for those of the lowest caste.
[65] They say that the length should be greater by a tenth, an eighth, a third, or even a single part; this is praised for those beginning with the Brāhmaṇa caste.
A house for residence must always be constructed for the commander-in-chief, for the king, for the four castes, and for those who are always honored by the king.
And for those born in between [the castes], it is held that [the distance] is less than that of their own father;
likewise, for forest-dwellers, it is within a hundred cubits.
The placement of the halls is proclaimed as being seventy less than fourteen times the extent of both the commander-in-chief and the king.
When that [measurement] is increased by thirty-five, it is declared to be an *alinda*;
likewise, [the measurement] is thirty-six cubits augmented by seven *aṅgulas*.
The great hall of a Brahmin should not exceed ten finger-breadths in length; likewise, that of a Kṣatriya is ordained to be greater by that same amount.
For a Vaiśya, it is thirty-five cubits and thirteen finger-breadths;
for a Śūdra, it is likewise [thirty-five] cubits joined with fifteen finger-breadths.
That site where a pathway exists at the front, occupying one-third of the hall, is named Soṣṇīṣa; it provides shade in the afternoon.
Where there is a pathway on both sides, that is called *sāvaṣṭambha*;
where there is a pathway all around, that is here called *susthita*.
All this is auspicious and fourfold among the four castes;
in its extent, it is a sixteenth part [of the whole] and likewise four cubits.
The height of the first terrace is reduced at the top;
in all the terraces, it is likewise reduced by one-twelfth from its height.
The wall should be made of baked bricks, with a width equal to one-sixth of its height;
it may also be constructed of wood or likewise of clay.
In all types of dwellings, measurement by the *garbha* (inner sanctum) is recommended;
[the measurement] of the house's width is [calculated] by adding eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) to fifty [units].
It should be joined [to the wall] at a distance equal to the width of the door, and its height should be twice that;
the thickness of the door-frames should be measured by one-sixth of the height.
The width of all dwellings is commended by the wise in finger-breadths;
and the top portion of the threshold should be one and a half times that width.

"‘Of the general and the king also, [it is] seventy-seven,’ etc. The meaning is as follows: having added seventy cubits (*karasaptati*) to the extent stated for the house of the general or the king, one should take half of that, divide that half into fourteen parts, and construct a hall (*śālā*) with whatever remains as its width. Thus, in a royal residence (*rājaveśman*) measuring one hundred and eight cubits in width, the hall becomes five cubits in measure. Regarding the phrase "extracted by thirty-five": in that same royal residence measuring eighty-nine cubits in width, when a division by thirty-five cubits is made, nineteen cubits remain; a porch (*alinda*) of that size should be constructed. An *udumbara* is a threshold (*dehalī*).

(On the Determination of Pillar Height) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the determination of the measurement of pillars. They know that this should always be seven times the height of the building on the site.
The width at the front should be one-eightieth [of the height], together with ninefold [proportions];
it should be square for the *rucaka* type, while the eight-sided is called the *vajra*.
The sixteen-sided [pillar] is the double-vajra; the thirty-two-sided is the dissolved.
That pillar which is circular in the middle region is known as the "circular" (vṛtta).
These five great pillars are praised for all types of building sites;
they are adorned with lotuses, creepers, vines, vases, leaves, and mirrors.
The spaces between the lotuses and the vases are one-ninth the height of the pillar;
the beam (tulā) is said to be equal to the pillar, while that which is less than this is called an atulā.
In all cases here, it should be reduced by one-third or again by one-fourth;
thus, at every stage, it is diminished by a quarter-part.
The entry for all [the deities] is by the southern side, along with their vehicles.
(The Ritual for the Doors) I shall now declare the doors that are praised here;
a door facing east toward Indra and Jayanta is commended in all cases.
The wise know that Yāmya and Vitatha are in the south;
Puṣpadanta is in the west, and he is praised as belonging to Varuṇa.
To the north of Bhallāṭa, however, the Saumya deity brings happiness;
likewise, in all dwellings, one should avoid piercing the door.
If the door is pierced by a street, there will be the destruction of the entire family;
if it is pierced by mud, there arises grief along with an abundance of faults for the young.
[68] Epilepsy will surely occur constantly through the piercing of a well;
pain will arise from a spring, and there will be danger from fire through a stake.
If [the rite] is performed by a woman with a pillar, there will be destruction caused by a deity;
if it is performed in the house with a house, there will be the destruction of the master of the house.
If it is pierced by impure refuse, the housewife shall become unchaste;
one should know that there is danger from weapons if it is pierced by the house of an outcaste.
If one avoids digging a depth twice the height of the foundation, no structural collapse occurs;
yet if the door opens by itself, it brings madness to the householders.
A wise man should know that if [the breath] itself is obstructed, there will be the destruction of his family;
if it exceeds [the proper measure], there is fear of the king, and if it is deficient, there is fear of thieves.
And that door which is above the door is known as the fear of Death;
it is distended in the middle region, and its width is excessive.
A *vajra* (thunderbolt-shaped) door in the middle of a narrow space causes the immediate destruction of the master;
likewise, a door that is constricted by another will bring about many evils.
The main entrance should not be excessively adorned beyond that;
rather, one should beautify the main entrance with water-jars and *śrīparṇa* creepers.
And one should also worship that daily with an offering of food, unbroken grains, and water.
(The Ritual for Planting Trees in the Home):
A banyan tree in the eastern quarter of the house fulfills all desires;
likewise, an udumbara tree in the southern quarter and an auspicious pippala tree in the western quarter [are likewise beneficial].

[69] Moreover, a Plakṣa tree to the north is auspicious, whereas those in the opposite positions lead to failure; likewise, thorny trees, milky sap-bearing trees, and fruit-bearing trees situated nearby [are unfavorable].
The loss of one's wife and the loss of one's progeny will occur respectively;
however, if one does not cut down those trees, one should plant auspicious ones in their place.
Punnāgas, aśokas, tilkas, śamīs, vakulas, and campakas; pomegranates, long peppers, grapes, and likewise pavilions of flowers.
With *jambīra*, betel-nut, *panasa*, and *ketakī* trees;
with *jātī*, lotus, *śatapatrikā*, and *mallikā* flowers; and with coconut, plantain leaves, and *pāṭala* blossoms.
It is fitting that this palace here spreads forth splendor.

‘Rathyā’ means a road. ‘Vedha’ here refers to being situated directly in front [of the door]. Regarding the phrase ‘twice the height’: if these [obstructions], such as roads and so forth, exist beyond the ground in front of the door at a distance twice the height (or length) of the door, then there is no ‘vedha,’ meaning no structural defect (*vāstu-vedha*). Sūta said:
“The head of a symmetrical dwelling is likewise elevated toward the north.”
Having examined [the site] as before, the wise man should proceed with the erection of the pillar.
‘Of the equal one’: of the Vāstupuruṣa together with the mind.

[70] A wise man should not have a dwelling constructed in the vicinity of a temple dedicated to the gods, near places of religious merit, or in the proximity of crossroads; such a house will be filled with suffering and grief.
(The Ritual for Entering a Planet): There are four ways of entering it; those from the front of its lap are auspicious.
To follow behind it repeatedly, turning to the right, is recommended.
The *apasavya* [wind] leads to destruction, and likewise the *śīrṇaka* blows from the south;
the one named *saṃpūrṇa* blows from the left, granting all desires to men.
Having thus considered the entrance, one should diligently begin the construction of the house;
then, at an auspicious moment proclaimed by the astrologer.
Having prepared a stone slab adorned with jewels and provided with all types of seeds,
four Brahmins should worship the pillar with garments and ornaments.
The artisan, wearing white garments and accompanied by those who have mastered the Vedas,
should likewise place that [image], which has been bathed and endowed with all medicinal herbs.
Equipped with various unbroken grains, joined with garments and ornaments,
accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, musical instruments, and the sounds of auspicious songs.
At twilight, one should feed the Brahmins; the fire-oblation, however, should always be performed with honey and clarified butter while reciting this mantra: “O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge [us].”
Likewise, one should act thus at the casting of the line, again at the raising of the pillar,
similarly at the raising of the door-beam, and likewise at the time of entry.
Likewise, for the pacification of the site, the Vāstuyajña sacrifice is fivefold:
the laying of the cord should take place in the northeast, and the planting of the central pillar in the southeast.
One should perform circumambulation and the scraping of the ground for Vāstoṣpati;
likewise, the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb should be on the right side.
Coral, gems, gold, fruit, polished rice, and water—
these are recommended for marking out the ground in all divisions of a building site.
One should never scratch the site with ashes, charcoal, or wood, nor with weapons, nails, or hides, nor with horns, bones, or skulls.
By these [signs], one should recognize suffering, grief, fear, and so forth;
when the entry into the house occurs, the artisan should observe them there.
Likewise, regarding the erection of pillars, the laying of foundation lines, and so forth, if a bird cries harshly while facing the sun, it portends the arising of auspicious or inauspicious results.
When the master of the house touches his own limb at the same time [as the astrologer],
a man should know that there is a dangerous thorn (shalya) in that particular part of the site.
Wherever there is a bird's cry immediately followed by the sound of elephants, horses, or wild beasts,
a wise physician should know that the arrow has originated from that particular part of the body.
When the thread is being stretched out, if it is leaped over by dogs or jackals,
or if there is a harsh and terrifying sound, one should know that a thorn (impurity) is present there.
If a crow cries sweetly in the northeastern direction,
one should know that there is wealth either in that region or in the portion presided over by the master.
If the thread is cut, death will occur; if the pegs are turned downward, disease;
likewise, if on embers, insanity; and if on skull-basins, agitation.
One who knows the scriptures should recognize signs of unchastity in women from [cracks] at the throat-thorns;
likewise, there will be the ruin of both the house-builder and the house itself if there is confusion regarding the placement of the artisans.
If the pitcher falls from the pillar's shoulder, one should predict diseases of the head;
if the pitcher is stolen, there will be the destruction of the entire family.
The wise know that when the pitcher is displaced from its place of death and broken, it signifies bondage;
but if it falls while still held in the hand, they know it portends the destruction of the householder.
If the site is devoid of seeds and medicinal herbs, one should predict danger from elemental spirits;
having placed [the ritual items] to the east and south, one should fix the parasol upon the pillar.
Then, the wise man should install the other pillars by circumambulating them clockwise;
for if they are installed counter-clockwise, they bring fear to men.
One should diligently perform a protective rite that destroys obstacles to the pillar;
likewise, one should place a fruit-bearing branch upon the top of the pillar.
One should construct it sloping toward the northeast, but one must not allow it to be confused with the cardinal directions;
this applies to the pillar, the house, the gate, and likewise the bedchamber.
If one is confused about the directions, there will be the ruin of the family, and the household will not prosper.
If one would cause the household to prosper, one must avoid everything [that leads to confusion].
[73] A site extended toward the east will always bring about enmities;
a site extended toward the south leads to death, without a doubt.
A site that has expanded toward the west causes the depletion of wealth;
likewise, one extended toward the north causes great distress.
Where there is an increase in the southeast (āgneya), that will bring about danger from fire;
if it increases in the southwest (rākṣasa) corner, it will cause the loss of wealth.
If the Vāyavya corner of the site is enlarged, it causes the provocation of diseases caused by wind;
if the Īśāna corner is always enlarged, there will be a loss of crops.
In the northeast, there should be the temple of the deities as well as the hall for peace;
likewise, the kitchen should be in the southeast, and the water-storage area on its northern side.
A wise person should place all the household utensils in the southwest;
he should also construct the latrine and the bathing pavilion outside.
Wealth and grain should be placed in the northwest, and the workshop for labor outside of that;
such an arrangement of the site will bring auspiciousness to the master of the house.
(The Ritual for Fetching Wood) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the excellent ritual for fetching wood,
excluding the five stars of Dhaniṣṭhā and, beyond that, the Viṣṭi yoga and others.
Then, on a day prescribed by the astrologer, the wise man should depart for the forest;
first, he should by all means perform an offering and worship to the tree.
A house-beam that falls toward the northeast is praised;
otherwise, one should know it to be auspicious when it falls toward the south or the west.
One should not place in a house wood produced from a milk-tree (kṣīravṛkṣa) that has been inhabited by birds or afflicted by fire and wind.
Likewise, wood broken by an elephant, or afflicted by lightning or a thunderbolt,
as well as wood that is dried out at the top, split, or crooked;
That which arises from a shrine or temple, as well as from a river confluence or a mountain,
and that which dwells in a cremation ground or a well, or originates from a pond and the like.
One who desires abundant prosperity should always avoid wood [from] thorny trees,
such as the *nīpa*, *nimba*, and *vibhītaka*.
One should avoid *śleṣmātaka* trees from ponds for use in house-building;
however, the *asana*, *aśoka*, *madhuka*, *sarja*, and *sāla* trees bring auspiciousness.
Fortunate people may construct an auspicious dwelling using sandalwood, breadfruit wood, dhanyā, deodar, or haridraka; it may be made with two, one, or all three of these types of wood.
Since that which is made by many would bring manifold fears,
it is better that a single *śiṃśapā*, *śrīparṇī*, or *tindukī* tree alone be used.
These, when not joined with others, bestow auspiciousness in building activities;
likewise, upon cutting down a tree, the wise man should recognize a lizard as being of yellow color.

In a mañjiṣṭha-colored [dream], one should recognize a frog; in a blue one, one should point out a snake. In a ruddy-colored one, one should know it to be a chameleon; in one with the luster of a mung bean, one should indicate a parrot.
One should recognize a mouse in a tawny [ant-hill], and one should indicate water in one that has the luster of a sword;
such a site in its entirety should be avoided in the work of building a dwelling.
But one should take what was previously cut, provided it is accompanied by auspicious omens and signs.

(Dhvajalakṣaṇam) When the length is multiplied by three and divided by eight, one should know that whatever remainder remains constitutes the first [category]; I shall now describe its eightfold divisions to you.
The banner, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey,
elephant, and crow— these are the remaining signs starting from the east.
The Dhvaja is auspicious when facing all directions, but especially when facing west;
the Siṃha should face north, and the Vṛṣabha should face east.
An elephant facing south is described as being composed of seven [units];
one [unit] is designated as a twice-born (dvija), and three are proclaimed to be a lion.
It is declared that one becomes a bull by [multiplying] by five; the wise man should exclude those situated in the angles and multiply that very [number] eightfold to form the heap of hands.
A wise person should know that when [the total] is divided by twenty-seven, the remainder is Dakṣa;
one should divide the remainder by eight, and whatever remains is considered the expenditure (vyaya).
"One should not cause an excess of expenditure, for that would produce defects;
when income is greater, there will be peace—thus said the Blessed Lord Hari."
Having placed the best of the twice-born in front, and having offered to the brahmins a full water-pot adorned with curd, unbroken rice, copper leaves, flowers, and fruits,
as well as gold and garments;
One should enter the house as an abode of auspiciousness and peace.
One should perform the *balikarma* according to the rules for *homa* prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*,
as well as the rite taught for pacifying the site (*vāstu*) of a temple; then, one should gratify the most excellent of the twice-born with various kinds of foods and edibles.
And wearing white garments, he should enter the dwelling while it is fragrant with honey-scented incense.

‘By two or by one’: when one should construct a house with trees of several species, then it may be done with two or three, but not with four, five, or more species; this is the meaning. ‘Saraṭa’ means a chameleon. ‘Mudgābhe’ means having a color similar to that of a mung bean. ‘Aśmantaka’ means a stone. ‘Khaḍgābhe’ means dark-colored. ‘When the length is multiplied by the width’: when the length is multiplied—that is, revolved—by the ‘width,’ which is the number representing the breadth, and as many cubits (*hasta*) as there result, having divided them into groups of eight and performed the division, that which remains is the *āya*. And that is divided into eight types according to the distinction of the *dvaja* and so forth. ‘The eastern and others’ refers to those situated in the eight directions starting from the east, respectively. ‘That very same’: the aforementioned mass of cubits for the length multiplied by the width. ‘When divided by eight on the right’: when the total mass of cubits for the asterism is divided into eight parts.
In the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-sūtra*:

Now, therefore, follows the examination of the site (*vāstu*). One should select ground that is not saline, not quarrelsome, and abounding in herbs and trees; on such ground where *kuśa* and *vīraṇa* grasses are plentiful, one should dig a trench and remove thorny and milky plants along with their roots. Where the *apāmārga*, *śāka*, *tilvaka*, and *parivyādha* grow, and where waters from all sides meet at the center and, after flowing clockwise around the site to be pacified, flow toward the east—provided they do not fall away—that place is entirely prosperous. One should cause the kitchen and the dwelling to be built on a spot where the water flows away together. For there, food becomes abundant. On ground sloping toward the south, one should have the assembly hall (*sabhā*) constructed; it becomes a place for gambling, and therein young gamblers become quarrelsome and short-lived. Where waters flow out from all sides, that site is conducive to well-being and free from gambling.

Now, one should examine the site (*vāstu*). Having dug a pit knee-deep, one should fill it with that very same earth. If there is an excess [of earth], it is excellent; if equal, it is mediocre; if deficient, it is censurable. After sunset, one should let water remain in it. If it remains full of water, it is excellent; if damp, it is mediocre; if dry, it is censurable. [The soil should be] white, sweet-tasting, and sandy for a Brāhmaṇa; red for a Kṣatriya; yellow for a Vaiśya. Having ploughed it a thousand times, one should measure it out as a square of equal sides according to the directions, or as a rectangle. With a branch of *śamī* or a branch of *udumbara*, while walking three times clockwise around it, one sprinkles it with an unbroken stream of water, reciting the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ. One should have shelters constructed between the bamboo beams and cause *avakā* plants and *śīpāla* grass to be placed in the pits; thus it is known: "No fire shall burn it. Having placed [a post] in the pit of the central pillar and having spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing east and north, one should pour water mixed with rice and barley, saying: "To the immovable one, the earthly, svāhā! Then, as it is being raised, one should consecrate it with: "Stay right here, O firmly established one! May the Tilvila and Irāvatī rivers reach you as you stand in the midst of prosperity. May the evil-doers not reach you. May a young boy, a child, be born together with you. May the jar of curds and the pitchers reach you."

While the bamboo beam is being set up, he recites: “O bamboo beam, ascend the pillar by means of Truth, bestowing upon us a longer and more extended life. He should establish the water-jar (*maṇika*) upon four stones covered with *dūrvā* grass, with the verse: “Born from the earth, the Araṅgara speaks aloud; bound in three ways by the triple-bond, may he bring us nourishment (*irā*) and drive away want. Then he pours water into it with the verse: “May King Varuṇa come with the wealthy waters; let him stay in this place rejoicing. Bringing nourishment and sprinkling ghee, may they dwell together with Mitra. Then he pacifies this spot with water containing rice and barley, having placed gold therein, while walking three times clockwise and sprinkling with an unbroken stream of water using the triplet beginning, “O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss. Having cooked a mess of sacrificial food (*sthālīpāka*) in the middle of the house, he offers oblations with each of the four verses beginning, “O Lord of the Dwelling (*Vāstoṣpati*), recognize us,” and having prepared the food and fed a Brāhmaṇa, he should cause him to say: “Auspicious is the dwelling! Auspicious is the dwelling!”

“*Avivadiṣṇu*”: where there is no one wishing to dispute with a disputant; however, if the reading is *avivādī*, the meaning is "free from dispute. “*Bhūmauṣadhivanaspativat*”: suitable for the abundant growth of herbs and forest trees. “*Parikhāya*”: having uprooted. “*Paricyādhaḥ*”: a particular species of royal tree (*rājavṛkṣa*). “*Pradakṣiṇaṃ śayanīyaṃ parītya*”: having circumambulated the bedchamber so that it is to the right. “*Prapatantyaḥ*”: going forth in abundance. “*Sarvasamṛddham*”: filled with everything, such as sons and so forth. “*Samavaśrave*”: at the place of the water-channel. “*Bhaktaśaraṇam*”: the kitchen. “*Sabhā*”: that is the assembly hall of the householder; if it is built on ground sloping toward the south, then it becomes a gambling den, therefore it should not be done in that way—this is the meaning. “*Pramāyukāḥ*”: prone to death. “*Vārttam*”: neither too excellent nor too inferior—this is the meaning. “*Sahasrasītam*”: ploughed an unlimited number of times. “*Śantātīyena*”: by means of the hymn beginning with “*śaṃ na indrāgnī bhavatam*. “*Avakāḥ*”: *śambuka* snails. “*Śīpālāḥ*”: moss (*śaivāla*).
Thus concludes the procedure for building works [79]. Now follows the consolidation of the kingdom.
Regarding this, Manu says: "In the administration of the kingdom, he should constantly practice this rule;
for a king whose kingdom is well-administered prospers in happiness."
He should establish a military outpost (*gulma*) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise for hundreds of villages, for the protection of the kingdom.
One should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The connection [of the words] is: "in two villages. "Gulma" means a troop of infantry. Āpastamba says:

"In villages and cities, he should appoint honest men of truthful character to guard the subjects and protect their wealth. Their attendants should likewise possess those same qualities. A city extending for one *yojana* on all sides must be protected from thieves; a village for one *krośa*."
[80] Manu says: Another affectionate minister of the king, being vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their private affairs.
In every city, one should appoint an overseer of all affairs,
occupying a high position and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.
He himself should personally inspect all those officials;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through his spies.
Likewise,
the village headman himself should gradually settle the disputes that have arisen in the village for the sake of the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten should report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, however, should personally announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Having thus performed all these duties that he ought to do for himself,
he should protect these subjects, being both disciplined and vigilant.
Whatever is to be paid daily by the village dwellers to the king—
such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth— the villagers shall obtain those things from him.
The officer of ten (daśī) shall enjoy the family [of the offender]; the officer of twenty (viṃśī), five families;
the superintendent of a hundred villages (grāmaśatādhyakṣa), a village; and the lord of a thousand (sahasrādhipati), a city.

‘Anuparikramet’: when those appointed by him are overcome by litigants, he should then fill them with his own force; this is the meaning. ‘Pariṇayet’: he should cause [the matter] to reach [its conclusion]. A *kula* is a portion of a village known as a *pāṭaka*. Viṣṇu states: “The village headman (*grāmādhyakṣa*) shall provide a remedy for the defects of the village. If he is unable, he shall report it to the district headman (*deśādhyakṣa*). If he too is unable, [he shall report it] to the district headman. The district headman, moreover, shall eradicate the defect with all his might.”

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: There must be constant supervision of mounts and warriors; their maintenance shall be two suvarṇas per month, with a review every six months or four months. When they have died, there should be gifts and compassion; when their services are known, there should be further grants. One should bestow honors upon those who excel in lineage, conduct, character, learning, and physical marks.

‘Gifts for those who have gone to heaven,’ and so forth. The king should provide gifts and compassion to the sons and other relatives of warriors who have died in the service of the state. However, in the case of well-known warriors, clothing and other items should be given even in excess of their regular gifts and wages; this is the meaning. Manu says: “The king should daily determine the livelihood for women and servants engaged in his services, in accordance with their rank and their work.”
A gift should be given to one who is lowly;
however, for one who is eminent, there should be a meal, clothing every six months, and a *droṇa* of grain every month.

The syntactical connection is: "six *paṇas*. "*Ācchādaḥ*" means a garment for clothing. Bṛhaspati says: "How can one who has been proclaimed as virtuous and celebrated in the assembly of people be described as devoid of virtue by that very same mouth?"
Therefore, one should not disturb the sovereignty or the livelihood of one who is faultless;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress, and likewise, the support [of the community] would perish.
‘Upagraha’ means acquisition.
One who has properly settled his territory and constructed a fortress according to the treatises should always exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns (the suppression of criminals).
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should a king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
In kingdoms, servants appointed to protect generally become deceitful and seize the property of others; one should therefore guard these subjects from them.
‘Nirdātā’ means one who reaps. ‘Kakṣa’ means grass. Yājñavalkya says:
“The king shall protect his subjects when they are being oppressed by flatterers, thieves, evildoers, perpetrators of great violence, and others—especially from scribes.”
Manu says:
That king who, through delusion and lack of oversight, oppresses his own kingdom,
shall before long fall from his sovereignty and from life itself, along with his kinsmen.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
[84] Kātyāyana says: Vedic scholars, widows, children, and those who are weak yet have families—
these, being dependent on the king's power, must be protected by the king with great effort.
For the protectorless, the king is the protector; for the homeless, the king is the home;
for the sonless, the king is the son; and for the fatherless, O monarch, the king is the father.
Where the king personally oversees legal affairs in accordance with dharma,
there the subjects, following virtuous conduct, shall dwell in happiness.
Manu:
Having received the Brāhmaṇical consecration according to the rule, a Kṣatriya must provide protection for all this [world] in accordance with justice.
"Brahmanical consecration" (*brāhmaṃ saṃskāram*) means the sprinkling of water performed by a Brahmin. Kātyāyana states:
"The constant protection of subjects and the clearing away of thorns."
And for the very purpose of honoring the twice-born, the king was established.
Bṛhaspati says: That protection of the subjects is declared by those who know justice to be threefold:
[protection] from the enemy's army, from the fear of thieves, and from those who are powerful and ignorant of justice.
The king should quell the fear caused by enemy forces through strategic means,
and he should provide daily judicial review for those oppressed by the powerful.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of royal execution,
he sacrifices day after day with sacrifices accompanied by hundreds of thousands of sacrificial fees.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one offers as oblation, and whatever one recites— of that,
the king becomes a sharer of a sixth part by virtue of providing protection.
Śaṅkha says:
A king does not attain heaven through vows, nor through fasting, nor through various kinds of sacrifices; he attains it through the protection [of his subjects].
Yama says:
Forest-dwellers, wandering mendicants, and Vedic scholars who maintain the sacred fires—these are givers of a sixth part [of the produce]; they do not pay gold to the king.
‘Of a sixth part’: of a sixth part of merit. Manu says:
“A king obtains a sixth part of all dharma through his protection.”
For one who does not protect [them], even a sixth part of their demerit falls upon him.
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls,
the customary share, and fines, shall immediately go to hell.
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part as tax,
is one who carries away the entire impurity of all the world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist,
who causes destruction, and who does not protect [but rather consumes] his subjects, is destined for a downward path.
That king who, having seized thousands of cows, gives them away without protecting them, becomes a thief; as a king, he partakes only in the fruit of the mere sound [of the gift].
‘Vipralopakam’ means that which causes the interruption of livelihood and so forth; this is the explanation. ‘Attāram’ means the enjoyer.
Thus ends the section on the consolidation of the kingdom (87). Now, the treasury.
In that regard, the Mahābhārata says:
"They say one who lacks wealth is weak; through wealth one becomes strong.
Everything is favorable for the powerful, and the possessor of a treasury overcomes all."
From wealth, O lord of men, come dharma, pleasure, and even heaven;
indeed, even the mere sustenance of life for the world cannot be accomplished without wealth.
One who lacks wealth does not perform religious duties properly;
for from wealth, action flows forth like water from a lake with its outlets open.
One who is without wealth and yet desires riches cannot acquire merit;
by means of wealth, further riches are secured, just as great elephants are captured by means of elephants.
For from wealth that has increased and been gathered from here and there,
all activities proceed, like rivers from mountains.
He is the best of kings whose treasury and records are constantly maintained by men who increase the wealth of the treasury and who are worthy recipients.
If someone should report to the lord of men that the royal treasury is being depleted,
he should be heard in private and protected from [intrigue by] the ministers.
‘Cetum’ means to collect.
[88] Manu says: “Purchases and sales, travel, and food along with its incidental expenses...”
And having duly considered their security and well-being, he should cause merchants to pay taxes.
Having observed how the king and the performer of actions are joined with their respective fruits, the king should always apportion taxes within his realm accordingly.
Just as water, fire, a calf, and bees take their food little by little,
so should the king take the annual tax from his realm in small amounts.
The king shall take one-fiftieth as tax on cattle and gold;
one-eighth, one-sixth, or even one-twelfth on grain.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
[89] Of leaves, vegetables, grass, and bamboo;
of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone.
Likewise: "For a Kṣatriya who, in times of distress, takes a fourth part as his share while protecting his subjects to the best of his ability, is released from sin."
In victory, his own duty is fulfilled; he should not turn his back in fear. Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he should collect the lawful tribute.
The toll on grain for the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; on manufactured goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide labor, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [shall pay no toll].

‘Adanti’ means they eat. ‘Ādyam’ means that which is to be eaten. ‘Vāryokasaḥ’ refers to aquatic creatures. By the word ‘dru’, a tree is denoted. ‘Āpadi’ means in times of distress, when the treasury is empty. Bṛhaspati says: “A cultivator shall pay a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part as tribute to the king, respectively, from fallow land, from land cultivated during the rainy season, and from land cultivated during the spring.”
[90] According to local custom, they should offer oblations to the spirits every six months or annually;
this is declared to be the ancient law for tillers of the soil.

‘Bhūta’ means as it is established. ‘Kīnāśa’ means a cultivator. Viṣṇu says: He shall take a sixth part of grain from the subjects for the sake of tribute [per year], and likewise from all crops; and two percent on cattle, gold, and clothes. From meat, honey, clarified butter, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, juices, vegetables, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and bamboo articles, he shall take a sixth part. He shall not impose taxes upon Brāhmaṇas, for they are the ones who provide the king with the tax of righteousness (dharma).
Kātyāyana says: "The king alone is traditionally held to be the owner of the earth; he is never the owner of other property. For he shall receive a sixth part of its fruit, and not otherwise."
Because the beings dwell within it, its lordship is proclaimed;
hence, one-sixth of their actions—arising from the causes of both the auspicious and the inauspicious—is [the king's share].
[91] Manu says: Even when dying, a king must not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor should a Śrotriya living within his realm suffer from hunger.

Āpastamba: A non-professional Vedic scholar (*aśrotriya*), women of all castes, and boys before the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics; those who dwell for the sake of learning; ascetics devoted to dharma; a Śūdra who washes feet; those who are blind, mute, deaf, or afflicted by disease; and those who have become useless through the possession of wealth. [In this context,] "secondary sexual characteristics" (*vyañjana*) refers to the growth of facial hair and so forth. "Useless through the possession of wealth" means those whose purpose has vanished in the accumulation of property. Manu: *Note: The provided text consists of the commentary of Haradatta on Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.29.1–3, followed by the citation of Manu.*
One who is blind, dull-witted, a cripple who moves about on a board, or one who is seventy years of age or older,
even if he is a learned Vedic scholar, shall not be made to pay tax by anyone.

‘Pīṭhasarpī’ means a cripple. Vasiṣṭha states: “Those who subsist on river-beds, marshes, forest-clearings, or mountain slopes shall be the *viṣkara* [tax-payers]; or those who live off them may pay it. However, one should collect the marriage-fee (*udvāhakara*) every month.
‘Forest-clearing’ (*vanadāha*) refers to a burnt forest. ‘Those who subsist on them’ are those who live by those very resources; that indeed is their means of livelihood.

Gautama: Artisans shall perform one day’s work for the king every month. By this, those who subsist by their own labor and boatmen are also explained. One should also provide them with food. "Artisans" refers to blacksmiths and the like; they shall perform for the king one day of work each month according to their own capacity, and nothing else should be taken from them. "Those who subsist by their own labor" refers to porters, dancers, and so forth. "Boatmen" refers to those engaged in the trade of boats and carts. [93] Manu:
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one destroys both oneself and them.
The non-collection of taxes such as the *kara* and *śulka* is "cutting off one's own root. The collection of more than what is appropriate is "cutting off the root of others. Yājñavalkya says:
"That king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means shall, before long, lose his prosperity and go to destruction along with his kinsmen."
The fire born from the suffering and oppression of the subjects does not turn back until it has consumed the king's lineage, his fortune, and his very life.
Kātyāyana says: For that king who, by unjust means, takes taxes, fines, a share of the grain, and tolls from his kingdom, he partakes in sin.
Manu says: A king, even if he is impoverished, must not take what ought not to be taken;
nor, even if he is prosperous, should he relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death.
From the enjoyment [of taxes], from the blending of castes, and from the protection of the weak, the power of the king is born; he prospers both in this world and after death.

Regarding the phrase “from the intermixture of castes” (*varṇasaṃsargāt*): the meaning is that no confusion of castes arises through marriage and other such relations between the castes—namely the Brāhmaṇas and others—and those of their own kind. Kātyāyana says:
“O Lord of Men, when a king conducts himself in this manner, having abandoned greed, his sons are born [in purity], and his kingdom and treasury increase.”
In the Mahābhārata: "That lord of the earth who possesses a great treasury acquired through righteousness rules the entire world, even if his retinue is exceedingly small."
Thus ends the section on the treasury [95]. Now,
the section on the army.
In that regard, the Mahābhārata states:
"In this world, both manifest and secret punishment have been ordained.
Therein, the manifest is of eight kinds, while the secret is more powerful."
Chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry, O Bhārata; laborers who are not exempt from service, and guides as the eighth.
O lord of the earth, a king who possesses an army that is devoted, joyful,
and well-nourished conquers the world even with a very small force.
‘Viṣṭi’ refers to a laborer who has been forcibly conscripted; ‘daiśikāḥ’ refers to persons belonging to a particular region.
Thus ends the section on punishment.
[96] 10 — Now, in that regard, Manu says: "A friend."
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend, even if that friend is weak, provided he is capable of enduring for the future.
One who knows the dharma, is grateful, and possesses a contented nature;
who is devoted, steadfast in his undertakings, and light—such a friend is highly praised.
Yājñavalkya says: Since the acquisition of friends is better than the acquisition of gold or land,
one should strive to attain that [friendship] and protect the truth with a concentrated mind.

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "O illustrious one, a friend inherited from one's father or grandfather, as well as the neighbors of an enemy, and an artificial friend— these are said to be the three kinds of friends."
In the Mahābhārata:
Friends are to be recognized and enemies are also to be understood;
this subtle truth, esteemed by the wise, is seen in this world. [97]
He who, seeing the suffering inherent in the purpose of living, does not live for that purpose— he would be a friend to him only so long as the opposite of that [suffering] does not occur.
There is no such thing as stable friendship, nor is there anything called permanent enmity;
friends and likewise enemies arise through the force of circumstances.
A friend becomes an enemy after the lapse of some time, and an enemy becomes a friend; for self-interest is more powerful.
Vyāsa says: No one is anyone's friend, and no one is anyone's enemy;
friends and likewise enemies arise through the force of circumstances.
Yājñavalkya says: The sovereign, the ministers, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Manu says:
The sovereign, the minister, the capital city, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements;
thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Regarding these seven constituent elements of the kingdom,
a king should understand that each preceding one is more serious than the next in terms of calamity.
In this seven-limbed kingdom, which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels anything else due to the mutual equality of their qualities.
For in various specific tasks, this or that factor is distinguished;
whichever factor establishes that task is said to be the most excellent in that regard.
‘Vyasanam’ means the cause of calamity; the word ‘faulty’ (doṣavat) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus ends [the section on] the friend.
[99] 11 — Now follows the protection of the prince, as found therein in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The prince must be protected by the ruler of the earth,
and he must also be attended by teachers and guards who are ever-vigilant.
One should instruct him in the sūtras concerning virtue, pleasure, and wealth, as well as the science of archery;
and one should always have him practice exercise with the chariot and the elephant.
One should have him trained in the arts by trustworthy persons and speak to him with feigned affection;
under the pretext of protecting his person, one should appoint guards for him.
One should not show attachment to him by those who are mean, greedy, or contemptuous;
rather, one should discipline him in such a way that he remains compliant even when he reaches the prime of youth.
One should not be led away from the path of the virtuous, which is so difficult to traverse, by the senses;
for it is impossible to instill virtues in one whose nature makes such cultivation unattainable.
He should be bound in a secret place with comfort;
for a family with an undisciplined youth quickly falls apart.
One should employ a disciplined person in all offices,
first in minor ones, and thereafter gradually even in major ones.
‘One who has reached youth’ means one who has attained adolescence. ‘In the beginning,’ that is, at the outset. In the *Mahābhārata*:
“A king who has sons is never devoured by his own kinsmen or even by his enemies;
therefore, a king should always protect and educate his son.”
The protection of the prince must be arranged by ministers who resemble himself,
through spies and various diverse means.
The grammatical connection is that protection must be provided by one's own neighbors and others.
Thus ends the protection of the prince [101].
12. Now follows the mantra.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having risen in the final watch of the night, having performed purification and composed his mind,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall."
Having caused all the subjects dwelling there to rejoice, he should dismiss them.
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "There are three kinds of persons in the world—superior, inferior, and middling.
Of these, when they are gathered together, I shall describe their virtues and faults."
Together with ministers who are well-versed in counsel, capable in determining policy,
or with allies who share the same purpose, and with kinsmen who have been long-standing associates.
He who, having deliberated with his ministers, proceeds to undertake an action and exerts effort toward that very end, him they call the best of men.
One deliberates on the matter, one applies his mind to the law, and one carries out the tasks; him they call the mediocre man.
He who, without having ascertained the merits and defects, abandons reliance on righteousness and neglects a task with the thought "I shall do it later," is the lowest of men.
Just as men are always classified as superior, inferior, or middling,
so too should mantras be understood as superior, inferior, or middling.
Having reached a state of unanimity through the eye of insight provided by the scriptures, the deliberation of ministers according to the rules of counsel— this they call the highest form of counsel.
When many opinions have arisen among ministers for the sake of accomplishing a purpose,
but they subsequently reach a state of unity, that counsel is known as middling.
When one proceeds by relying on the opinions of others,
and there is no cohesion in their unanimity, that counsel is called the lowest.
That wherein both profit and loss, as well as doubt, are examined, should be known as counsel; the remainder, indeed, is valor.

‘With those who have the same purpose’ means with those who share the same objective. Manu says: “Having ascended a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place, or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate until dawn.”
The king whose counsel ordinary people do not discover even when they have gathered together enjoys the entire earth, even though he be destitute of a treasury.

[103] ‘In a place free from noise,’ meaning in a secluded spot. Yājñavalkya says: Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, one should keep that counsel well-guarded, so that others do not know it until the results of the actions have come to fruition.
Manu says:
At the time of reciting the mantras, one should exclude those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, animals, the very aged, women, barbarians, the diseased, and the deformed.
Those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, deride a mantra; therefore, one should be careful regarding them.
‘Tairyagyonāḥ’ means those born of animal wombs, such as parrots, starlings, and the like. In the Mahābhārata: “A wise person should devise these gateways for the disclosure of secrets;
furthermore, one who desires prosperity should guard them constantly.”
Arrogance, sleep, contempt, and self-originated pride;
placing trust in wicked ministers, as well as an unskilled messenger.
[They should be] those who know the reality of the determination of mantras, who understand the qualities of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya),
who are capable, of noble birth, devoted, and whose conduct has never been previously reproached.
[He appointed] those who were knowledgeable in ethics, knowledgeable in legal procedures, experts in the meaning of history,
perceivers of gestures, knowers of expedients, and brave heroes born of noble lineage.
Those who are skilled in all affairs, who have mastered the science of archery and missiles,
who know how to construct fortifications and machines, and who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the treatises on Dharma.
Those who are noble-minded, patient, wise, and proactive; those who understand how to provide remedies for the future and possess firm resolve in the present.
O Bhārata, they know the states of enemies, friends, and neutrals; firm in their vows, they are naturally guarded and as immovable as mountains.
Having thoroughly examined all [candidates] with his intellect, the king should appoint as ministers those who are virtuous, not miserly, and likewise free from all deceitful motives.

Having assembled with those who are capable of bearing the burden of his kingdom like excellent oxen, the protector of the earth— whose counsel is kept secret and whose senses are subdued— [should rule].
O bull among the Bharatas, one should apply effort toward the practice of seeing [the truth].
"Those who have never been reviled before," meaning those not insulted by speech; "those who have transcended all guiles," meaning those free from all deceit. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"A king should not deliberate on a secret counsel alone, nor with too many people."
One should not board a leaky boat, nor one that has not been examined.
[105] In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "Many who possess the intellect of cattle, being ignorant of the scriptures,
desire to speak out of audacity once they have been admitted into the deliberations on counsel."
For those who, having abandoned the rise of what is beneficial, devote themselves to the opposite, should be suspected by the wise as being in the form of ministers, though they are actually enemies.
For those men who, out of audacity, speak of what is harmful as if it were beneficial, should be regarded as excluded from counsel; having committed an offense, they should be discarded.
Indeed, ministers who have allied themselves with enemies act here to cause the destruction of their own master by making him perform contrary deeds.
Manu says: He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, successful in their aims, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions,
he should, in all matters concerning them collectively, act for their own benefit.
But the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brāhmaṇa among all [his ministers].
One should always place full confidence in him and entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, one should then commence the task.

In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "Whatever is pleasing, beneficial, and entirely consistent with the dharma of the virtuous— those ministers should speak such words, especially while counsel is being deliberated."
When a task has arisen,
a minister must indeed speak only what is beneficial, even at the cost of what is pleasing, in order to lead his own master toward the excellence of virtue.
O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are rare indeed.
With "the ministers" being understood from the previous context, Manu says:
"Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon general matters:
peace and war, the strategic position, revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired."
At midday and at night, being rested and free from fatigue,
one should contemplate virtue, pleasure, and wealth, either alone or together with them.
The acquisition of those things which are mutually contradictory,
the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons.
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining matters of business,
the conduct within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
[107] He should diligently examine the entire eightfold business, the five groups,
as well as loyalty and disloyalty, and the conduct of the circle of states.
He should diligently [ascertain] the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest,
the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy.
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
The five others are known as ministers, the kingdom, forts, wealth, and the army;
each of these has been described briefly, totaling seventy-two.
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the enemy's ally;
immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party.
One who is situated at a great distance, independent, neutral, and possessed of power,
yet is a source of obstruction to the objectives of the circle of states— that one should be known as the middle king.
Likewise: "The wise say that an enemy who is intelligent, of noble birth, generous, brave, capable, grateful, and powerful is difficult to overcome."
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and compassion;
he was always liberal and possessed the virtues of one who remains impartial.
Likewise,
he should win over all of them by means of conciliation and other such expedients,
whether employed individually or collectively, as well as through personal prowess and statesmanship.

‘Station’ (*sthāna*) is fourfold, distinguished as the army, the treasury, the city, and the kingdom. ‘Accumulation’ (*samudaya*) consists of agriculture, crafts, guilds, marketplaces, trade, cattle, customs duties, fines, and so forth. ‘Protection’ (*gupti*) is the defense of the kingdom and other territories. ‘Settlement of acquisitions’ (*labdhapraśamana*) is the application of gifts and honors toward deities, hermitages, the learned, and the righteous. ‘Of these’ refers to virtue, wealth, and pleasure. ‘Acquisition’ (*samupārjana*) is their production in a proper and non-contradictory manner. ‘Spies’ (*praṇidhayaḥ*) are secret agents. ‘The eightfold business’ (*aṣṭavidhaṃ karma*) is as stated by Uśanas: “In taking and in giving, likewise in commanding and in forbidding...”
And in the fifth, in the speaking of the meaning and in the observation of conventional usage.
Likewise engaged in the purification of punishment as well as in the purification of the self,
the king who performs the eightfold duty goes to heaven, honored by Śakra.

‘The group of five’ (*pañcavarga*) is a collection of five types of spies. They are as follows: [109] people who know specific regions, crafts, and languages that inspire trust; likewise, those disguised as hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the deaf, the mentally dull, the blind, and so forth; likewise, actors, dancers, singers, and the like; likewise, women who move within the inner quarters; and likewise, ascetics (*śramaṇa*) and others. These groups of spies must be understood by oneself and by others for the purpose of knowing their activities. ‘Loyalty and disloyalty’ (*anurāgāparāgau*) means that the loyalty or disloyalty of the minister, domestic priest, commander-in-chief, crown prince, doorkeeper, and others should be known from one’s own group of five types of spies. ‘The conduct of the middle king’ (*madhyamasya pracāram*): In this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*), there are these four royal natures (*rājaprakṛti*): the seeker of conquest (*vijigīṣu*), the enemy (*ari*), the middle king (*madhyama*), and the neutral king (*udāsīna*). Among them, the one who possesses the qualities of a king and is intent on conquering is the seeker of conquest. The enemy is of three kinds: natural (*sahaja*), artificial (*kṛttrima*), and the neighbor of one’s own territory (*svabhūmyanantara*). The ‘middle king’ is one capable of suppressing both the enemy and the seeker of conquest when they are not united. The ‘neutral king’ is one capable of suppressing the enemy, the seeker of conquest, and the middle king when they are not united. Of each of these four primary natures of the circle, there are two further natures—each having an enemy and a friend. These eight, together with the original four, make twelve. ‘The minister,’ etc.: the five natures beginning with the minister belong to each of the twelve natures; thus, from six sets of twelve, there are seventy-two.

[110] In the Mahābhārata: For one who desires victory, there are the enemy, the friend, the enemy’s friend, and beyond that, the friend-of-a-friend and the enemy’s friend; these are to be known as the primary allies.
The rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the rear-caller (*ākranda*), and the rear-supporter (*pārṣṇyāsāra*) from behind,
as well as the support for the rear-caller (*ākrandāsāra*), are to be known by those who contemplate the circle of states.

In times of conflict, a king should augment his rear-attackers (*pārṣṇigrāha*) and his ally (*abhisāra*), as well as his rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), by means of the ally’s rear-enemy (*rājākranda-abhisāra*) and likewise by means of the rear-enemy’s rear-enemy (*tathākranda*).
One who desires the status of a neutral king should oppose the enemy’s ally, as well as the friend of that enemy’s ally,
by means of his own ally and the ally of his own ally.
A self-possessed king should protect [his subjects] through the power of his spells, his majesty, and his valor.
‘Vardhayet’ means he should cut it.
Thus ends the mantra.
Now, the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya).
Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, sitting encamped, dividing one's forces, and seeking refuge."
Having considered both sitting and marching, as well as making peace and waging war,
one should employ the strategies of double-dealing or seeking protection after examining the task at hand.
One should know that alliance is of two kinds, as is conflict with a king;
likewise, there are both marching and encamping, as well as the double policy and seeking refuge.

A peace treaty should be understood by the wise as being of four kinds: that which involves a common expedition, that which is the opposite, and those associated with the immediate present or the future.

War is declared to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of a specific objective, whether at the improper time or at the right time; and that waged against a friend, even when no such occasion has arisen.
Traveling alone when a time of urgency has arrived, or traveling together with an ally according to one's desire— these two types of marching are taught.

When one's power has gradually diminished, whether by fate or by one's own past actions, neutrality is declared to be of two kinds: that arising from the constraint of a friend, and that arising from the decline of one's own strength.
The maintenance of both the army and the sovereign for the sake of accomplishing the task is declared to be of two kinds as "duplicity" by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy.
Seeking refuge is considered to be of two kinds: for the sake of accomplishing one's objectives, or when being oppressed by enemies, seeking the protection of the virtuous.
When one perceives that one's own superiority will be certain in the future,
or that there is excessive suffering at present, then one should resort to peace.
When he considers all his constituent elements to be exceedingly strong and himself likewise highly exalted, then he may consider undertaking war.
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit,
and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is completely depleted of both mounts and forces,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect,
he should then divide his army into two parts and accomplish his own purpose.
But when one becomes most vulnerable to the attack of enemy forces, then one should quickly seek refuge with a powerful enemy who is righteous.
One should constantly serve with all efforts like a teacher that person who effects the suppression of the subjects and of the weak.
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from taking refuge, he should then engage in fair combat without hesitation.
A king who knows the principles of policy should employ every means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to himself.
One should examine all future undertakings as well as those of the present,
and the merits and defects of all past ones, according to their true nature.
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who understands the remaining consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies.
He should manage everything in such a way that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not overcome him; this is the summary of political strategy.
Likewise:
Through spies, through the application of energy, and through the very execution of actions,
one should constantly ascertain the strength and weakness of both oneself and the enemy.
Having reflected upon all afflictions as well as calamities,
and having weighed their relative gravity and lightness, one should then undertake the task.
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when utterly exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings.
Thus ends the section on the sixfold policy.
[115] 14 — Now, the expedition.
In this regard, Manu says:
"When the lord sets out upon a vehicle toward the enemy's kingdom,
he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule."
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition,
or else toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra, according to his strength.
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy.
Yājñavalkya says:
When one should march against the enemy's kingdom that is endowed with the quality of truthfulness,
while the enemy is weak and one's own self possesses joyful mounts and men.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "When a king perceives that he is being overwhelmed by a rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*) due to a more powerful enemy, then he should undertake a military expedition."
Having stationed a superior force at the rear as a reserve,
he should march forth against the enemy who is afflicted by celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents.
He was tormented by the oppression of bears, afflicted by malevolent planets,
beset by the calamity of his own army, and likewise oppressed by famine.
And when his internal anger has arisen, the king should swiftly march against the enemy,
provided there is an auspicious throbbing of the body and likewise the sight of a good dream.
Likewise:
when an auspicious omen, a favorable sign, or a lucky occurrence has arisen, one should proceed toward the enemy's city;
moreover, throbbing on the right side of the body is praised as auspicious.
Likewise, on the left side of the back and the heart, a mark or a pimple is to be known as inauspicious,
just like a throbbing.
The opposite of this is prescribed for all women;
even on the right side, it is especially auspicious on a praiseworthy limb.
Otherwise, there is the accomplishment of the desired or censured result through silence,
when the signs of impending death appear to the twice-born.
And the propitiatory offering should be performed with gold.

In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa, regarding matters auspicious and inauspicious, there are the words of Trijaṭā: "In a dream, I saw Rāma swallowing this entire city, with all its buildings, and drinking a great deal of blood."
Rāghava, having comfortably ascended a divine palanquin made of ivory that travels through the air and is yoked to a thousand elephants, [proceeded].
And today in a dream I saw one clothed in excellent white garments,
stationed upon a white mountain surrounded by the ocean.
And I saw Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, wandering about mounted upon a great elephant resembling a mountain and possessing four tusks.
Then those two tigers among men, blazing with their own splendor and wearing white garlands and garments, presented themselves before Jānakī.
Then, from the front of that city, Jānakī took her place upon the shoulder of the elephant stationed in the air, who was held by her husband.
Then, leaping up from her husband's lap, that lotus-eyed woman was seen by me rubbing the moon and the sun with her hand.
Then that excellent elephant, mounted by those two princes and by the large-eyed Sītā, proceeded around Laṅkā.
Rama himself, wearing white garlands and garments, arrived with Lakshmana in a chariot yoked by eight white bulls.
"And Rāvaṇa was seen by me on the ground, sprinkled with oil,
wearing red garments, intoxicated, and drinking while wearing a garland of *karavīra* flowers.
Today, Rāvaṇa fell from the Puṣpaka aerial chariot before my eyes.
He was seen by the woman laughing, shaven-headed and wearing yellow garments, while being reviled.
[118] Adorned with red garlands and unguents, he traveled by means of a chariot yoked with donkeys and entered the Gomaya lake in the southern direction.
Having bound the ten-necked one by the throat, the dark-complexioned woman,
dressed in red and possessing a terrifying countenance, drags him toward the southern quarter.
The ten-necked one was seen by me repeatedly as a boar, as a porpoise, and as a camel, traveling toward the southern direction.
And I beheld an assembly accompanied by song, instrumental music, and dance,
consisting of Rākṣasas wearing red garlands and red garments.
And this city of Laṅkā, seen once teeming with elephants and horses,
has now fallen entirely into the ocean, its walls and gateways shattered.
Having drunk the oil, all the Rākṣasa women in Laṅkā, which was rough with ashes, began to dance and laugh with loud voices.
And all these foremost of Rākṣasas, Kumbhakarṇa and the others,
were seen wearing yellow garments as they played in a pool of cow dung.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Now I shall describe the omen regarding the sight of dreams:
the growth of grass or trees upon any part of the body other than the navel."
Pounding [the head] with the dregs of bell-metal, shaving the head, likewise nakedness,
wearing soiled garments, anointing the body with oil, and being smeared with mud.
Jumping from a great height, riding on a swing,
applying collyrium, and wearing mud, iron, or even heated metal ornaments.
Likewise, there is the act of climbing trees with red flowers, as well as a *caṇḍāla*,
and similarly mounting boars, bears, donkeys, and camels.
The eating of cooked meat, oil, and *kṛśara* rice;
dancing, laughing, marriage, and even [sexual] intercourse.
Playing musical instruments that lack strings,
wading into a stream, traveling, and bathing with cow-dung water;
Likewise, by means of mud-water and also by earth-water,
there is entry into the mother’s womb as well as ascending the funeral pyre.
The falling of the banners of Śakra, the falling of the moon and the sun,
and the appearance of portents both celestial and terrestrial.
The wrath of gods, brahmins, kings, and gurus,
as well as embracing young maidens and sexual intercourse with men.
There will be the wasting away of one's own limbs, the performance of purgation and emesis,
a journey toward the southern direction, and likewise an affliction by disease.
One should predict the loss of fruits, the destruction of houses, the falling down of dwellings,
as well as the sweeping away of the home and the loss of wealth.
There is suffering even from Piśācas, Kravyādās, monkeys, and outcastes;
likewise, there is oppression by others, and from that, the arising of calamities.
Likewise, wearing saffron-colored robes, sporting with women,
as well as drinking oils, bathing, and using red garlands and ointments.
"Likewise, 'playing with women' means playing with a woman dressed in saffron-colored robes.
One should point out such inauspicious dreams;
however, not mentioning them is auspicious, as is sleeping further."
Bathing with *kalka*, oblations with sesame seeds, the honoring of Brahmins,
the chanting of praises to Vāsudeva, and likewise his worship.
Listening to the *Gajendramokṣa* should be known as the destroyer of bad dreams;
however, dreams occurring in the first watch of the night bear fruit within a year.
In the second [case], it is seen after six months; in the third, after three months;
and in the fourth, after merely one month—for one who observes this, there is no doubt.
Whether it be on a single night, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
one should predict the fruition for that person who is seen there afterwards.
Therefore, after a good dream, a subsequent dream is not praised; however, seeing mountains, palaces, or elephants, and mounting a bull, is auspicious.
O twice-born one, there was likewise the movement of trees with white flowers;
the appearance of trees and grass upon the arms, as well as the possession of many arms.
Likewise, there is the state of having many heads and the appearance of grey hair;
wearing very white garlands and wearing very white garments.
The swallowing of the moon, sun, and stars, as well as their cleansing; the embracing of Indra’s banner and likewise the act of raising it aloft.
O twice-born one, there shall be the swallowing of earth, water, and clouds, as well as the act of slaying enemies,
victory in disputes, at dice, and likewise in battle.
The eating of raw meat, fish, and milk-rice;
the sight of blood; and bathing with blood.
The drinking of wine, blood, and liquor, as well as milk;
being entwined on the ground by intestines, and likewise a spotless sky.
Milking at ease is recommended for female buffaloes and likewise for cows;
it is also the same for female elephants that are not emaciated, as well as for mares.
Likewise, auspicious acts consist of showing favor toward gods, Brahmins, and teachers,
as well as performing ablutions with water drawn from the horns of cows.
O King, it should be known that one who has fallen from the moon indeed bestows sovereignty;
likewise, there is both the consecration to kingship and the severing of the head.
[122] Death and being burned by fire; burning of houses and the like by fire;
the acquisition of royal insignia; and the playing of stringed instruments and the like.
Likewise, crossing over water, leaping across a boundary,
and the birth of female elephants, mares, or cows within one's house [are auspicious omens].
Likewise, mounting [a vehicle], the barking of dogs, and the auspicious sight of excellent women, as well as obtaining them and embracing them.
For living beings, being bound with fetters is blessed, as is being smeared with excrement; even the sight of kings and their friends is a blessing.
Beholding the images of deities as well as pure waters.
Furthermore, O knower of dharma, best among those who support others, by seeing these auspicious dreams, a man effortlessly attains prosperity and the acquisition of wealth on this earth.
And likewise, the one who is afflicted also attains liberation from disease.
Manu says: Having performed the rites at the base according to the rule, as well as the preparations for the journey,
having secured a place of refuge, and having properly stationed spies;
Having purified his threefold path and his sixfold strength,
he should march toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a protracted campaign.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a friend who serves one's enemy and remains hidden, as well as one who has gone abroad and returned; for such a person is indeed a most dangerous foe.
‘According to the method for the next world’ means according to the method of battle. In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
“One should deploy an army consisting mostly of infantry and elephants during the rainy season;
and one consisting of chariots and horses during the winter and the cool season.”
O lord of men, he may lead an army consisting largely of donkeys and camels during the summer,
or one equipped with the fourfold forces during the spring or the autumn.
