That lord of the earth who possesses an army consisting largely of infantry may attack an enemy who has taken refuge in difficult terrain.
Likewise, a king should advance against an enemy stationed in a pleasant region covered with trees,
or similarly in one that is somewhat marshy, provided he possesses many elephants.

A king should march with an abundance of chariots and horses toward a field that has level paths; likewise, he should conquer fortified cities with an abundance of ships when approaching a region abounding in water.
A king who has many donkeys and camels should always employ his enemy,
even while that enemy is held in captivity, during the rainy season.
One should attack an army stationed in a region afflicted by falling snow during the summer;
likewise, one should attack it at the time when fodder and fuel are abundant, during the king’s birth-star period.
O knower of dharma, autumn and spring are traditionally considered the two common seasons.

Having ascertained the [suitability of] the twice-born, the place, and the time, and likewise having understood fate and the three periods of time, the king should march forth according to the opinion of those who know the seasons.
Being contemplated by those who know the mantras of the twice-born.

Manu says: He should march along that path in the staff-array (daṇḍavyūha), or the wagon-array (śakaṭavyūha), or the boar-array (varāhavyūha), the crocodile-array (makaravyūha), the needle-array (sūcīvyūha), or the eagle-array (garuḍavyūha).
From whatever direction one might fear danger, from that side one should extend the army;
then, one should personally take up position in the lotus formation (*padmavyūha*).
He should station the commander-in-chief and the army supervisor in all directions;
or, whichever direction he might suspect danger from, he should designate that as the "east."
He should station trusted men as military outposts here and there in numbers of one hundred—
men who are skilled in both their positions and in combat, fearless, and authoritative.
[125] Śaṅkha and Likhita say:

The horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is indeed a royal ritual (*rājakratu*); no one who is not a sovereign emperor (*sārvabhauma*) is worthy of performing it. One who intends to sacrifice with the horse sacrifice should march against the territory of another, provided he is endowed with the advantages of place, time, and power, and possesses abundant fodder, fuel, and water for his military operations. Having prepared all necessary equipment along the route, he must be knowledgeable regarding the qualities and strategic methods of forts, essential supplies, ministers, the terrain, and the recruitment of troops. Being prudent toward his assembly (*parṣad*), he should follow a well-known path that is beneficial. Just as the terrain is, so should be the deployment of forces; the king, skilled in providing food, drink, and encampments, and expert in anticipating and countering dangers at every station, should fight the enemy with full attention.
Yājñavalkya says:
Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom, he obtains all that very same dharma when bringing another's kingdom under his control.
Manu says:
Having besieged the enemy, one should remain encamped or harass his kingdom;
and one should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, water, and fuel.
One should break down the tanks as well as the walls and moats;
one should launch a frontal assault upon him at night and likewise cause terror.
Having besieged the enemy, one should not incite internal strife; rather, one should fight for that purpose alone.
When fate is favorable, one seeking success through recitation should fight with those who are free from fear.
Likewise: "While he is thus victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control through the strategic means beginning with conciliation."
If, however, they do not abide by it through the first three expedients,
one should bring them under control gradually by force, having assailed them with punishment.
Yājñavalkya says:
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment—these means, when properly employed, lead to success; yet punishment is the resort for those who have no other way.
Manu says: Among the four means of policy, conciliation and the others, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant increase of the kingdom.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "O best of men, O King, [the means are] conciliation, sowing dissension, as well as bribery, punishment,
indifference, illusion, and sorcery."
Seven applications have been declared; listen as I describe them to you.
Conciliation (sāma) is said to be of two kinds: the true and the untrue.
Even there, untruth leads only to the reviling of the virtuous;
likewise, O best of men, a virtuous person is won over through effort and conciliation.
Those who are of noble lineage, upright, constant in dharma, and have conquered their senses can be won over by conciliation;
one should not employ conciliation toward those who are not truthful.
One should employ truth and conciliation, as well as praise of [the recipient's] lineage, character, and so forth,
and likewise describe the services and honors already performed for them.
By this very method, one should manifest one's own gratitude;
thus, through conciliation, they should be brought under control and made devoted to the Dharma.
Although there is a Vedic text stating that even by means of conciliation the Rākṣasas may be won over,
nevertheless, when employed against the wicked, this very method is not beneficial.
The wicked understand the person who knows the Sāman only as "excessive suspicion"; therefore, that [quality] is avoided among them.
Likewise:
"And those who are mutually hostile, angry, fearful, or insulted—against them one should employ sowing of dissension; for they are considered capable of being overcome through division."
One should show one's own hope and show fear of another;
for in this way, one may cause division, and having divided them, bring them under control as is fitting.
Indeed, unity, when devoid of dissension, is difficult to withstand even for Śakra;
therefore, those expert in policy praise dissension alone.
The queen, the crown prince, as well as the commander-in-chief, O twice-born one,
the ministers, the counselors, and likewise the princes.
The internal anger of kings is declared to be terrible;
"atiśaṅkitam" means that in which there is excessive suspicion or imprecation. "Sāmavedinam" means one who employs conciliation (the Sāma).
[This is stated] in the Brahmapurāṇa.
One should never, under any circumstances, cause division within one's own faction;
for it is only in the absence of fear from a foreign kingdom that one can maintain a secure fortress, treasury, and territory.
"Even subjects whose roots are firmly established perish through internal dissension alone;

'without fear from a foreign kingdom'—the meaning is that when there is dissension within one's own faction, even forts and other defenses perish even in the absence of danger from an enemy army. [129] In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
Among all means, giving is considered the most excellent;
by giving well in this world, one conquers both worlds.
Even though men who are free from greed and profound are like the ocean,
they nevertheless become partial toward those who do not take [their wealth].
Those who cannot be brought under control by the three means [of conciliation, gifts, and sowing dissension] should be subdued by force; for force is the most effective means of subduing them.
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa:
"In that regard, conciliation should be employed toward those who are noble and virtuous;
bribery toward the greedy; and sowing dissension toward those who are suspicious—this is the settled rule."
In the same way, punishment must always be inflicted upon the evil-minded.
Manu says: One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, or by all these means combined or separately; never by war.
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight,
and defeat likewise occurs in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
Likewise:
When the three aforementioned expedients have all been exhausted,
one who is thus well-equipped should fight in such a manner that he may conquer his enemies.
Likewise: One should make a few soldiers fight in close formation, but one may extend many as one desires;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.

One should fight with chariots and cavalry on level ground; with elevated elephants on high ground; with bows on terrain covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other handheld weapons on firm ground.
One should employ the men of Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena— both tall and short alike— in the vanguard of the fierce divisions.
Having arrayed the army, he should inspire it with joy and closely examine those who are deeply distressed;
he should also discern the gestures of even those fighting at a distance.
In the *Mahābhārata*:
"A Brahmin, especially, must fight against the aggression of a king.
Gautama, following the rule that the king’s authority is superior, states: "And there shall be no retreat for those who stand firm in battle. Yama says:
The field of a Kṣatriya is in his chest, while the Brahman is established in his back;
therefore, one should protect one's back in battle so as not to become a slayer of a Brahmin.
Manu says:
When challenged by enemies who are equal, superior, or inferior in battle, a king,
mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya, must not retreat from the fray.
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another and fight with their utmost strength, never turning their backs, go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with those that are barbed, nor with those smeared with poison, nor with those whose tips are set ablaze with fire.
"[They are] contending with one another," is the ellipsis. "Digdhaiḥ" means smeared with poison. Baudhāyana says:
One should not fight with those who are terrified, intoxicated, insane, distracted, unarmed, women, children, the elderly, or Brahmins—except in the case of an assassin (ātatāyin).
Gautama says:

There is no fault in killing in battle, except for those who are without horses, charioteers, or weapons; those with joined palms; those with disheveled hair; those who have turned their backs; those who are seated; those who are on the ground or mounted on a tree; and those who cry out "cow" or "Brahmin."
Manu says: One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with joined palms;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."

One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unprepared for battle, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should not strike one who is suffering from the loss of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away.
Devala says: One who eats grass, one who covets another's property, the lazy, one who has sought refuge,
a eunuch, one oppressed by others, one who merely wears the marks of an ascetic, the elderly, the fallen, and a child.
In a righteous war, warriors should not be killed when they are not in a state of distress; this is how they should be known.
Yājñavalkya says: Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land, without turning their backs and with weapons free from deceit, go to heaven like yogis.
[133] Devala said: For the sake of his subjects, a Kṣatriya should fight and completely sacrifice his own life;
he thereby naturally attains the entire fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Slain by enemies in battle with a weapon, while not turning his back,
he attains the auspicious world of Śakra, won by his own heroism.
In battle, for every weapon hurled at him by hosts of enemies while he stood as a hero facing the front, he performed that many sacrifices.
He who touches the blood flowing from wounds or the dust of the earth remains certainly in the world of the gods for that same length of time.

There is no duty for kings equal to the sacrifice of one’s own body in battle. Those who die for the sake of protecting cows, Brahmins, friends, and wealth attain the world of the gods. Āpastamba says: “When a king is slain while seeking to recover the property of Brahmins that has been stolen, they call him a sacrifice whose sacrificial post is his own self and whose sacrificial fee is infinite.

Here, “the property of Brahmins” refers to what has been seized by thieves and others. “Seeking to recover” means desiring to win back after having defeated them. The meaning is that a king who is killed while fighting is himself the very embodiment of the sacrificial rite. Vyāsa says:
Those who, devoted to the duty of the warrior class (kṣatradharma), were slain by sharp weapons—they have gone to the abode of Brahmā; of this I have no doubt.
Neither by sacrifices nor by sacrificial fees, nor by austerities nor by knowledge do mortals go to heaven in the same way as warriors slain in battle.
For there is no unrighteousness more evil for a Kṣatriya than flight;
indeed, the path of righteousness through battle is truly superior as a way to heaven.
Yājñavalkya: When [the army] is broken, the words [of command] are equal to the sacrifice because they cause retreat;
the king takes away the merit of those who have been killed while fleeing.
Manu:
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies,
takes upon himself whatever evil deed his master has committed.
Whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter,
the husband takes all of that from one who is killed while retreating.
Parāśara says:
For those of sinful intent who turn their backs and flee, abandoning their fallen master in battle, there is the sin of killing a Brahmin at every step.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The servant who abandons his lord in an instant as he sets out for battle—
that fool, by that punishment of the king, goes to hell."
By conquering the enemy, one attains wealth; for one who has died, there is the supreme goal. There is no means of expiation for one's master’s funeral cake equal to the path of battle.
O Sage, whatever blood flows from arrows as they strike anywhere, by that very means one indeed casts off all evil along with it.
In that same way, whatever suffering one endures through doubt—
that is a most terrible austerity, beyond which there is nothing greater in the world.
For one who has died, there is no funeral rite, no period of impurity, and no water-libation;
for what indeed could one wish to do here that is greater than battle?
Thousands of excellent apsarases, afflicted by desire, rush toward a hero slain in battle, thinking, "He shall be my husband."
When one who, remaining healthy, desires to depart without abandoning his companions,
the gods led by Śakra act toward him as he stands there.
When a distressed person cries out loudly in the presence of a hero, O Brahmin,
if that hero does not protect him from evil, he shall partake in the fate of hell.
If one is slain for the sake of protecting brahmins or cows,
that hero, having abandoned his life, attains the world of Indra.
Likewise:
Having gratified the king in battle and having stood at the forefront of other kings,
that man who does not seize wealth after victory has taken his place in heaven.
If he crushes kingdoms but does not carry off their wealth,
and if he is slain right there, that man has attained heaven.

Likewise: those kings devoted to righteousness who were slain for the sake of their subjects, and those who were struck down by fire or lightning, or killed by lions and tigers; [for all these, one should perform the śrāddha].
And they all reached this city of Airāvatī.
[137] Manu says: Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all types of property, and base metals— whatever one conquers belongs to him.
"And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually."
Gautama says:

The victor shall receive the booty acquired in battle; however, the mounts belong to the king, as do the special shares when there is no separate victory. As for other property, the king shall distribute it according to merit.
Manu says: Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety.
[138] But having understood that all of them desire the same thing,
he should install a member of their own lineage there and establish a formal covenant.
And one should establish authorities for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and one should honor him with jewels together with the principal men.
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving causes pleasure;
therefore, the timely acquisition of desired objects is praised.

“[He should grant] exemptions” means that even what is due to the king, he should relinquish some portion for the sake of winning the affection of the people. “Authorities” means that whatever laws exist in a particular region, those must be protected exactly as they are. “Appropriate to the time” means that even that which causes displeasure is praised when considered in light of the timing. Viṣṇu: Upon capturing an enemy city, the king should consecrate a member of that [enemy’s] family; he should not exterminate the royal lineage, except in the case of a royal family that lacks noble descent.
[139] Kātyāyana said: Even if a king is wicked, his kingdom shall not perish,
because he does not proceed toward unrighteousness without the consent of his subjects.
Yājñavalkya: Whatever custom and whatever legal practice is established in a family in a particular region,
that very same must be maintained when it has come under one's authority.
[Now, regarding human effort:
Manu says: "All this action is dependent upon the ordinance of both fate and human exertion."
In that regard, while destiny is inconceivable, human action exists within the realm of man.
An expedition endowed with both divine and human factors accomplishes all objectives;
in such an undertaking, the divine factor prevails in its excellence, while the human factor remains equal.
Some of those with wise intellects maintain that the fruit [of action] arises through human effort, some through destiny, and others through both.
The conception of a fetus in a woman occurs when there is the presence of both divine and human factors;
even when union with a man has taken place, it does not succeed in the absence of the divine factor.
For destiny never at any time, nor anywhere, yokes a human being—
who is here rendered helpless— to the fruits of gain or loss.
Even if one encounters fate before one's eyes by chance, like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence,
a person is not joined with that fate except through human effort.
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "But that man who, being devoted to fate alone, does not undertake his duty,
quickly becomes destitute and intent on flight."
Likewise: "The despondent one of inferior vigor who always conforms to fate,
but the undaunted and spirited one does not conform to fate."
He who strives to overcome destiny through human effort never sinks, even when his purpose is thwarted by fate.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Destiny, human effort, and time, O Supreme Person—
these three combined indeed lead to the fruit for a human being."
The attainment of fruits is seen through the conjunction of cultivation and rain;
they are praised during the rainy season, but never at any other time.
Vyāsa says: Fate, ordinance, necessity, inherent nature, time, the planets, the Lord, action, and destiny.
Fortunes, merits, and the conjunction of destiny are synonyms for that which was performed in the past.
One should know that "fate" (daiva) is the action performed by oneself in a previous body;
whereas "human effort" (puruṣakāra) is said to be that which is performed here in this life as something distinct.
[Thus ends the section on human effort.
Manu says:
Or, being disciplined, he may march along with [the enemy], having carefully concluded a treaty.
Perceiving a friend, gold, or land as the threefold fruit.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and likewise the ally within the circle of states,
one should obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy.
Viṣṇu: "When attacked by an enemy, he should protect his kingdom with all his soul, and he should protect himself from every side.
Manu:
[He should protect a land that is] secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle.
A king should relinquish his land for the sake of his own soul, without hesitation.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune, and protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one must protect oneself above all else, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together,
the wise man should overcome them by employing every means, both those that are combined and those that are separate.
Relying upon these three— the practitioner, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of the self.
Thus concludes the section on journeys.
Now, regarding the duties of one who has been consecrated,
Manu says:
"He should apply himself day and night to the mastery of the senses."
And one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control.
One should diligently avoid these ten calamities arising from desire, as well as those eight born of anger, which have miserable ends.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self.

Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony of song, dance, and instrumental music, and idle wandering— this is the tenfold set of qualities born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, jealousy, and the spoiling of property;
along with verbal and physical harshness—this is the eightfold group born of anger.
One should strive to conquer greed, which the ancient seers know to be the root of both these; for both these classes originate from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— know that this group of four, in their respective order, is the most grievous among the set born of desire.
One should always know that this triad— inflicting punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth— is always difficult to endure, even within the group born of anger.
Among this entire group of seven interconnected vices,
one should know that each preceding one is more grievous for oneself than the one that follows.
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
one who suffers calamity sinks lower and lower, while one who dies free from calamity goes to heaven.
In the Mahābhārata: "Drinking, dice, women, hunting, singing, and instrumental music—
one may enjoy these with moderation, for addiction to them is indeed harmful."
But one who, even while associating [with others], does not fall away from dharma and artha—let him associate with that person at will; he should not practice the conduct of a fool.
One should not be devoted solely to sensual pleasure; one should pursue all [aims] at all times.
One should practice virtue in the first stage, wealth in the middle, and sensual pleasure in the final stage.
The world recoils from one who abandons both dharma and artha to follow only desire, as if from a snake that has entered the house.
Therefore, one who prioritizes dharma and has restrained the self should pursue wealth;
having inspired confidence in all beings, he should bring them under his control through conciliation.
One who is endowed with virtue, wealth, and pleasure rejoices both in this world and in the next.
Likewise: "People even criticize the rain-cloud for raining upon salt-wastes, and for raining too softly into vessels; how much more so, then, the lord of the earth?"
Likewise:

One should speak kindly without being fawning; one should be brave without being boastful; one should be a giver who does not shower gifts upon the unworthy; and one should be bold without being harsh.
Viṣṇu: "One should not cut off the doors of income, nor should one shower wealth upon unworthy recipients. "Doors of income" refers to the sources from which wealth is produced. In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"And the king should avoid all vices."
For the sake of gathering the world, he should appear to be addicted to worldly vices.
Likewise:
A king should avoid two kinds of corruption regarding wealth:
the corruption of wealth itself, and likewise corruption by means of wealth.
The destruction of ramparts, the neglect of fortresses and other defenses,
the squandering of wealth, and its mere dissipation— these are declared to be [the causes of decline].
Giving at an improper place or time, giving to an unworthy recipient, and the corruption of wealth through the promotion of unwholesome actions— these are declared to be faults.
Lust, anger, pride, arrogance, greed, and likewise exhilaration—
this internal group of six enemies must be conquered by the ruler of the earth.
Having achieved victory over these, he should then secure victory over his servants;
having secured victory over his servants, the king should conquer the people of the city and the countryside.
Having achieved victory over them, he should then conquer external enemies;
a king should not be mild, for one who is mild suffers decline.
One should not behave with harshness, for people tremble before one who is too severe;
a ruler should avoid jesting with his servants.
In this world, servants treat with contempt a king who has fallen under the sway of pride.
Manu says:
Every day, he should inspect the works, those afflicted by labor, and the draft animals;
as well as the fixed income and expenditure, the mines, and the treasury.
Yājñavalkya: One should seek to acquire what has not been obtained through righteous means; what has been acquired, one should protect with effort;
what has been protected, one should constantly increase; and what has been increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients.
Uśanas [says]:
"In taking and in giving, as well as in commanding and forbidding,
in the fifth [matter], namely speech, and in the observation of legal proceedings."
Constantly devoted to the purification of punishment as well as the purification of himself,
the king who performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by Śakra.
In the Mahābhārata:
A king who has disciplined his own self should always practice humility;
for a monarch whose self is disciplined is never humiliated.
One should not behave improperly simply because one has attained sovereignty; for lack of discipline destroys prosperity, just as old age destroys the most excellent beauty.
Having received the Vedic consecration according to the prescribed rite,
the Kṣatriya lord of men should acquire the sciences in accordance with the proper method.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple knowledge (trayī) and the science of government (daṇḍanīti);
from logicians, the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī); and from the people, the practical applications of the economic arts (vārtā).
No one knows everything; there is no such thing as an omniscient being.
There is nowhere any person in whom knowledge reaches its ultimate perfection.
One should extract the essence from everything, even from the chatter of the most excellent or the prattle of a child, just as one extracts gold from stones.
A wise man should exert effort in the science of archery and in history,
as well as in riding elephants, riding horses, and in the maneuvers of chariots.

Two parts are prescribed for the purpose of the Itihāsas, one part for the Three Vedas, and another part for archery and related sciences; thus the day is traditionally remembered as being divided into four parts.
One should serve those women whose three things—birth, learning, and conduct—are pure; for association with them is weightier even than the sacred scriptures.
By constantly performing worship of the guru, attending upon the elders,
and listening to the sciences, one attains the highest good.
Indeed, without having understood what has been heard and without having served the elders,
it is not possible to know dharma and artha, even for those equal to Bṛhaspati.
O lord of men, you should always attend upon those advanced in knowledge;
whatever they may say, you should listen to it and carry it out without hesitation.
Even if a lord of the earth attends upon a thousand fools,
or even ten thousand, there is no assistance to be found in them.
Even a single wise man who knows the treatises and has attended upon his teachers can bring great prosperity to a king or a prince.
That man who does not listen to his well-wishing friends— who are always desirous of his welfare,
wise, and learned— brings joy to his enemies.
A person should conduct themselves properly from the very beginning;
in this way, one does not grieve with regret over a past matter.
He who may be a master of wealth but is not a master of his senses falls from his sovereignty in this world due to his lack of mastery over the senses.
O King, he who restrains the impulse that arises from desire and joy becomes a vessel for prosperity; whereas he who later succumbs to delusion does not.
The wise should not despise those who are inferior, superior, or middling;
for there is no place at any time for intoxication in those consumed by pride.
For the lowliest there is fear of non-existence; for those of middle rank, fear of death;
but for the most excellent of mortals, the supreme fear is of dishonor.
He who seeks to please the world through the four means of action, mind, speech, and sight— the world does not become pleased with him.
He who never adopts a haughty appearance, nor boasts even of his prowess, who does not speak excessively and who endures dispute;
Everywhere he receives such praise.

[151] Following the phrase "more so for the king," Gautama says: "Exertion in victory, especially in times of fear, and movement with chariots and bows. "Exertion" (*yoga*) means effort. "In victory" refers to the necessity of applying effort toward bringing oneself, the senses, ministers, and others under control. "In times of fear"—that is, when an attack by another is imminent—one must make a special effort for the sake of protection. "Movement" (*caryā*) means wandering; the meaning is that this should be performed while equipped with mounts and weapons. Manu says:
"He should always have his rod of punishment raised, and he should always manifest his prowess."
One should always move about with careful restraint, constantly watching for the vulnerabilities of the enemy.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly wields the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod alone.
One should conduct oneself solely without guile and never with guile;
being always well-restrained, one should perceive the guile employed by an enemy.
An enemy should not discover one's own vulnerability, but one should cut through the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, one should conceal one's own weak points and protect one's own openings.
One should contemplate one's goals like a crane, exert valor like a lion,
smear oneself with guile like a wolf, and dart away like a hare.
Likewise:
A lord of the earth should be both severe and mild after considering the task at hand;
a king who is both severe and mild becomes esteemed.
Regarding the term "king," Viṣṇu states:

He should possess the Sudarśana [discus] and be one who maintains antidotes against poison and mantras; he should not consume anything unexamined; he should speak with a smile first; and he should not knit his brows even toward those deserving of death.
"Agada" means medicine. [This is stated] in the Matsya Purāṇa.
People, constantly overwhelmed by suffering, always experience agitation toward a haughty king whose mind is ever-arrogant.
A king should not be dilatory in any of his undertakings;
for a king who is dilatory, the failure of his works is certain.
In matters of passion, pride, arrogance, anger, and sinful deeds,
as well as in performing what is unpleasant, a procrastinator is praised.
One should not mount a rogue elephant, nor likewise an untamed horse;
one should not approach an unknown woman, nor should one dwell at a festival for the gods.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

A king whose livelihood is under his own control, whose treasury is based on his own confidence, who personally supervises his duties, and who has desisted from the wealth of Brahmins, beholds prosperity for a long time.
Yama said: One who has been asked should not say "no," and one who is consecrated should not speak untruth;
he should not retreat in battle—the gods know him as a true Kṣatriya.
A donor, a performer of sacrifices, a hero, and one devoted to the gods and the twice-born—
he, impartial toward all beings, protects the earth for a long time.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Oh, the greatness of endurance! Oh, the great fruit of giving!
Hariścandra went on foot and yet attained the sovereignty of Indra."
Yama says:
One should discern an internal fault by means of outward appearance;
being constantly suspicious of those who are trustworthy, one should always protect them with one's power and remain ever-vigilant.
One should exercise restraint over the wicked and provide protection for the virtuous;
furthermore, one should attend upon the elders at the proper times in due order.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should rely upon stability, increase, and decrease regarding one's own side and the opposing side;
one should distinguish between these states of stability and so forth, and at the proper time, collect wealth and goods.
Manu: Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to the Brāhmaṇas— these constitute the supreme welfare of a king.
Nārada said: "The constant favoring of the virtuous and likewise the restraint of the wicked—
this is recorded as the duty of kings, and from it shall also come their prosperity."
His function consists of protecting the subjects, serving the elderly and the wise,
presiding over legal proceedings, and guarding himself.
Yama said:
He who is impartial toward all beings, skilled in discerning right from wrong,
and who does not perform his duties alone— he attains the earth for eternity.
Likewise: "That king who, like the rain-cloud, like a great tree, is the one upon whom all beings depend for their livelihood, shares in the world of Śakra."
Kātyāyana says:
That king who goes forth under the complete sway of anger without proper discernment shall dwell in a terrible hell for half a kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"A king, having risen daily, should worship the gods and the twice-born;
he should perform the propitiation of the sacred fire and behold sandalwood and clarified butter."
When the lunar day and the asterism are suitable for hearing, one should carry out what the physician has prescribed.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: Every day, the king should inspect his stores of ghee, behold auspicious objects, give away a tawny cow (kapilā), converse with those who are well-adorned, consult physicians, and address elders with smiles, deliberation, and humility.
Yājñavalkya: Having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers,
and having seen the astrologers and physicians, he should give a cow, gold, and land.
And then he visited the houses of the householders and those of the Vedic scholars.
Regarding the assembly hall, Bṛhaspati says:
Having occupied it in the forenoon, he should look upon his aged ministers and dependents,
and likewise listen to the gods as well as the treatises on dharma and artha.
Manu says:
"For the king was indeed created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are established in their respective duties in due order."
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his attendants,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon Brahmins who are learned and advanced in the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.
One should constantly serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who always serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
From them, even one who is already self-disciplined should constantly learn the Vinaya;
for a king who is self-disciplined never perishes.
Those who dwell in the forest have even obtained kingdoms through discipline;
many kings, however, along with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline.
Vena was ruined through his lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa,
Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi.
Pṛthu obtained the kingdom through discipline, as did Manu; Kubera obtained wealth and sovereignty, as well as eternal knowledge of the science of government (daṇḍanīti),
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the science of the self (ātmavidyā), and the undertaking of all forms of economic activity (vārtā).
Yājñavalkya: Having performed his protective rites and risen, he should personally inspect income and expenditure;
then, having attended to legal matters and heard petitions, he may eat according to his desire.
Manu says: Having thus deliberated upon all this with his ministers, the king,
having exercised himself and bathed at midday, shall go to the inner apartments to eat.
There, one should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are self-controlled, knowledgeable of the proper time, and reliable, while using mantras that neutralize poison.
[158] One should wash all his belongings with water that neutralizes poison,
and, being self-restrained, he should always wear jewels that counteract poison.
And women, having been thoroughly examined by means of ointments, water, and incense,
and being well-prepared with their dress and ornaments, should touch him with composed minds.
One should exert effort in this manner regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food,
as well as in bathing, grooming, and all forms of ornamentation and the like.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "The king must also be protected from poison; learn my stratagem for that purpose. For the sake of sport, the king may keep wild animals and birds."
One should first examine food, as well as fire and other such things,
and likewise clothing, vehicles, ornaments, food, and shelter.
But a lord of the earth should not even touch anything that has not been previously examined;
for one whose face turns dark and whose eyes roll, who is distressed and looks about with agitation—[such a person is to be avoided].
The *śyāvāsyacakra* has a slightly dark and white facial disc;
it gazes here and there after having administered poison or despair.
With his upper garment slipping off, dejected, he hides himself behind pillars, walls, and the like; he feels ashamed and likewise stumbles.
A man who constantly scratches the ground, moves his neck, plucks at his feathers,
or rubs his head should always be observed with suspicion.
O King, one should examine these and other such signs of a poisoner: his voice becomes shrill during actions, and certainly even when those actions are contrary to his nature.
Then, filled with haste, one should examine that food in the fire:
the fire will have the color of Indra’s bow (a rainbow), be dry, and be accompanied by sparks.
It is of a single color, foul-smelling, and crackles intensely;
from seeing its smoke, a disease of the head arises in living beings.
O King, flies do not settle upon poisoned food;
yet once settled, they perish as soon as the poison is perceived.
O best of kings, the gaze of the cakora bird becomes disenchanted,
and likewise, O monarch, the voice of the cuckoo undergoes a transformation.
The gait of the swan falters, the king of bees hums,
the crane approaches in rut, and the cock crows.
The parrot cries out, O King, and the maina likewise vomits;
the golden bird goes elsewhere, as does the kāraṇḍava toward death.
The monkey urinates, O King, and the jīvajīvaka bird faints;
the mongoose’s hair stands on end, and he weeps behind one's back.
O King, a peacock feels joy at the sight of poison,
and poisoned food, O King, takes a long time to digest.
Likewise, it becomes soured, cooked, and like something stale;
its flavor and fragrance are ruined, and it is thus joined with the moonlight.
The dryness of solid substances and the formation of bubbles in liquids,
as well as the production of a garland of foam in substances containing salt, [arise from this].
O best of kings, the line of crops is copper-colored, that of milk is blue, that of wine is like the hue of a cuckoo, and that of water is likewise.
Likewise, black and brown insects are found in fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), and honey-colored and dark ones in kodrava;
furthermore, blue and yellow insects are found in buttermilk (takra).
That which resembles water belongs to clarified butter; that with the luster of a pigeon belongs to curd-whey;
that which is green belongs to honey; and likewise, that which is reddish belongs to oil.
Even for fruits that are unripe, ripening occurs quickly;
likewise, there is excessive moisture in those that are ripe, and likewise, wilting in those that have been submerged.
There is softness of hard things and the opposite of softness;
likewise, there is the settling of fine fibers and an excessive growth of body hair.
There is a dark discoloration, especially of garments,
and metals and gems become smeared with dirt and mud.
O best of kings, one should recognize the loss of fragrance in ointments and garlands,
as well as the withering of leaves.
O King, a yellowish radiance should likewise be known in the water;
furthermore, the teeth, lips, and skin become dark, as does the body’s thinness.
O best of kings, such signs as these are to be recognized.
Therefore, the king should always remain protected by means of jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and antidotes.
Protected by these [precepts] and avoiding negligence, the king [shall remain steadfast].
The king is the root of the tree of subjects; through its protection, the kingdom attains growth.
Therefore, the king’s protection must be undertaken with diligent effort.
O descendant of the solar and lunar lineages, you must perform this entirely.
Manu says:
Having eaten, he should indeed divert himself with the women in the inner apartments;
and having thus passed the time, he should again consider his duties.
Likewise, being adorned himself, he should inspect the armed host,
as well as all the mounts, garments, and ornaments.
Yājñavalkya:
Gold brought by messengers should be deposited in the treasury;
then, accompanied by his ministers, he should inspect the thieves and dispatch envoys.
Then he may move about at his own pleasure, or associate with his ministers;
having inspected the forces, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he should also engage in song and dance, and recite his sacred study.

Manu says: Having performed the twilight devotions, the king, bearing his weapon, should listen within the inner apartments to the reports of those who reveal secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again for the purpose of eating, surrounded by women.
Having eaten there a little more, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to bed at an unconventional time and rise with his fatigue dispelled.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The king’s rising from sleep shall be signaled by the sound of conchs, drums, and trumpets. Yājñavalkya says:
"He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise awaken to that same sound;
having awakened, he should reflect upon the scriptures as well as all his duties."
And then he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and among others.
‘Among their own’ refers to one’s own vassals and so forth; ‘among others’ refers to other lords of the earth. Manu says:
“A lord of the earth who is free from illness should maintain this very conduct;
but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his chief minister.”
Kātyāyana says: Due to an abundance of valor, learning, and wealth, and especially because of their power,
the minds of kings constantly fall into delusion for these reasons.
Therefore, the mind must always be awakened by the twice-born regarding the duty of kings;
one should not transgress the words of the Vedas, which are supremely purifying and meritorious.

Viṣṇu: "In all matters, the king shall be dependent upon the astrologer. Likewise: "He should pacify divine afflictions through rites of propitiation and auspicious ceremonies; and he should ward off the attacks of enemy armies by means of constant military preparedness. He should appoint as his domestic priest one who is well-versed in the Vedas, the Itihāsas, and the Dharmaśāstras, who is of noble birth, free from physical defects, and devoted to austerity."
‘By constant application to weapons,’ meaning by being devoted to the practice of arms; [thus says] Gautama.

And he should appoint a Brahmin as his domestic priest (*purohita*), one who is endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, youth, and good character; one who is upright in conduct and ascetic. Impelled by him, he should perform his duties. For it is known from scripture: "The Kṣatriya power that is impelled by the Brahman prospers and does not falter. He should also pay heed to whatever those who contemplate divine portents might declare, for some maintain that even security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) depend upon them. He should perform in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*) rites associated with prosperity—such as propitiatory, auspicious-day, *svastyayana*, longevity, and auspicious ceremonies—as well as those intended for causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent magic, and the ruin of enemies. Other rites are to be performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as has been stated.
‘Produced by that’ means authorized by that. ‘Enchantment’ (*saṃvanana*) means bringing under control. ‘The ruin of enemies’ (*dviṣadvyṛddhiḥ*) means the absence of prosperity for one’s foes.
[166] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “One should perform two hundred-thousand oblations (*lakṣahoma*) in this manner every year.”
And one should perform a *koṭihoma* with diligence, which bestows freedom from all fear.
According to the ritual rules of the Atharvaveda, accompanied by mantras and the family priest, he performed the daily rites, those performed for specific purposes, and likewise the occasional rites.
During an eclipse of the sun or moon, or when an earthquake or portentous omen is observed,
a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) that destroys misfortune must be performed at that very moment.
Yājñavalkya says:
And he should appoint a domestic priest who is well-born, knows the omens of the gods,
and is likewise skilled in the science of government (daṇḍanīti) as well as in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda].
In the Mahābhārata: "A king who has a chief domestic priest shall indeed attain his welfare,
he who always practices the dharma as instructed by the Brāhmaṇas."
To that extent, that wise man remains long in fame;
the royal priest becomes a partaker of that perfected merit.
Yājñavalkya:

For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, he should likewise choose officiating priests (ṛtvij) and should also perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings.
Manu says:
One should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this inexhaustible treasure of the Brahmins is ordained as belonging to the Brāhmaṇas.
Neither thieves nor enemies carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should establish an inexhaustible treasury among the Brahmins.
It does not overflow, it does not suffer distress, and it never perishes;
for what is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is indeed superior to the Agnihotra sacrifice.

Kātyāyana says: When a king properly grants to a petitioner what was requested without causing him distress, that gift for the sake of dharma saves an infinite number of beings; such is the nature of this gift.
That which is acquired by kings through conquest according to justice, having defeated their enemy—that is pure and must be given; never that which has been obtained otherwise.

Regarding the duties of kings, Viṣṇu states: "One should not seize land given by another from Brāhmaṇas; one should bestow all kinds of gifts. Regarding the duties of kings, Āpastamba states: "By giving land and wealth to Brāhmaṇas according to their merit out of consideration for his dependents, a king conquers infinite worlds. Kātyāyana says:
"By the power of the sound of the Vedas, the Vedas themselves reside in heaven."
They too rejoice there, satisfied by the honoring of the twice-born.
Therefore, kings should always perform the worship of the twice-born with great effort;
by that means, they shall repeatedly attain the status of Śakra as well as the sovereignty of men again and again.
The term "the king" being understood, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"Having honored a Brāhmaṇa, he should give a gift preceded by [stating] the occasion; to the others—[namely] the miserable, the afflicted, the helpless, the deformed, widows, children, and the elderly—he should provide maintenance with medicine, shelter, food, and clothing."

[169] Vasiṣṭha: And when the king has died, one should provide incidental support [to his relatives]. By this, the conduct toward parents is explained. The king shall maintain the king’s chief queen, paternal uncle, and maternal uncle; their daughters-in-law and other wives of the king shall receive food and clothing, or they may depart if they do not wish [to remain]. The king shall maintain eunuchs and those who are insane, because the inheritance goes to them.
“Incidental” (*prāsaṅgika*) means the honoring of Brahmins in connection with the *śrāddha* ceremony. — Manu:
The king should always honor a learned Vedic scholar, those afflicted by disease or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, one born of a noble lineage, and the virtuous.

Gautama: "A king should support *brāhmaṇas* who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), as well as non-*brāhmaṇas* who lack livelihoods, those who do not pay taxes, and those who are students (*upakurvāṇa*). Āpastamba:

"In his residence, he should provide lodging for guests who are *śrotriyas*, according to their merit. He should provide them with dwellings, beds, food, and drink. He must not live in a manner that exceeds his teachers or his ministers. Śaṅkha and Likhita: [The same].

Even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, if they are unable to subsist, may wait upon the king. Both of them should assist him according to their ability by performing their own respective duties; so too should artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras.
Manu says:
"In whose kingdom, however, a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger..."
Because of that hunger of his as well, the kingdom perishes before long.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, he should determine his means of livelihood;
and he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son.
When this [dharma] is protected by the king, it is practiced daily;
thereby the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
[172] Yama says: That king, along with his kingdom, prospers through the splendor of Brahmanic power, in whose realm the twice-born indeed study during the first and middle watches of the night.
Whatever sin a king commits through negligence, whether he endures it or not,
the Brahmins dwelling in his kingdom pacify that by means of silent recitation.
A king, having risen in the morning, should always honor the brahmins;
by the grace of the brahmins, the deities dwell in heaven.
Whatever these others declare, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, one should do exactly that and not otherwise; for in this matter, the Brāhmaṇa is the authority.
Likewise:
those who protect the ancient treasure, which is indivisible, uncuttable, beginningless, and inexhaustible;
Having honored those twice-born ones, the lord of the earth shall become invincible, like the king of the gods in heaven.
Indeed, armor can be pierced by an iron arrow or even by a shaft;
yet the blessing of a Brahmin is exceedingly difficult to breach, even by a thousand thunderbolts.
[173] Manu says:
"Neither the Kṣatriya without the Brāhmaṇa prospers, nor does the Brāhmaṇa without the Kṣatriya flourish.
When joined with both Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya, one prospers both in this world and in the next."
Yama said: The king is the tree; the Brahmin is its root;
the citizens are the leaves; and the ministers are its branches.
Therefore, the king must protect the Brahmins;
when the root is guarded, there is no destruction of the tree.
For fire burns when near; a Brahmin burns from afar.
What is scorched by fire grows back, but what is scorched by a Brahmin does not grow.
By the curse of the Brahmins, the consumer of oblations became an eater of all things,
the ocean became undrinkable, and Purandara became fruitless.
The moon, consumption, saline wastes upon the earth,
the resin of trees, and the defeat of the Dānavas.
The splendors of the high-souled Brahmins are indeed infinite;
therefore, a king should bow before the Brahmins with constant discipline.
‘Viphala’ means one who is without testicles. Manu says:
“Even when he has fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke a Brahmin.”
For they, being enraged, would instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts.
By whom was fire made all-consuming, the great ocean rendered undrinkable, and the moon made subject to waning; who would not perish by provoking them?
If provoked to anger, they could turn the worlds into non-worlds and the world-protectors into non-protectors;
they could turn gods into non-gods—who could prosper while harming them?
Who, desiring to live, would harm those who always abide supported by them— the gods and the worlds— whose wealth is Brahman alone?
Just as fire is both sublime and unsublime, a great deity;
so too is the Brāhmaṇa, whether ignorant or learned, a great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
rather, when oblations are offered into it at sacrifices, it is even more highly honored.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable activities,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are indeed the supreme deity.
Even when the Kṣatriya power has increased in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇa alone shall be its restrainer;
for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
In the Mahābhārata: "There are eight preliminary signs of a man who is about to perish:
first, he hates the Brāhmaṇas; then, he opposes the Brāhmaṇas."
He seizes the property of Brahmins, seeks to kill Brahmins,
delights in reviling them, and does not rejoice in their praise.
He does not remember them in times of need and becomes envious when asked for help;
a wise man, having recognized these faults through his intelligence, should avoid such people.
Likewise,
Bhīṣma said:
"O Bhārata, this is the most important duty for a consecrated king."
The permission of the Brahmins is for one who desires ultimate happiness.
Know this, O bull of the Bharatas, as that which must be performed by a king in this world:
he should always honor those who are learned in the Vedas, those who have completed their vows, and the elderly.
And he [honored] the citizens and countryfolk, as well as the learned brahmins,
with conciliation, the granting of enjoyments, salutations, and likewise with sacrifices.
This is the most important duty for kings; they should always keep this in mind:
they should protect these [subjects] just as they protect themselves and their own sons.
The king should also honor those among them who are most worthy of worship;
when they are at peace, that entire kingdom shines forth in splendor.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, following the word "the king":
"He should constantly worship the gods, sages, and nāgas who are present;
and he should always offer an oblation (*bali*) to the piśācas at the time of the twilights."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"O Lord of the Earth, Kārttikeya is declared to be always worthy of worship by kings;
they declare that there is no one else to be worshipped by kings other than Kārttikeya."
The hero who, while going forth to battle, worships the Son of Kṛttikā,
conquers his enemies just as Indra conquered the Dānavas in combat.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the son of Śaṅkara;
for when he is worshipped with devotion using various *campaka* flowers, O King, [he grants his grace].
He is liberated from all sins and shall indeed go to the abode of Śiva.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "She is divided by difference of names, yet non-different in the ultimate sense;
she is Śivā, Nārāyaṇī, Gaurī, Carcikā, Vimalā, and Umā."
She is to be constantly saluted and worshipped by those empowered by her—
by kings for the sake of victory— with respect to the sword, the dagger, the sandals, and the cloth.
Furthermore, by having Cāmuṇḍā of manifold forms depicted in a book,
or by having a parasol made for her banner, that king shall conquer his enemies.
Thus concludes the duties of the king.
[178] 15— Now follows the procedure for the procession of the deity (*devayātrāvidhi*), as set forth in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
In the six months beginning with Vaiśākha, as well as in the temples of the gods,
a festival procession must always be performed every year.
The journey for Brahman should always be undertaken on the first lunar day (pratipad),
and on the second lunar day (dvitīyā) for the gods, during the commencement of studies, and at great festivals.
On the third lunar day, a very beautiful rite should be performed for Bhāgīrathī;
then, on the fourth day, one should perform it for Vināyaka and the Nāgas.
By the word "atha" in the phrase "then on the fourth," the fifth [tithi] is indicated.
On the sixth, [the offering is] for Skanda; on the seventh, for the Sūryas respectively;
and on the eighth, for Purandara and for Rudra with his attendants.
On the ninth day, offerings should always be made to Durgā and the other Mothers;
on the tenth day, an offering to the Earth should be performed, provided with all necessary implements.
On the eleventh day, an offering should be made briefly to Vidhātṛ Viśvakarman;
on the twelfth day, it should be made to the high-souled Viṣṇu, together with his weapons.
On the thirteenth day, however, [one should offer] to Kāma; on the fourteenth, to Kapardin;
on the full moon day, to the gods, and likewise to the Moon.
On the new moon day at the end of the lunar festival,
or on the fourteenth or fourth day, one should perform offerings for the ancestors here somewhere, as well as for Yama, the King of the Ancestors.
On the twelfth or the full moon day, [the rite] for the Nāgas should be performed on the fifth day;
that for Nārāyaṇa should always be performed on all lunar days.
And by one desiring to undertake a journey, worship of Vināyaka with heaps of modakas should be performed at the outset on each day.
On the second day, the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti) should be performed in due order;
likewise, on the fourth day, one who knows the scriptures should perform worship to the Gandharvas.
On the fifth day, [an offering] should be made to Sthānanāga with milk and milk-rice;
on the sixth day, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins.
On the seventh day, the ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed after making the site well-protected;
the temple of the deity should be made white with lime and decorated with paintings.
One should likewise have a theater constructed as ordained for the gods;
there, one should worship the principal deity with garlands, garments, wreaths, gold, and other offerings.
Then the bathing of the image should be performed according to the sequence of the Kalpa-śākhā,
accompanied by auspicious recitations, songs, dances, and the like, as well as fire offerings and the presentation of bali-oblations.
Then, at the conclusion of the bathing ceremony with hymns, auspicious water should be brought by the citizens preceded by dancing, accompanied by great magnificence.
From that ever-present sacred site (tīrtha),
using whatever new jars were obtained according to the requirements of place and time, [he performed the rites] with elephants, horses, bulls, and men.
With that water, the image should be bathed on the ground according to the scriptures;
and the bathing ground should be prepared, free from all defects.
On the day the journey arrives, one should have a gabled pavilion constructed,
adorned with flowers, garlands, garments, and banners.
Having placed there an image that is very delicate and most beautiful, accompanied by the sound of a thousand bells and endowed with all splendors;
And the gabled pavilion should be carried by elephants, horses, men, and bulls,
according to the requirements of place and time, and adorned with garments, garlands, and other ornaments.
The king should be followed by his army behind the deity,
and he should be followed from a great distance by the ministers dispatched for that purpose.
Whomever that deity approaches while being worshipped,
he must always offer hospitality to him with incense and other offerings.
With shouts of "kṣveḍita" and "utkṛṣṭa," and with the sound of victory-instruments,
one should perform a circumambulation of the city according to tradition.
Then, having worshipped that image,
one should lead it to the temple while performing a great festival filled with song and dance.
Then, hundreds of thousands of lamps should be offered by the king upon that stage for the sake of illuminating it for those who wish to behold the Great-souled One.
Having thus gladdened the people with various well-spoken verses,
he should set in motion the wheel of Dharma for the sake of compassion toward all.
On the third day, he should observe the skill of those who live by the stage;
he should give them wealth according to his ability and avoid deceit.
At the time of the inspection, those who are principal should be honored in due order,
preceded by respectful treatment and according to the rules with betel, flowers, and other offerings.
At the conclusion of the journey, the spirits should always be worshipped with offerings and services,
and thereafter even the night-wanderers should be honored with sacrificial oblations.
Thus, for those desiring to behold the festival of the invisible forms,
he abandoned his own doubt through supreme devotion at the time of twilight.
Having understood that "all exists," with a stainless mind,
the exclusive deities should be worshipped in the month of Vaiśākha as before.
In every house, women should be honored by the householders as the deities of the home;
and that king who, with a composed mind, observes these rules of conduct, [attains success].
Endowed with sons and grandsons, he shall possess long life and wealth;
he attains victory everywhere and goes to eternal heaven.
Whenever this word of Viṣṇu is transgressed by people in this land,
then the crops perish due to terrible floods of water.
Excessive rain, drought, famine, and likewise death [arise from these];
therefore, one should diligently abandon hypocrisy, pride, and greed.
Having made a firm resolve, one should carry out that word which has been spoken by Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the ritual for the procession of the gods.
[182] 16— Now follows the great festival of Kaumudī.
In that regard, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"From morning onwards, the king issues the command for the Kaumudī festival,
the night of the god Rudra, which destroys the Asuras."
Let the city be made ready with streets well-swept and sprinkled; let all the inhabitants of the city be clad in gathered garments.
Wearing garlands and having bathed their heads, the married couples should proceed in due order;
let the singers sing and the actors and dancers dance.
Let banners be raised in houses, on streets, and in marketplaces;
and let your houses always remain well-smeared with plaster.
They were graced by various kinds of kings with heaps of flowers;
they all possessed garlands and were filled with forest wreaths.
And let lamps be placed everywhere along the royal highways and in the houses at night, set close together with wicks of abundant oil.
Let the youths wander about on all sides together with their women,
sporting, laughing, singing, and devoted to dancing.
Let the musical instruments be played, let the celestial women dance,
and let there be auspicious worship of Mahādeva with perfumes, flowers, and the like,
as well as various offerings and great couches.
And lamps of various forms, as well as drinks and kṛśara porridge.
Offer various fruits, meat both cooked and raw,
and objects adorned with gold and jewels to the Lord.
Let animals be slaughtered here and let the best of the twice-born be fed;
whatever man dwelling in this city should fail to do all this at any time, [let him be punished].
The highly illustrious king shall inflict corporal punishment upon him;
the king himself, moreover, should be self-controlled, tranquil, pure, and of restrained mind.
Day after day, one should diligently bathe Rudra with pure *pañcagavya* and fragrant oil.
With milk, clarified butter, curd, and many auspicious juices;
with flowers, fruits, seeds, and gems, all accompanied by water.
With fragrant ashes and scented water,
the king himself [poured] from each of one hundred and ten jars.
Day after day, O Vyāsa, he should consecrate Tryambaka with perfumes,
flowers, incense, recitations, and offerings.
Having worshipped them, the king should then feed the Brahmins and others;
having performed [the rites] with sacrificial animals, goats, jewels, and offerings of food,
clothing, and wealth, he should return to his home while being praised.
Thus concludes the Great Festival of Kaumudī.
Now follows the procedure for raising the banner of Indra (Indradhvaja),
as described in the Devīpurāṇa.
Under an auspicious lunar mansion, a favorable *karana*, and a propitious, lucky moment,
the astrologer and the master builder, accompanied by assistants, should go to the forest.
One who is enjoined to a procession according to the ritual for the installation of a goddess should go and seek out an auspicious tree, such as the *priyaṅgu*, *dhava*, or *arjuna*.
One should take these five auspicious trees—the Udumbara and the Gajakarṇa—for the purpose of a banner; however, my son, one should avoid trees grown in a deity’s grove.
One should fashion the Kanyā, Adhyuttamā, and Yaṣṭī images according to the measurement of cubits:
eleven cubits for the first, O child, and nine or five cubits for the others.
One that is unattached, infested with worms, or inhabited by birds; one grown on an anthill, in a cemetery, or in a forest; one that is withered or hollow.
One should avoid a tree that has been watered by a jar, one that is not censured even by women, one struck by lightning or a thunderbolt, and one that has been burnt.
If these are unavailable, one should make [the insignia] from campaka, mango, or likewise from śāla wood;
for the purpose of Śakra’s emblem, it must never be made from any other tree whatsoever.
One should take pure water produced from a pure place that brings about auspiciousness;
then, facing either east or north, one should worship the tree.
"O Lord of Trees, O Tree, the king honors you for the sake of a banner; this is the truth, so let it not be understood otherwise."
At night, an offering should be given in a pit, in the cardinal directions, and likewise at a tree;
having made your dwelling at a great tree in the forest, you may indeed go elsewhere.
They guard the banner of the King of the Gods here and there;
having worshipped the tree, one should then cause a fragrant offering to be presented.
At dawn, having seen auspicious dreams and other such signs, he should cut down the tree while facing either north or east, using an axe smeared with honey.
Falling toward the northeast, silent, without a wound, and unattached to another tree is auspicious; otherwise, one should abandon it.
One should discard eight finger-breadths from the base; one should cast the tip into the water, and likewise, O child, one should bring it out by means of a cart or oxen.
When the staff, being straight or slightly curved, is led with effort before the city by youths endowed with strength;
If the wheel is round, the prince and the domestic priest suffer defeat;
if the rim is broken, one should shatter the enemy force; likewise, if the felly is broken, there is ruin.
But if the axle of the chariot should break,
one should perform a propitiatory rite there with the mantra "indraṃ yaccha" or with "jātavedo maya".
Having led her thus, one should have her seated in the city at an auspicious moment;
one should cause decorations to be made at the gate, in the city, along the streets, and even in the houses.
Accompanied by the sharp sounds of drums, the auspicious songs of the guild of courtesans,
and the Vedic chants of the twice-born, he should lead her to where he shall raise [the banner].
One should then wrap her, as she stands there, with garments fashioned by a painter or artisan—
auspicious, fine, and newly cut, arranged in the proper order.
In the first sector are the maidens known as Nanda and Upananda;
the goddesses named Jaya and Vijaya are established in sixteen sectors.
Having bowed to Ambikā, the conqueror of enemies, and then to the deity of the banner,
one should determine those [measures] after having established them according to the dimensions of the banner.
The wise one should make the remaining [garments] deficient by a sixteenth part;
the Self-Existent One himself gave the first [set] of multicolored cloths.
In ancient times, Viśvakarman gave the second [disc], which was well-proportioned and square; Śakra himself gave one that was eight-cornered and blue-red.
Yama gave Kṛṣṇa, Varuṇa a great silk garment,
Vāyu a madder-dyed lotus-shaped cloth, and the gods a boar.
And he gave that [meter] which is blue in color and variegated by the fire of the Vedic meters;
and Agni gave the eighth, which is the *vṛtta* meter, in his own color.
Indra further gave him a neck-ornament resembling lapis lazuli;
Sūrya gave one in the shape of a wheel-mark, while the Viśvedevas gave a lotus.
The sages also know that [mark] to be blue, with the luster of a blue lotus;
and it is broad, placed upon the head by Śukra and Guru.
Even houses of various kinds were given by the mothers;
whatever was given by whomsoever became that person's ornament for the banner.
One should recognize that as fate; yet one may also raise it up by means of machines and the like. A staff that drags along excellent land destroys the kingdom.

By the sound of clapping hands from children, one should predict the destruction of the country; a scattered sound portends the death of the king, while a completely calm sound brings about auspiciousness.
Curds and unbroken grains (akṣatas) should be offered as oblations with the mantras of Śambhu, Sūrya, Yama, Indra, Indrā, Dhanada, Varuṇa, Agni, and Nāga.
The wise one should cause Śukra, Skanda, Guru, and Rudra to recite [the mantra] along with the Apsarases;
having offered oblations according to the rule, he should likewise gaze upon the flame of the fire for a hundred thousand times.
[188] Brilliant with excellent splendor and flowers, vast and radiant as the sun,
having the appearance of a red *aśoka* tree, and auspicious with the sound of a chariot-drum.
The sounds of conchs, drums, and clouds are auspicious when the fire is kindled;
one should also raise banners upon plantain trees and sugarcane stalks.
And various other ornaments should be raised upon the banner of Śakra on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, for they are auspicious.
Then, during the month of Āśvina, on the bright fortnight, one should raise [the banner] under the asterism Śravaṇa;
it should be accompanied by the sounds of cowherds, troupes of actors, and the resonance of drums and kettledrums.
It was brilliantly illuminated by canopies, banners, and splendid flags,
and consecrated with the mantras of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra, as well as the Siṃharakṣa mantra.
It should be firmly situated within the mother's womb, with its auspicious gateway directed forward,
suspended yet turned upward, with its membrane unbroken and even.
O Lord, the banner born of Indra should not be raised too hastily;
a wise man should protect that which has been raised from crows, owls, and pigeons.
One should not provide shelter there even for birds;
rather, one should raise the banner of Indra according to the ritual procedure with the mantra.
[189] Having worshipped a well-constructed and well-mechanized pleasure-device,
one should perform a night vigil with the recitation of Indra-mantras.

The royal priest, who is always an astrologer and ever devoted to auspicious rites of pacification, [should act thus]; for the fall of a comet would slay the king, while its falling banner signifies the death of the queen.
One should always provide a cushion for the crown prince;
by the falling of the archway, the kingdom shall perish, and there shall be a depletion of food at the banner.
When the staff of Indra has fallen, one should appoint another king;
when a swarm of worms appears, there is danger from locusts and thieves.
When [the balance] is perfectly established, peace prevails for both the king and the city;
it remains so for as many years as there are years in a yuga, even while he stands up.
The daughters of Indra, intent on sacrifice, should delight in the ritual;
and when [the image] has fallen, the worship should be performed at its rising exactly as it was before.
At night, no most auspicious deed has been seen that has not been observed by young crows;
likewise, a king who performs such a sacrifice together with his subjects [attains success].
Whether in a kingdom, a city, or a market town, if the king acts in this manner,
he should erect at the city gate a Paurandara banner raised high with a bull and a lion.
It is considered the banner of all terrors, the destroyer [of enemies], and the bestower of victory;
thus did Hari previously obtain this banner from the one whose vehicle is the bull.
Then Brahmā [received it] from him; from that Brahmā, Śakra received it;
he gave it to Soma, and from him it passed to Dakṣa.
From that time onwards, kings have continued to erect this banner even to this day;
thus, whatever king should cause such a victory-bringing banner to be made, [he shall attain success].
The earth, together with its wealth and its islands, shall come under his control.
Thus ends the procedure for the raising of Indra’s banner.
[191] 18— Now, the Mahānavamī worship; now, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the worship of the Goddess.
In that regard, the Devīpurāṇa states:
Brahmā said:
"When the terrible Mahāvīra, who struck fear into both gods and asuras, had been slain..."
The gods who are devotees of the Goddess are numerous, as are the rākṣasas.
Having arrived and seen that invincible buffalo slain,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśāna, Indra, Candra, Yama, and Anila [approached].
Then the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Grahas, Nāgas, and Guhyakas—
all those gods having assembled, praised the Goddess with devotion.
And she, the destroyer of fear, granted a boon to all the worlds;
and the beings offered an oblation to her with the flesh of buffaloes and goats.
In the pure [quarters], hundreds and thousands of conchs and kettledrums were sounded,
along with the sharp sounds of dundubhi drums and mardala drums.
O Śakra, best of gods, one who is devoted to the Goddess should cause that day to be adorned with banners, flags, mechanical devices, and the like, beautified by bells and chowries.
Thus, O child, on that day which was crowded with spirits and ghosts,
a great and eternal worship was performed by all the gods.
[192] Those who, at midnight on the eighth day at the end of the month of Āśvina, when the clouds have ceased, worship the Goddess who destroys the enemies of Mahiṣa;
Those who slaughter animals with devotion become possessed of great strength;
and those who offer a sacrifice intended for the destruction of all beings [attain the same].
The Goddess is pleased with them for as long as the kalpa of Śaṅkara;
they sport with various enjoyments in the celestial world, which is so difficult to attain.
For them there shall be no mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor shall there be fear of enemies;
neither gods, nor planetary spirits, nor Daityas, nor Suras, nor Pannagas [shall cause them harm].
O Lord of the Gods, they oppress those who have taken refuge at the feet of the Goddess,
as long as earth, wind, space, water, fire, moon, and planets exist.
And for that long, Caṇḍikā shall always be worshipped on earth,
especially during the rainy season, in the month of Āśvina, and on the eighth lunar days.
And on the ninth day, the "Great Sound" (Mahāśabda) shall attain renown in the world;
O Indra, Lord of the Gods, this bestows the fruit of dwelling in heaven.
But the distinction between the higher and the lower is proclaimed by means of the yoga of action.
Indra said:
"O dear one, I wish to hear about the fasts, vows, and other observances pertaining to the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, which occurs every year."
Brahmā said: Listen, O Śakra, I shall explain according to what you ask—
that which bestows great siddhi, is auspicious, and destroys all enemies.
For the sake of benefiting the entire world, and especially toward those who follow the path of the earth,
this must be performed by the Brahmins and others, as well as by the Kṣatriyas who are the guardians of the world.
[193] Likewise, it was performed by Vaiśyas for the sake of cattle-wealth, by Śūdras seeking the happiness of sons,
by women for the sake of good fortune, and by others desiring wealth.
O Indra, king of the gods, this great vow of immense merit, which was practiced by Śaṅkara and others,
should be performed by those endowed with devotion to the Goddess.
O Śakra, when the sun is situated in Virgo, beginning from the day of Śuklā Nandikā,
one should subsist on unasked food, observe a fast, eat only at night, or else subsist on air alone.
Bathing at dawn, having conquered the pairs of opposites, worshipping Śiva three times a day,
