and engaged in recitation and fire-offerings, he should always feed virgins.
O best of gods, on the eighth day one should have nine auspicious houses made of wood, or at least one, according to one’s means.

On that [sword], the Goddess should be fashioned, either of gold or even of silver; or, endowed with the proper characteristics, she may be carved from wood. One should then worship her upon the sword or the spear.
Provided with all offerings such as garments, jewels, fruits, and so forth,
one should have chariots, palanquins, and the like prepared, as well as perform divine worship and sacrificial rites.
One should perform a diverse worship with flowers and other offerings, bilva fruits, jasmine, punnāga, and campaka; one should pay homage on the eighth lunar day.
With a single-minded and well-purified mind, the king should recite the mantra before Durgā;
when half the night remains, he should offer an animal for the sake of victory.

Having recited "Kālī, Kālī" according to the ritual rules over a five-year-old [victim] endowed with auspicious marks and perfumed with fragrant scents and incense, one should strike him with a sword.
[194] Having taken the blood and flesh arising from that,
it should be offered to the Nairṛtas during worship and other rites, consecrated with the Mahākauśika mantra.
In front of that [image], the king should bathe after having worshipped it with an umbrella;
then, having struck it with a sword, he should offer it to Skanda and Viśākha.
The wise man should bathe the Goddess with milk, clarified butter, water, and other substances;
having worshipped her with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood, he should offer incense.
Flowers, jewels, and new, unwashed garments should be offered;
furthermore, a very abundant food offering should be presented to the Goddess by those who are well-purified in mind.
Those devoted to the Goddess, as well as maidens and young women, are to be honored;
one should satisfy the twice-born, the poor, the blind, and even the heretics with food and drink.
Those men who are devotees of Nandā and who observe the great vows,
having especially worshipped that form made of wool, [attain their goal].
The worship of the Mothers and the Goddesses should always be performed at night;
one should raise banners, parasols, flags, and the like in the temple of Ambikā.
One should perform the chariot procession, the offering of oblations, and the securing of safety, filled with the loud sounds of resonant musical instruments;
for by these means, and by the immolation of animals, the Goddess is pleased.
The best of gods, through devotion, obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
this worship on Mahanavami grants all desires.
[195] O child, for all castes, this has been proclaimed by you through devotion;
by performing it, one obtains fame, sovereignty, sons, long life, and the wealth of prosperity.
Thus concludes the worship of Mahānavamī.
[196] 19. Now, the procedure for the marks (*cihna*),
as found in the *Devīpurāṇa*:

Brahmā said: From the beginning of the month of Kārttika, a man who subsists on milk, who is devoted to the Goddess, who eats only vegetables or barley-gruel, who bathes in the morning, and who bows to Śiva— [attains the fruit].
One should perform the sesame oblation with curd, milk, ghee, and other offerings;
one should do so with the mantra of the Goddess—listen, O Hari, to the meritorious fruit thereof.
One joined with great sins, or even associated with minor offenses, is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter, because Śivā is omnipresent.
Or another person engaged in meditation may, according to this rule,
worship Śivā herself, or cause her to be worshipped by someone else.
For him there shall be no disease, nor fear caused by enemies;
neither shall there be calamities from portents or malignant planets, nor shall the kingdom perish.
The seasons are always endowed with their natural excellence, the clouds bestow auspiciousness,
all crops reach full maturity, and there are no thieves.
The cows yield abundant milk, the Brahmins are devoted to their sacred rites,
all the women are faithful to their husbands, and the kings bring about peace and security.
Through the worship according to the ritual of Carcikā, the nurse-nature (dhātrī) shall abound with fruits and flowers, and the crops shall be full of flavor; of this there is no doubt.
“Victorious one, auspicious one, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā— homage be to you!”
With this very mantra, one should perform recitation and fire-oblation;
for, O child, when remembered at dawn and well-worshipped, she is the slayer of buffaloes.
Just as at the rising of the sun, he quickly destroys evil;
for him upon whose banner is Umā mounted on a lion, there is no destroyer of enemies.
O child, she who stands at the door is worshipped; she has no fear born of enemies.
Mahāmāyā, seated upon a monkey, is the destroyer of all foes.
In Vṛṣa one should grant whatever is desired; in Kalabha, supreme prosperity; in Haṃsa, the fulfillment of Dharma and Kāma; and in Barhiṇa, the granting of beloved sons.
Mounted on Garuḍa, Mahāmāyā is the destroyer of all diseases;
seated upon a buffalo and stationed upon a banner, she pacifies Mahāmārī.
In all undertakings, kings should employ the trident-bearing Carcikā, who stands upon a lotus and is fashioned from silver; she bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.

O Indra among gods, that excellent goddess who resides in the realm of the pretas, who constantly bestows all fears through the striking down of sacrificial animals, is worshipped while holding a blue lotus in her hand.
But for one desiring spiritual accomplishment, she should be stationed at the tip of the ritual mark (cihna),
having been honored with perfumes and flowers and well-adorned with garments and gold.
One should raise at the front of the *śohā* a banner adorned with fruits, rice, barley, and awned grains, or a large, beautiful cloth.
The fly-whisk, the water-pot, the conch, the parasol,
and the canopy shall indeed bestow the fruit of success upon a king who desires accomplishment.
“Homage to Viśveśvarī, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, and you who take away the heads!
I shall hoist the banner that brings the happiness of a stream of wealth.”
Thus ends the rule concerning the marks.
[199] 20— Now, regarding the abandonment of speech (*vāg-utsarga*), it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
On the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika,
or on a day following it, whoever performs the rite of setting a bull at liberty shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of gold, the gift of cows, and the gift of land,
that fruit is obtained multiplied ten millionfold by the ritual release of a cow.
Therefore, in a delightful place, abounding in green grass, free from pits,
devoid of gravel and stones, and resounding with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums;
Having erected two pillars situated in the east and west,
one should construct there [a structure] made of *darbha* grass or else of bamboo reeds.
In the center, O Brahmins, was a beautiful long rope joined with a woolen blanket,
flanked on both sides by those accompanied by the sound of the Vedas.
Having performed it in this manner according to the rules, one should then cause the ritual relinquishment (utsarga) to be made;
first, the Hotṛ priest, accompanied by the patron (yajamāna), proceeds.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as cattle and other subjects,
and likewise others outside the castes, with the exception of the Caṇḍālas.
They go forth joyful and delighted, filled with laughter and contentment—
whosoever king acts thus within his city, village, or town.
All the mental faculties of the people perish for a long time in the Nandana grove;
the king does not die prematurely, and he prospers with his sons and grandsons.
The gods become well-pleased, as do the mothers;
O child, one shall attain Goloka and obtain all desires.
‘Calamities’ (*īti*) are well known. As it is said: excessive rain, drought, rats, locusts, parrots, and kings who have drawn too near—these six are recorded as calamities.
Thus concludes the release of the cow.
Now, the stream of wealth (vasordhārā).
In that regard, the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa states: Agastya said:
"The Goddess, who bestows all desires, is established as the Vasordhārā."
In that manner, I shall tell it to you; listen for the increase of merit.
This supreme [mantra] has been declared by me for all the gods;
however, it is considered especially bestowing long life and health when established in the fire.
Situated in the Kuṇḍa, she bestows victory, the acquisition of land, and what is dear to men, as well as learning, good fortune, sons, and so forth.
Therefore, for the sake of prosperity, the auspicious Vasordhārā,
which bestows the fruits of all desires, should be worshipped by the king according to his capacity.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Grahas, Viṣṇu, we Yakṣas along with the Kinnaras— all of us,
whose mouths are the sacrificial fire, bestow both seen and unseen fruits.
The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and gifts such as jewels, clarified butter, and sesame seeds—these they call great gifts; among them, the stream [of water] is distinguished as superior.
Whatever fruit is obtained by feeding tens of millions upon tens of millions of Brahmins,
that same fruit would be gained even by a single person who is peaceful and delights in virtuous conduct.
One obtains that very thing by offering a stream [of water] into the sacrificial fire;
there is no doubt regarding this Vyatīpāta, and it is proclaimed to be subtle.
O King, at the solstice, as well as during the "poisonous" period and likewise the intercalary day,
one obtains the rare results of gifts and fire-offerings that are otherwise difficult to attain.
Therefore, for the sake of prosperity, a king who desires victory in both the seen and the unseen worlds should perform the Vasordhārā rite,
which brings about all desired objects and happiness.
Whether equally, or half by half, for a season, a month, half a month, or a day— by performing [the rite] according to one's means, the eternal fruit is obtained.
Whoever, having fashioned an image of the Goddess, should pour a stream of clarified butter into the fire for even a single day, shall obtain his desired fruit.
The fountain-house may be located near the Devīmātṛs, or in the vicinity of Śiva and Viṣṇu, or even that of the Sun, Prajāpati, or Vāsava.
In all ancient places, whether naturally formed or consecrated by human effort,
on divine mountains, and at the confluences of rivers.
O King, by bestowing desired objects according to the prescribed rite in various caves, within the interiors of houses, or upon the ground, one obtains those very things.
Now, the house in general should have equal lines, be open to the light,
possess a layout purified according to the Vāstu principles, and measure eleven cubits at most.
One should have it made as three, five, seven, ten, or nine;
or twenty less one, but one should not make it more than twenty.
It may be constructed of baked brick, stone, or wood, provided with a veranda and arched gateways,
and adorned with five, seven, or nine windows.
Arranged as the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], it is expanded by a gradual increase;
it has a smoke-vent at the top and is especially luminous.
The assembly should include the gods, or else it should be together with the deities;
in its center there should be a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing auspicious characteristics such as being one cubit in size.
Alternatively, it may be square or lotus-shaped;
the Śakra-vṛtta bestows victory on the earth, while the [lotus] shape grants the fruits of desire.
The *śākram* [pit] is square;
in the lotus [pit], one finds victory, health, and the granting of the fruits of yoga.
The remaining pits should be constructed according to the rule by the wise practitioner.
For all homas, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) dedicated to Indra is the most excellent;
its width should be equal to its depth, and it should be provided with three tiers (mekhalās).
One should make the measurement of the pit four, three, or two finger-breadths;
for each doubling of the pit's size, one should double the measurement according to the requirements of the fire-oblation.
O Brahmin, having thus prepared it, he should then place the vessel along with its chain—
whether made of gold, silver, or copper— and endowed with the proper characteristics.
It should be joined with four rings and secured with iron chains;
in its center, O child, a hole should be made using a rod.
A wise person should properly prepare a vessel made of copper, measuring four finger-breadths in size, for the purpose of pouring out the clarified butter.
Just as one should proceed with one nāḍī in nine and a half palas,
the oblation for the two fires consists of five hundred and seventy [grains].
O child, one should act exactly as Pūrṇā would go, and not otherwise.
There should be a golden chain, a cubit in length, shaped like a serpent.
Then, having supported it from below by means of a thread tied through the opening,
one should cause a jewel or a lotus, together with an *aśvattha* tree, to be fashioned at its base.
In this manner, one should prepare the vessel and the clarified butter with twice or even three times the amount of material according to their form, as enjoined by the deities for the consecration.
O best of kings, I shall also state here a brief summary:
the seasons, months, fortnights, days, and nights are the same as previously described.
O child, one should determine [the auspicious time] from the ascendant when it bestows all desires;
and in matters requiring immediate action, one should act with devotion at a favorable moment.
For a moment, the Goddess should be beheld as she who is all-pervading and auspicious;
likewise, the principles, the elements, the planets, the serpents, and the threefold auspicious qualities [should be seen].
In the daily and occasional fire-offerings (homa), one should cause the offerings to be given through the application of mantras;
for whichever deity a person is devoted to, one should bring that deity into close proximity.
One should visualize the *saṃgrahas*, the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), the mothers, and the auspicious serpents in all fire-offerings (*sarvahomas*); the Goddess is established within these.
Indeed, she is the gross form of all; when the Goddess is pleased, she yields great fruit.
O child, one should perform the consecration of the time, the offerings, the perfumes, and so forth.
Just as one endowed with prosperity should cause [offerings] to be given at all times,
so too should one install the Mothers, the spirits, and the World-Protectors.
Or [images] made of gold, silver, or copper, characterized by their respective locations;
[one should offer] incense, flowers, and oblations, perfumes, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in due order.
To the Mothers, the World-Protectors, and the Planets, offerings should be presented according to the prescribed rule,
using the Heart-mantra and the ancient Root-mantras.
Alternatively, one may have all the common rites performed, including those pertaining to the Vedas,
using the Atharvanic procedures or the previously mentioned mantras, just as in former times.
One should offer abundant food along with sacrificial offerings accompanied by profuse fees with great effort; never otherwise.
One should recognize that there is danger in cutting [the tree]; one should have half of it used for that purpose.
Wherever [it is needed], one should employ it with the Mahāvyāhṛti oblation.
One should offer the bell with the root mantra,
the ghee with the heart mantra, and warm it with the mantra of the head or the crest-mantra.
Having likewise protected the fire with the *kavaca* mantra, one should cause it to be offered;
with the *astra* and *netra* mantras, one should cast everything everywhere.
One should worship the world-protectors, the planets, and the nāgas with half of twelve [offerings];
one should also worship Śiva and the others, Sanaka and the others, as well as the gods and the others.
O one of great wisdom, in the case of permanent rites and specifically those occasional ones,
there are groups of five, seven, and nine, beginning with the ritual actions.
O child, at that time, the color, smell, sound, as well as the forms and transformations of the fire should be understood as indicators of success or failure.
At its conclusion, O child, she who grants all desires must be honored,
so that the auspicious goddess may be present in all fire-offerings.
O thousand-rayed one, O great splendor, homage to you who possess many forms;
homage to you, the blue-throated one, the yellow-robed, O Purifier!
Salutations to the one who holds the sacrificial ladle and girdle in his hand;
salutations again and again to the purifier who consumes the cosmic egg, who eats all things, and who is omnipresent.
Salutations indeed to Durgā, to the one of fierce form, to the one whose gender is feminine, to self-luminous splendor, to the one in the form of Vasu and the Aśvins, and to the destroyer of all.
O Rudra, you are the performer of terrible deeds, the slayer of the terrible, the Supreme Lord;
you are Viṣṇu, the protector of the worlds, and you are remembered as Brahmā, the creator.
And you, O God, are the soul of all, abiding in the bodies of the world-protectors:
for Indra, for Agni, O God, and for Yama, the eater of flesh.
Salutations indeed to Varuṇa, Anila, Soma, and the god Īśa;
to Sūrya, to him who is the form of Candra, to Bhūsuta, and to Budha.
To Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Sauri, Rāhu, and Ketu; to the one who possesses the form of all the planets, and who has the form of the Mothers of Beasts.
Rain, creation, maintenance, and prosperity—salutations to you, the agent and the bestower of boons!
Salutations to you, O Mother of Skanda; salutations again and again to the Father of Skanda!
O All-pervading Lord, whether in a sacrificial pit, or in a mandala, or on a consecrated mound,
or even in a kitchen— by offering oblations to you there, O God, a man shall obtain his desired object.
He who constantly performs oblations with ghee, milk, meat broth, grain, sesame seeds, rice, kuśa grass, and barley— whether out of devotion or even out of lack thereof— [attains the highest state].
Thus, even a man devoid of wealth who is free from sin [attains this];
how much more so for one who performs the daily oblation with the *vasordhārā* into the fire?
One should cause the oblation to be offered with the Sarvamaṅgala mantra;
for the abodes of the world-protectors, however, [one should offer] with the syllable *Oṃ* followed by the words ending in *namaḥ*.
O best of kings, the oblation for all [the deities] should be performed with their respective mantras;
the food should be diverse, pure, and consecrated with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
The Brahmin should perform the fire-oblation according to the rules, or he should cause the offering (bali) to be presented;
the king, wearing white garments, accompanied by his army and his mounts, [should likewise do so].
One should worship the jewel of the parasol and other such objects, as well as one’s mother, father, the twice-born,
teachers, kinsmen, and all those people who are devoted to their respective stages of life (āśramas).
One should honor actors, dancers, courtesans, young girls, widows,
and those who are distressed, blind, or miserable by giving them food.
Having performed the installation in this manner, one should constantly recite [the mantra] a hundred times each at dawn, midday, and the evening twilight; therein, peace is proclaimed.
It brings about for the king and his kingdom the results previously described.
(Thus concludes the procedure for the installation of the stream of wealth.
[It is stated in that very same place:
Brahmā said:
Resplendent with the hue of molten gold, bearing the brilliance of the sun and vermilion,
he is auspicious, resembling the conch, the kunda flower, the moon, and the lotus, and like ghee and milk.
One that has the luster of a victory banner, the luster of an *aśoka* flower, or resembles lac and a lotus brings auspiciousness for all undertakings; indeed, the opposite brings failure.
The auspicious sound of flutes and lutes, like the thunder of clouds and the blast of conchs, is honored by the calls of bulls, elephants, peacocks, crows, and cuckoos.
Fragrant with saffron, agallochum, camphor, madana, and gorocanā,
and possessing the scent of māṃsī, cardamom, kuṣṭha, tagara, and white sandalwood, he is worshipped.
A hand shaped like a swan, a ploughshare, a water-pot, or a lotus is auspicious;
likewise, hands shaped like a lion, a peacock, a mountain, or a fly-whisk bestow what is desired.
A fire that smokes, smells of nectar, resembles a parrot or a bee,
has broken flames, or is red— such a fire is not desired for any rite.
With its flame well-consolidated, praised, blazing upwards, or even licking [the oblation],
the fire in the sacrificial pit is auspicious, radiant, and a granter of boons.
Such is Vaiśvānara, who is always established in the sacrifice;
he bestows success in all undertakings, whether on a journey or under the banner of Indra.
O Brahmin, a stream that flows too thin from pride is not auspicious;
nor is one that is excessive praised, for it brings about famine and strife.
That which flows on may break, or the fire may be extinguished;
even that [fire] might seek another king, as would a stream that falls outside.
The Vajra river is of great form, enchanting, and effectual;
golden and the color of gold, its stream leads to the increase of sovereignty.
That which falls continuously and as if spreads the fire,
that stream of wealth undoubtedly extends to the king and the kingdom.
Ghee from a cow that is fragrant, healthy, pure, and free from worms and insects is praised; it is highly esteemed for the Vasudhārā rite.
In the absence [of these], one should offer fragrant incense or very beautiful clarified butter;
a stream of ghee, honey, and milk wards off all afflictions.
An oblation with pieces of *guḍūcī* and mango leaves is auspicious;
[an oblation with] *aśvattha*, *mālatī*, and *dūrvā* bestows long life, health, and sons.
O child, this auspicious goddess bestows good fortune and prosperity without hesitation;
when she is properly honored, she fulfills all desires and makes them fruitful.
O King, sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) must be offered at all times with constancy;
likewise, clarified butter (ghṛta) is prescribed for all times, as well as for specific occasions according to their requirements.
One should examine those [signs] regarding the purified ghee here;
in all fire-offerings, one should observe the auspicious flame, its power, and its fragrance.

O King, the stream [of water] should be offered by those who are self-restrained, moderate in their food, masters of the meaning of all scriptures, and devoted to the recitation of mantras and the performance of fire-sacrifices— indeed, by such as these.
One should neither speak to nor look upon those who are deficient in their religious vows, the greedy, those devoid of dharma, the outcasts, or those who engage in idle chatter at all times.
Then one should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra ending in the dative case;
for one who performs daily oblations, this brings good fortune, but otherwise it would be fruitless.
In the case of the ordinary stream [of breath], one hundred recitations should be performed at each of the morning,
midday, and evening twilights for the fulfillment of all desires.
Vasu is the substance, clarified butter is the sacrificial oil, and it is the immortal oblation desired for the rite;
therein the stream should always be poured, for that is considered the "stream of Vasu" (vasordhārā).
By Vasu, by the great-souled Dakṣa who desires offspring,
by me, by Viṣṇu, O Śakra, and by Rudra together with Umā.
And as she held herself in her true form, fallen into the stream,
the Goddess, the bestower of all desires, arrived in her presence.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should cause the wife of Vasu to be given away;
there is no merit greater than this, O best of monarchs.
Even for a single day, the king who desires prosperity and wishes to conquer the kingdoms of others should perform the offering of the stream of wealth (vasordhārā).
[211] O child, know that this stream should always be offered for the destruction of enemies;
however, the daily fire-oblation must never be interrupted under any circumstances.
He who causes the gods to turn away incurs a great fault,
except in the absence of materials, in the absence of ghee, or when there is fear arising from kings or thieves.
O best of kings, if the stream does not flow, then there is no defect;
having performed the fire-oblation, one should ask for forgiveness from the God of gods.

Furthermore, O child, when [the time] arrives, the installation should be performed according to the prescribed rites during the great month of Āśvina, specifically on the eighth and ninth lunar days.

O best of beings, [the gift] should be offered on the full moon of Kārttika, Māgha, and Caitra, as well as under the asterisms of Citrā and Rohiṇī; and on the full moon of Vaiśākha, O Jyeṣṭha, it should be given under the asterism of Jyeṣṭhā.
The twelfth day of Āṣāḍha is prescribed, as well as the eighth and the full moon of Nabhas;
O child, [the conjunction] with Rohiṇī occurs in Nabhasya on the fourth lunar day, a Tuesday.
On all the transits [of the sun],
on those involving Jupiter and Saturn, during lunar and solar eclipses, and at the time of consecration rites and sacrificial ceremonies.
It should be given during the festival of the son's birth, at the consecration with birth-flowers,
on the path, when bound by a vow, in times of great terror, and upon the appearance of Ketu.
To pacify the afflictions caused by the planets, a propitious stream [of water] should be offered;
thus, one should cause the stream to flow according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
For him, the entire earth, together with its mountains and oceans, is successfully attained;
merit equal to that of a horse sacrifice arises from a single daily oblation.
Even if one performs a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices at night and likewise a hundred Agniṣṭomas,
mental anxieties and physical ailments shall never arise for him.
One shall obtain long life, health, and sovereignty, and at its conclusion, one shall be happy.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the stream of wealth (vasordhārā).

Thus ends the section on the Duties of Kings (*Rājadharmakāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara Bhaṭṭa, the Minister for Peace and War under the illustrious Great King Govindacandra.
May there be auspiciousness.
